entries.note: The practice of choosing a Roman consul was abolished in 541 and the title was added to imperial titles. This continued until the time of Emperor Leo VI in 887.

entries.label: Constans II is the last emperor to visit Rome
entries.note: AD663 – Constans II is the last emperor to visit Rome, and the city gradually slips out of imperial control.

entries.label: Pepin the Short, King of the Franks, defeats Lombards
Basil I initiates reconquest of southern Italy
Second Novel of Romanus I
entries.note: Second Novel of Romanus I; extension of pre-emption right

entries.label: Invasion of Bulgaria by Svitatoslav, Prince of Kiev
Fiscal and administrative reforms of Alexius
Byzantine Rump States
entries.note: Byzantine Rump States: Empire of Nicaea Empire of Trebizond Principality of Theodoro Despotate of the Morea Despotate of Epirus

entries.label: Latins begin to occupy Latium Vetus
Offices of Roman Dictator and Master of the Horse created
Office of quaestor opened to plebeians
Patricians agree to allow Plebeian Consuls to be elected
entries.note: 366 BC: Patricians agree to allow Plebeian Consuls to be elected (the first being Lucius Sextius Sextinus). By this, Plebeians acquire de facto right to be elected Censor or appointed Dictator. As a concession, the Plebeians allow the Patricians to create the offices of Praetor and Curule Aedile, and allow only Patricians to run for these offices.

entries.label: Office of Praetor peregrinus created
entries.note: 242BC: The office of the praetor qui inter peregrinos ius dicit, a Praetor with jurisdiction over foreigners, was created.

entries.label: Gaius Servillius Geminus
entries.note: Gaius Servilius Geminus Roman statesman who served as the Consul in 203 BC, Dictator in 202 BC, and Pontifex Maximus from 183 BC to 180 BC.

entries.label: Lex Gabinia Tabellaria: required a secret ballot in elections of all magistrates
Fall of Sejanus
entries.note: Lucius Aelius Seianus (20 BC – AD 31), commonly known as Sejanus, was an ambitious soldier, friend and confidant of the Roman Emperor Tiberius. An equestrian by birth, Sejanus rose to power as prefect of the Roman imperial bodyguard, known as the Praetorian Guard, of which he was commander from AD 14 until his death in AD 31. While the Praetorian Guard was formally established under Emperor Augustus, Sejanus introduced a number of reforms which saw the unit evolve beyond a mere bodyguard into a powerful and influential branch of the government involved in public security, civil administration, and ultimately political intercession; changes which would have a lasting impact on the course of the Principate. During the 20s, Sejanus gradually accumulated power by consolidating his influence over Tiberius and eliminating potential political opponents, including the emperor's son, Drusus Julius Caesar. When Tiberius withdrew to Capri in 26, Sejanus was left in control of the entire state mechanism as de facto ruler of the empire. For a time the most influential and feared citizen of Rome, Sejanus suddenly fell from power in 31, the year his career culminated with the consulship. Amidst suspicions of conspiracy against Tiberius, Sejanus was arrested and executed, along with his followers.

entries.label: Year of the 4 Emperors
entries.note: AD69 - Year of the Four Emperors After the assassination of Galba, Otho and Vitellius briefly become emperors before Vespasian's accession to power in the end of the year; Flavian dynasty begins.

entries.label: The Five Good Emperors (Nerva, Trajan, Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius)
Anicius Faustus Albinus Basilius
entries.note: Last ordinary Consul in Roman history.

entries.label: Heraclius opens his Persian campaigns and reconquers the East
Siege and capture of Ravenna by Lombards; end of Byzantine rule in North Italy
Arab corsairs seize bases in Sicily and Crete
entries.note: Arab corsairs seize bases in Sicily and Crete. Muslim piracy disrupts trade and communication between Constantinople and the West.

entries.label: Constantine VII sponsors revival of arts and letters
Fall of Antioch to Seljuk Turks; disruption of pilgrimage routes
Emergence of a Turkish, Muslim civilization in Anatolia
Despotate of the Morea
entries.note: The Despotate of the Morea was a province of the Byzantine Empire which existed between the mid-14th and mid-15th centuries. Its territory varied in size during its existence but eventually grew to include almost all the southern Greek peninsula now known as the Peloponnese. The territory was usually ruled by one or more sons of the current Byzantine emperor. Its capital was the fortified city of Mystras, near ancient Sparta, which became an important centre of the Palaiologan Renaissance.

entries.label: Brutus of Britain
entries.note: Geoffrey of Monmouth, a Benedictine monk living in the 12th century AD, wrote a fabricated history of the kings of Britain (Historia regum Britanniae). In this history Britain is said to receive its name from Brutus, the first of its kings. According to him, Brutus was the son of Silvius and the grandson of Aeneas.

entries.label: Betrayal of Tarpeia
entries.note: 750 BC - Tarpeia betrays Rome because of greed and attempts to hand it over to the invading Sabines.

entries.label: • Titus Lartius Flavus
entries.note: First Roman Dictator in 501 or 498

entries.label: Repeated constitutional crises and unrest at Rome
entries.note: 121BC: The first Senatus consultum ultimum was passed, granting the consul Lucius Opimius emergency powers to defeat the partisans of Gaius Gracchus. 100BC: Assassins hired by Marius's political allies Lucius Appuleius Saturninus and Gaius Servilius Glaucia beat to death Gaius Memmius (tribune), a candidate for the consulship.

entries.label: Boethius
entries.note: AD510 Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (Boethius)

entries.label: Flavius Symmachus (West)
entries.note: Son of Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (Boethius), consul in AD510.

entries.label: Creation of the exarchates of Africa and Italy
East Roman army reorganization
entries.note: AD640 - The Roman legion of the East Roman army is disbanded, and the theme systems is introduced.

entries.label: Publication of Ecloga; administrative and military reorganization
Defeats at the hands of Bulgars and Abbasid armies
Visit and conversion of Queen Olga (Helga) of Kiev
Empire of Trebizond
entries.note: The Empire of Trebizond was one of the successor rump states of the Byzantine Empire, along with the Despotate of the Morea and the Principality of Theodoro, that flourished during the 13th through to the 15th centuries, consisting of the far northeastern corner of Anatolia (the Pontus) and the southern Crimea. | The Empire of Trebizond was conquered eight years after the Fall of Constantinople when its eponymous capital surrendered to Ottoman forces after it was besieged in 1461.
351 BC: Elected : first non-patrician Dictator
Last Roman Dictator until Sulla in 82-81 BC

entries.label: • Dictator: Caesar
entries.note: 45 BC: Granted Dictatorship for life.

entries.label: Flavius Boethius (West)
entries.note: Son of Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (Boethius), consul in AD510.

entries.label: Heraclius issues Ecthesis, proclaiming Monothelete (“one will”) doctrine
The last exarch of Ravenna is killed by the Lombards
First Novel of Romanus I establishing pre-emption right in land reform
Conquest of Bulgaria by Basil II
Debasement of currency and fiscal crisis
The patrician Lucretia was raped by Lucius Tarquinius Superbus' son Sextus Tarquinius
Cato the Elder is elected censor
The Vandals take Carthage
entries.note: 19 October 439 AD The Vandals take Carthage. Geiseric, king of a new Vandal-Alan coalition, leads them from their base in Libya to successfully take possession of Carthage and the richest provinces of the western Empire. With this development, vital tax revenues, critical in allowing the Empire's remaining armies to be maintained, are directly threatened.

entries.label: Failure in Africa
entries.note: AD 468 African provinces are now beyond the reach of Rome. The last attempt to regain the rich North African provinces fails as the Vandals destroy an Eastern Roman expeditionary force, led by the general Basiliscus, off the coast of North Africa. With the weakness of the West exposed, the other barbarian powers established on Roman soil, rapidly take as much territory as they can, with Rome powerless to stop them.

entries.label: Flavius Belisarius
entries.note: Flavius Belisarius (c. AD500 – AD565) General of the Byzantine Empire. He was instrumental to Emperor Justinian's ambitious project of reconquering much of the Mediterranean territory of the former Western Roman Empire, which had been lost less than a century previously.

entries.label: Disintegration of Byzantine rule in the West
Clash between Constans II and Pope Martin I
Council of Hiera; proclamation of Iconoclastic doctrine
Appointment of John Cucuras as Domestic of the East
Revolt of George Maniaces; collapse of Byzantine Italy; Normans, under Robert Guiscard, conquer southern Italy (1046–1071)
Battle of Myriocephalon: Seljuk Turks defeat Manuel I
entries.note: 1176 Battle of Myriocephalon: Seljuk Turks defeat Manuel I; Byzantine withdrawal from central Anatolia

entries.label: Principality of Theodoro
entries.note: The Principality of Theodoro, also known as Gothia or the Principality of Theodoro-Mangup, was a Greek principality in the southern part of Crimea, specifically on the foothills of the Crimean Mountains. It represented one of the final rump states of the Byzantine Empire and the last territorial vestige of the Crimean Goths until its conquest by the Ottoman Empire by the Ottoman Albanian Gedik Ahmed Pasha in 1475.

entries.label: Villanovan culture
entries.note: The Villanovan culture was the earliest Iron Age culture of central and northern Italy, abruptly following the Bronze Age Terramare culture and giving way in the 7th century BC to an increasingly orientalizing culture influenced by Greek traders, which was followed without a severe break by the Etruscan civilization. The Villanovan culture and people branched from the Urnfield culture of Central Europe. The Villanovans introduced iron-working to the Italian peninsula; they practiced cremation and buried the ashes of their dead in pottery urns of distinctive double-cone shape.

entries.label: Villanovan I: (c. 1100 BC to c. 900 BC)
Villanovan II: (c. 900 BC to c. 700 BC)
Pomerium defined
entries.note: Pomerium: the sacred boundary of Rome

entries.label: Expulsion of Tarquinius Superbus
entries.note: 509 BC - Lucius Brutus founds the republic and expels the Etruscans and Tarquin the Proud from Rome. Following Lucretia's suicide, Lucius Junius Brutus called the Curiate Assembly, one of the legislative assemblies of the Roman Kingdom. The latter agreed to the overthrow and expulsion of Lucius Tarquinius Superbus and to a provisional constitution under which two consuls acted as a joint executive and a Curiate Assembly held legislative power, and swore never again to let a King rule Rome. It further elected Lucius Junius Brutus and Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, Lucretia's husband, as consuls.

entries.label: First non-patrician Praetor elected
entries.note: 337 BC: Elected the first non-patrician Praetor (Q. Publilius Philo)

entries.label: Augustus' coinage reform
entries.note: 23BC: Coinage reform of Augustus: Augustus centralized the minting of and reformed the composition and value of the Roman currency.

entries.label: Attila and the Huns attack
entries.note: AD 441 Attila and the Huns attack. Attila and Bleda attack cities of the East Roman Balkans. As a result, Eastern armies are withdrawn from a joint expeditionary force whose purpose was the restoration of Carthage and its surrounding provinces to Roman control. Consequently, the Western Empire is forced to recognise Vandal control of the richest parts of North Africa. Due to the significant loss of revenue, the Western Empire must now face the fact of a serious decline in its own military capacity.

entries.label: Romulus Augustulus is deposed
entries.note: 4 September 476 AD End of Empire - Romulus Augustulus is deposed. Able to exploit the discontent of his army over pay arrears, Odoacar, commander of the last Roman army of Italy, deposes the last western Emperor, Romulus Augustulus. With so many provinces falling out of imperial control, he is forced to pay his soldiers in land because tax revenues are insufficient. Afterwards, the Senate in Rome sent an embassy to the Eastern Emperor Zeno, and bestowed upon him the Western imperial insignia, a clear message that the West neither required nor could support any imperial claimant.

entries.label: Justinian I begins to restore the empire in the west
Decline of classical cities in Anatolia, the Balkans, and Italy
Byzantine revival under the Macedonian Dynasty
entries.note: AD 843–1056 - The Macedonian dynasty is established and the leads the Empire to a military, cultural and territorial revival. Byzantine scholars record and preserve many of the remaining ancient Greek and Roman texts. | AD 1025 - With the death of Basil II, the zenith of the Empire's power is passed and the long decline of the Byzantine Empire begins.

entries.label: Flowering of Byzantine arts and Platonism at Mistra (Sparta) in Greece
Founding of Alba Longa
entries.note: Alba Longa was an ancient city of Latium in central Italy, 19 kilometres (12 mi) southeast of Rome, in the Alban Hills. Founder and head of the Latin League, it was destroyed by Rome around the middle of the 7th century BC. In legend, Romulus and Remus, founders of Rome, had come from the royal dynasty of Alba Longa, which in Virgil's Aeneid had been the bloodline of Aeneas, a son of Venus.

entries.label: The Senones sack Rome
entries.note: Among other artifacts, books were destroyed. The history of Rome up to this point had to be mostly reconstructed and is sometimes unreliable or mythological.

entries.label: Augustus adopts his grandsons
entries.note: 17BC: Augustus adopted the sons of Agrippa and Julia, his grandsons Gaius Caesar and Lucius Caesar, as his own sons.

entries.label: Year of the Six Emperors
entries.note: 238 - Year of the Six Emperors The Senate supports a revolt of Gordian I and Gordian II in Africa. These two are defeated by an ally of Thrax, and the Senate appoints Balbinus and Pupienus as co-emperors. They are soon assassinated, and Thrax is killed in a mutiny. The young Gordian III becomes emperor.

entries.label: Alaric I
entries.note: Alaric I (d. 410) was the King of the Visigoths from 395–410. Alaric is most famous for his sack of Rome in 410, which marked a decisive event in the decline of the Roman Empire. | AD 395 - Becomes King of the Visigoths

entries.label: Avitus declared Emperor
entries.note: 9 July 455 AD Avitus is declared western Emperor. Acclaimed by Theodoric II and recognised by the Roman Senate, he nonetheless is reliant on the Visigoths for his position - the first time this has occured in the West. The decline in Rome’s military capacity has reached a point where it is now forced to include barbarian powers, albeit within its borders, in the process of imperial selection.

entries.label: Flavius Paulinus
entries.note: Decius Paulinus was a Roman aristocrat and politician who served as the last consul of the Roman Senate in AD534. After his term, consuls would be appointed in the East alone.

entries.label: War with Tsar Symeon of Bulgaria
House of Habsburg
entries.note: AD1642-1645) House of Wittelsbach

entries.label: Legendary dispute between Rome and Alba Longa (during the reign of Tullus Hostilius)
First dictatorship of Cincinnatus
entries.note: During the first dictatorship of Cincinnatus, the Aequians staged an offensive, breaking a truce. Cincinnatus defeated the Aquians at the Battle of Mount Algidus and after a triumph, returned to his farm after sixteen days.

entries.label: Marcus Porcius Cato Uticensis (Cato the Younger)
Tiberius retires to Capri, governing Rome by proxy
Massacre at Thessalonica; Ambrose forces the penance of Theodosius I
Fall of the western Roman Empire
entries.note: AD475 – Julius Nepos forced to flee to Dalmatia by his magister militum Orestes. Orestes proclaims his own son Romulus Augustulus as western emperor. AD 476 – Germanic general Odoacer kills Orestes, forces Romulus Augustus to abdicate and proclaims himself King of Italy. Traditional date for the fall of the western Roman Empire. The Eastern Roman Empire (later known as the Byzantine Empire) continues on. 480– Julius Nepos, still claiming to be emperor, is killed in Dalmatia.

entries.label: Carolingian Dynasty
entries.note: The term "sacrum" (i.e. "holy") in connection with the medieval Roman Empire was first used in 1157 under Frederick I Barbarossa. Charles V was the last Holy Roman Emperor to be crowned by the Pope. The final Holy Roman Emperor-elect, Francis II, abdicated in 1806 during the Napoleonic Wars that saw the Empire's final dissolution. | Widonid Dynasty

entries.label: Charles V
entries.note: 1516 - Charles V becomes king of Spain | 1519 - Charles V elected Holy Roman Emperor | 1529 - Charles V crowned Holy Roman Emperor at Bologna (the last such crowning by the Pope) | 1556 - Abdicates in favor of his younger brother Ferdinand I as Holy Roman Emperor and his son Philip II as King of Spain.

entries.label: Latin kings of Alba Longa
entries.note: The Latin kings of Alba Longa (Latin: rex Albanus, lit. King of Alba), also referred to as the Latin kings of Rome, or Alban kings of Rome, are a series of legendary kings of Latium ruling mainly from Alba Longa. In the mythic tradition of the founding of Rome, they fill the 400-year gap between the settlement of Aeneas in Italy and the establishing of the city walls of Rome by Romulus and Remus. It was this line of descent to which the Julii claimed kinship. After the defeat and destruction of Alba Longa and the incorporation of Latium into the Roman state, the Alban kingship is succeeded by the series of kings usually called "Etruscan," though only a few members of this line were brought in from neighboring Etruria to reign. | King of the "Aborigines", who gave his name to the new state of the Latins to be ruled from Laurentum by Aeneas and his own daughter Lavinia, given in marriage to Aeneas.

entries.label: Latinus
entries.note: The son of Aeneas and his Trojan wife Creusa, also known as Iulus, from which the gens Iulia was said to derive. Founder of Alba Longa (1151 BC), 30 years after the founding of Lavinium).

entries.label: Tiberinus Silvius
entries.note: Reportedly slain in battle near the Albula river and his body was carried away by it. The river was renamed Tiber.

entries.label: Romulus Silvius (in Livy) or Alladius (in Dionysius)
Second dictatorship of Cincinnatus
entries.note: Cincinnatus was called upon to accept a second dictatorship by the patricians to prevent Spurius Maelius from seizing power; the patricians suspected Spurius of using wheat to purchase the support of the plebeians, to set himself up as a king. Gaius Servilius Ahala was appointed magister equitum in order to stop Maelius; following an attack by Maelius, Ahala slew him. Cincinnatus again resigned his dictatorship and returned to his farm after 21 days.

entries.label: Vercingetorix
entries.note: Vercingetorix (c. 82 – 46 BC) was a king and chieftain of the Arverni tribe who united the Gauls in a failed revolt against Roman forces during the last phase of Julius Caesar's Gallic Wars. Despite having willingly surrendered to Caesar, he was executed in Rome.

entries.label: Augustus married Julia to his chosen successor, Marcus Claudius Marcellus
Constantinople is made the capital of the Empire
entries.note: AD 330 - Constantine makes Byzantium into his capital, which is renamed "Constantinople" (The City of Constantine). It would remain the capital of the Byzantine Empire, with a half-century exception, for over a thousand years.

entries.label: The Empire is permanently split into East and West
entries.note: AD 395 - The Empire is permanently split into eastern and western halves, following on the death of Theodosius I. Christianity becomes the official state religion of the Empire and others, such as Roman polytheism are proscribed.

entries.label: Tribute to the Huns
entries.note: AD447 - The eastern emperor agrees to pay the Huns a yearly tribute of 2100 pounds of gold.

entries.label: Frederick II
entries.note: Frederick II (26 December 1194 – 13 December 1250) One of the most powerful Holy Roman Emperors of the Middle Ages and head of the House of Hohenstaufen. His political and cultural ambitions, based in Sicily and stretching through Italy to Germany, and even to Jerusalem, were enormous; however, his enemies, especially the popes, prevailed, and his dynasty collapsed soon after his death. Historian Donald Detwiler,wrote of him: "A man of extraordinary culture, energy, and ability – called by a contemporary chronicler stupor mundi (the wonder of the world), by Nietzsche the first European, and by many historians the first modern ruler – Frederick established in Sicily and southern Italy something very much like a modern, centrally governed kingdom with an efficient bureaucracy." Viewing himself as a direct successor to the Roman Emperors of Antiquity, he was Emperor of the Romans from his papal coronation in 1220 until his death; he was also a claimant to the title of King of the Romans from 1212 and unopposed holder of that monarchy from 1215. As such, he was King of Germany, of Italy, and of Burgundy. At the age of three, he was crowned King of Sicily as a co-ruler with his mother, Constance of Hauteville, the daughter of Roger II of Sicily. His other royal title was King of Jerusalem by virtue of marriage and his connection with the Sixth Crusade. He was frequently at war with the Papacy, hemmed in between Frederick's lands in northern Italy and his Kingdom of Sicily (the Regno) to the south, and thus he was excommunicated four times and often vilified in pro-papal chronicles of the time and since. Pope Gregory IX went so far as to call him the Antichrist. Speaking six languages (Latin, Sicilian, German, French, Greek and Arabic), Frederick was an avid patron of science and the arts. He played a major role in promoting literature through the Sicilian School of poetry. His Sicilian royal court in Palermo, from around 1220 to his death, saw the first use of a literary form of an Italo-Romance language, Sicilian. The poetry that emanated from the school had a significant influence on literature and on what was to become the modern Italian language. The school and its poetry were saluted by Dante and his peers and predate by at least a century the use of the Tuscan idiom as the elite literary language of Italy.

entries.label: Aeneas
entries.note: A noble Trojan leading a force fleeing from the collapse of Troy. Listed as the first Latin king by both Livy and Dionysius. He founded Lavinium in 1181 BC, where he would rule the Latins until his death.

entries.label: Aventinus
entries.note: The Aventine Hill was reportedly named after him.

entries.label: Sibylline Books acquired
entries.note: King Tarquin was approached by the Cumaean Sibyl, who offered him nine books of prophecy at an exorbitant price. Tarquin abruptly refused, and the Sibyl proceeded to burn three of the nine. She then offered him the remaining books, but at the same price. He hesitated, but refused again. The Sibyl then burned three more books before offering him the three remaining books at the original price. At last Tarquin accepted, in this way obtaining the Sibylline Books.

entries.label: Conflict of the Orders
entries.note: The Conflict of the Orders, sometimes referred to as the Struggle of the Orders, was a political struggle between the plebeians (commoners) and patricians (aristocrats) of the ancient Roman Republic lasting from 500 BC to 287 BC in which the plebeians sought political equality with the patricians. It played a major role in the development of the Constitution of the Roman Republic. Shortly after the founding of the Republic, this conflict led to a secession from Rome by the Plebeians to the Sacred Mount at a time of war. The result of this first secession was the creation of the office of plebeian tribune, and with it the first acquisition of real power by the plebeians.

entries.label: Great earthquake of Asia Minor: massive relief by Emperor Tiberius
Gallic Empire
entries.note: The Gallic Empire (Latin: Imperium Galliarum) The modern name for a breakaway part of the Roman Empire that functioned de facto as a separate state from 260 to 274. It originated during the Crisis of the Third Century. It was established by Postumus in 260 in the wake of barbarian invasions and instability in Rome, and at its height included the territories of Germania, Gaul, Britannia, and (for a time) Hispania. After Postumus' assassination in 268 it lost much of its territory, but continued under a number of emperors and usurpers. It was retaken by Roman emperor Aurelian after the Battle of Châlons in 274.

entries.label: Alans, Vandals, and Sueves cross the Rhine
entries.note: 31 December 406 AD Significant numbers of Alans, Vandals, and Sueves cross the Rhine into Roman Gaul. The Western Empire's frontiers had already been compromised the previous summer with the invasion of Italy by Radagaisus. Coupled with the forces of the Huns shifting further westward, the balance of strategic power in central Europe was inexorably turning against the interests of Rome.

entries.label: Charlemagne
entries.note: 768 - Becomes King of the Franks

entries.label: Otto II
entries.note: The beginning of the light colour indicates Election. The beginning of the dark colour indicates Coronation.

entries.label: Maximilian I
entries.note: He was never crowned by the Pope, as the journey to Rome was blocked by the Venetians. He proclaimed himself elected emperor in 1508 (Pope Julius II later recognized this) at Trent, thus breaking the long tradition of requiring a papal coronation for the adoption of the Imperial title.

entries.label: Reforms of Publius Valerius Publicola are promulgated
entries.note: 509 BC The consul Publius Valerius Publicola promulgated a number of liberal reforms, including opening the office of senator to all Roman citizens and placing the treasury under the administration of appointed quaestors.

entries.label: The offices of the Tribuni militum consulari potestate were established
entries.note: A collegium of three patrician or plebeian tribunes, one each from specific Roman tribes (the Titienses, the Ramnenses, and the Luceres), would hold the power of the consuls from year to year, subject to the Senate.

entries.label: Office of Praetor established
entries.note: 366BC: The office of Praetor, which took the judiciary responsibilities of the consul and could be held only by a patrician, was established.

entries.label: Last Plebeian Secession
entries.note: Lex Hortensia ends Senate veto power over Plebeian Council Conflict of the Orders ends.

entries.label: Augustus married Julia to his general and stepson Tiberius
First Visit of Hadrian to cities of Asia Minor
Palmyrene Empire
entries.note: The Palmyrene Empire (260–273) A splinter empire that broke away from the Roman Empire during the Crisis of the Third Century. It encompassed the Roman provinces of Syria Palaestina, Egypt and large parts of Asia Minor. The Palmyrene Empire was ruled by Queen Zenobia for her infant son Vaballathus. The capital of the short-lived empire was the city of Palmyra. In 270, Aurelian became Roman Emperor. After defeating the Alamanni, who had invaded Italy, Aurelian turned his attention to the lost eastern provinces - the Palmyrene Empire. Asia Minor was recovered easily; every city but Byzantium and Tyana surrendered to him with little resistance. The fall of Tyana lent itself to a legend; Aurelian to that point had destroyed every city that resisted him, but he spared Tyana after having a vision of the great philosopher Apollonius of Tyana, whom he respected greatly, in a dream. Apollonius implored him, stating: "Aurelian, if you desire to rule, abstain from the blood of the innocent! Aurelian, if you will conquer, be merciful!" Whatever the reason, Aurelian spared Tyana. It paid off; many more cities submitted to him upon seeing that the emperor would not exact revenge upon them.

entries.label: Constantine the Great dies. Baptized shortly prior to his death
entries.note: AD 337, May 22 Constantine the Great dies. Baptized shortly prior to his death.

entries.label: Sack of Rome
entries.note: 24 August 410 AD The sack of Rome by Alaric and the Visigoths. The Western Roman Emperor Honorius fails to protect the old imperial capital which is sacked for the first time in almost 800 years. As a result, he communicates with the British provinces, advising them to look to their own defence. Faced with multiple threats including both the Visigoths and the Rhine invaders, the Empire starts to abandon outlying territories in an effort to concentrate its forces closer to home.

entries.label: Interregnum
entries.note: Roman authority in Italy was briefly re-established under Justinian, though his gains were lost under his successor Justin II, after a new Germanic tribe, the Lombards, invaded from the north and established their kingdom in 568.

entries.label: The Habsburg emperors claimed the Italian crown until 1801. The empire continued to include Italian territories until its dissolution in 1806.
Kingdom of Italy as a client state of France (1805 - 1814)
The Plebeian Council was reorganized by tribes rather than curiae
Roman soldiers earn their first salary
The Lex Hortensia is passed
entries.note: This made resolutions of the Plebeian Council (plebiscites) binding on all Romans, they formally only applied to plebeians.

entries.label: Murder of Tribune Tiberius Gracchus
entries.note: 133 BC: Tribune Tiberius Gracchus secures agrarian reform and is was beaten to death by a mob of senators led by the Pontifex Maximus Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Serapio (consul 138 BC).

entries.label: Gaius Cilnius Maecenas
entries.note: Gaius Cilnius Maecenas (68 BC to 8 BC) An ally, friend and political advisor to Octavian as well as an important patron for the new generation of Augustan poets, including both Horace and Virgil. During the reign of Augustus, Maecenas served as a quasi-culture minister to the Emperor. His name has become a byword for a wealthy, generous and enlightened patron of the arts.

entries.label: Iceni Rebellion
entries.note: 60-61 – Boudica, queen of the Iceni, leads a rebellion in Britain.

entries.label: Hadrian creates the Panhellenion
entries.note: c. AD 125 - Hadrian creates the Panhellenion, the league of Greek cities with great sanctuaries and games throughout the Roman world.

entries.label: Antonine Wall abandoned for the last time
Ascession of Shapur I
entries.note: AD 242 Shapur defeats Rome. The Sassanian Shah Shapur I unites the territories of what is today Iran and Iraq to create a Persian superpower that inflicts significant defeats on three different Roman Emperors. After over half a century of struggle, the stability of Rome's eastern front is restored, but the cost is enormous. To fund the necessary doubling of its armed forces, taxes have been significantly raised, and the threat posed by the might of the Persians is only temporarily arrested, not extinguished. Should another major threat appear, Rome will now find it has little spare capacity left to meet it.

entries.label: Britannic Empire
entries.note: AD286-296 - The Britannic Empire A short-lived breakaway state of the Roman empire in the late Roman Period. It was formed as a result of the revolt by the naval commander Carausius. It ended when Carausius's usurper, Allectus, was defeated by the Emperor Constantius I in 296.

entries.label: Battle of Adrianople
entries.note: 9 August 378 AD Disaster at Adrianople. Roman Emperor Valens and two-thirds of his elite field army are killed in battle with the Goths. The defeat can be traced to the rise of the Huns on the fringes of Europe causing tens of thousands of Gothic refugees to arrive on the Danube by late AD 376. Valens, already at war with Persia, had no choice but to admit them into Roman territory. But faced with Roman hostility, within a space of two years, the Goths reorganised themselves into a powerful military coalition which handed Valens and his army a massive defeat.

entries.label: Visigoths given Gallia Aquitania
entries.note: AD 418 A treaty gives Gallia Aquitania to the Visigoths. Honorius' hand is forced and the Visigoths settled permanently, with full imperial recognition, in southwestern Gaul. The weakness of the western Empire's military now proves insufficient in dealing with the multiple invaders now established on its soil. With this treaty, Romes hopes to use the Goths to help defeat the Rhine invaders who have by now occupied most of the Iberian peninsula.

entries.label: Theoderic
entries.note: Theoderic becomes the first Ostrogothic King of Italy

entries.label: Harodingians
entries.note: Bavarian dynasty, First Restoration

entries.label: Frederick II was never crowned King of Italy
College of the tribune of the Plebs amended
entries.note: 459 BC: The college of the tribune of the Plebs is raised from two to ten tribunes.

entries.label: Lex Licinia Sextia established the right of plebeians to hold the consulship
A census counted about 270,000 residents of Rome
The number of quaestors was increased to twelve
Tribunate and death of Caius Sempronius Gracchus
Marcus Agrippa
entries.note: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa (c. 23 Oct or Novr 64/63 BC – 12 BC) Roman statesman and general. He was a close friend, son-in-law, and lieutenant to Augustus and was responsible for his most important military victories, most notably at the Battle of Actium against the forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. As a result of these victories Octavian became the first Roman Emperor, adopting the name of Augustus. Agrippa was also father-in-law of the second Emperor Tiberius, maternal grandfather to Caligula, and maternal great-grandfather of the Emperor Nero. As aedile, he effected great improvements in the city of Rome, restoring and building aqueducts, enlarging and cleansing the Cloaca Maxima, constructing baths and porticos, and laying out gardens. He also gave a stimulus to the public exhibition of works of art. It was unusual for an ex-consul to hold the lower-ranking position of aedile, but Agrippa's success bore out this break with tradition. As emperor, Augustus would later boast that "he had found the city of brick but left it of marble", thanks in part to the great services provided by Agrippa under his reign.

entries.label: Second visit of Hadrian to Asia Minor
Alboin
entries.note: Began his reign before the Lombard Kingdom was established in Italy.

entries.label: Victor Emmanuel II
entries.note: Victor Emmanuel II (1861–78) Former King of Sardinia and first king of united Italy.

entries.label: Victor Emmanuel III
entries.note: Victor Emmanuel III (1900–46) King of Italy during the First World War and during the Fascist regime of Benito Mussolini.

entries.label: First Plebeian senators appointed
entries.note: First Plebeian (commoner) senators appointed (conscripti) to fill vacancies created by the overthrow of the monarchy

entries.label: Tribal Assembly created
entries.note: 447 BC: Tribal Assembly created: two quaestors elected for the first time.

entries.label: A law was passed which required the election of at least one plebeian censor every five years
The number of Praetors was increased to six
Jugurtha is imprisoned
entries.note: The Numidian king Jugurtha is imprisoned in the Mamertine Prison.

entries.label: Sibylline Books destroyed
entries.note: The Books were burned in AD 405 by the General Flavius Stilicho, who was a Christian and regarded the books as Pagan and therefore evil.

entries.label: Cleph
entries.note: From an unnamed dynasty

entries.label: Arioald
entries.note: Non-dynastic king

entries.label: Charles V was the last emperor to be crowned king of Italy or to officially use the title
Cispadane Republic
entries.note: The Cispadane Republic was a short-lived client republic located in northern Italy, founded in 1796 with the protection of the French army, led by Napoleon Bonaparte. In the following year, it was merged with the Transpadane Republic (formerly the Duchy of Milan until 1796) to form the Cisalpine Republic. The Cispadane Republic was the first Italian sovereign State to adopt the Italian tricolour as its flag.

entries.label: Umberto I
entries.note: Umberto I (1878–1900) Approved the Triple Alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary. Assassinated in 1900 by an anarchist.

entries.label: Umberto II
entries.note: Umberto II (1946) The last King of Italy who was pressured to call a referendum on whether Italy would retain the monarchy; Italians voted to become a republic instead of a constitutional monarchy.

entries.label: Due process rights granted to all Roman citizens
entries.note: 504 BC: Consul Publius Valerius Publicola grants due process rights to all Roman citizens; criminalizes all future attempts to plot to seize a tyranny

entries.label: Earliest surviving document of the Roman State
entries.note: The comitium contains the earliest surviving document of the Roman State. A cippus found on the second stratigraphic level, dated to 450 BC, informs citizens of their civic duties.

entries.label: Leges Genuciae
entries.note: 342 BC - Lex Genucia passed: no man can hold the same office before 10 years have elapsed from the first election. Second law passed, disallowing any man from holding two offices at once. Charging interest on loans was also banned.

entries.label: The number of quaestors was raised from four to ten
Lex Villia annalis
entries.note: Minimum ages set for the cursus honorum offices and a requirement of a minimum of two years in private life between offices.

entries.label: Lex Calpurnia
entries.note: Permanent extortion court established

entries.label: Caesar sent to govern Further Spain
entries.note: 61–60 BC: Caesar sent to govern Further Spain. He reforms administration and leads a highly aggressive punitive campaign. On his return to Rome he gives up the prospect of a triumph to stand for election for the consulship.

entries.label: Destruction of Pompeii
entries.note: AD79 August 24, An eruption of Vesuvius destroys much of Pompeii and Herculaneum

entries.label: Rule of the Dukes (Ten year interregnum)
Lucius Sicinius Vellutus leads the first Secessio Plebis: the plebs abandoned Rome for the nearby Monte Sacro
Taranto appealed to Epirus for aid against Rome
Attalus III of Pergamum bequeaths his kingdom to Rome
Caesar elected as military tribune
entries.note: 72 or 71 BC: Caesar elected as military tribune and probably serves against Spartacus.

entries.label: Charlemagne captures Pavia, the capital of the Lombard kingdom
John
entries.note: (senior co-emperor for the underage Baldwin II)

entries.label: Plebiscites now law
entries.note: 449 BC: Plebeian Council resolutions ("plebiscites") given full force of law over Plebeians and Patricians, but still subject to Senate veto.

entries.label: The Romans negotiate a treaty with Alexander I of Epirus
Caesar elected to the quaestorship
entries.note: 69 BC: Caesar elected to the quaestorship and serves in Further Spain

entries.label: North Africa et al
entries.note: Northern Africa, Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and the Balearic Islands

entries.label: Theophanu
entries.note: Theophanu (c. 955 – June 15, 991) Niece of the Byzantine Emperor John I Tzimiskes. By her marriage with Holy Roman Emperor Otto II, she was Empress consort of the Holy Roman Empire and held regency as Empress dowager upon her husband's death in 983. Her name is derived from Medieval Greek Theophaneia (Θεοφάνεια), "appearance of God" (Theophany). | 972 Marriage of Otto II to Princess Theophano; Byzantine-German alliance

entries.label: Marriage between patricians and plebeians allowed
The Romans gain control of Neapolis (Naples)
Caesar is curule aedile
entries.note: 65 BC: Caesar is curule aedile with Bibulus, who complains about being outshone. He also gives gladiatorial games in honour of his father.

entries.label: details
entries.note: Civil Wars and Usurpations during the Crisis of the Third Century 238 – Year of the Six Emperors between various generals against Maximinus Thrax and after his murder. 238 – Battle of Carthage – Troops loyal to the Roman Emperor Maximinus Thrax defeat and kill his successor Gordian II. After Gordian I and Gordian II are defeated by a pro-Maximinus Army following an attempt to overthrow the emperor, Maximinus is assassinated. Pupienus, Balbinus, and Gordian III replace him, but the former two are assassinated within months and only Gordian III survives. 240 – Failed usurpation of Sabinianus in Mauretania 248-249 – Failed usurpations of Jotapianus in Syria and Pacatianus in Moesia. 249 – Emperor Philip the Arab killed and overthrown by rebels at the Battle of Verona and replaced by Decius. 250 – Failed usurpation of Licinianus in Rome. 251 – Failed usurpation of Titus Julius Priscus in Thrace. 252 – Failed usurpation of Cyriades in Syria. 253 – Usurpations of Aemilianus and Valerian: Emperors Trebonianus Gallus and Volusianus murdered by their soldiers and replaced by Aemilianus. Valerian raises the Rhine legions in revolt, while Aemilianus is killed by his own soldiers. 254 – Failed usurpation of Uranius in Syria. 260 – Failed usurpations of Ingenuus and Regalianus in Pannonia; possibly of Sponsianus in Dacia. 260-261 – Failed usurpation of Macrianus Major, Macrianus Minor, Quietus and Balista in the East 260-274 – The breakaway Gallic Empire 261 – Failed usurpations of Lucius Piso and Valens Thessalonicus in Achaea. 261-262 – Failed usurpation of Mussius Aemilianus and Memor in Egypt. 267 – Failed usurpation of Maeonius in Palmyra. 268 – Failed usurpation of Aureolus in the West. Emperor Gallienus murdered by his soldiers and Claudius Gothicus proclaimed Emperor. 270 – Usurpation of Aurelian against Quintillus. 270 – Palmyrene invasion of Egypt – Palmyrene victory 272 – Battle of Immae – Aurelian defeats the army of Zenobia of Palmyra 272 – Battle of Emesa – Aurelian decisively defeats Zenobia. 271 – Failed usurpations of Felicissimus in Rome and Septimius in Dalmatia. 274 – Battle of Châlons – Aurelian defeats the Gallic usurper Tetricus, reestablishing central control of the whole empire. 275 – Aurelian murdered by the Praetorian Guard and replaced by Marcus Claudius Tacitus 276 – Usurpation of Probus against Florianus. 280 – Failed usurpation of Julius Saturninus in the East. 280-281 – Failed usurpation of Proculus and Bonosus in the West. 282 – Probus assassinated by his soldiers. The new emperor Carus may have been involved in the plotting. 283-285 – Failed usurpation of Sabinus Julianus. 284-285 – Usurpation of Diocletian against Carinus 285 – Battle of the Margus – The usurper Diocletian defeated the army of the Emperor Carinus, who was killed.

entries.label: Twelve Tables of Roman law published
entries.note: 449BC - The Decemviri publish the Twelve Tables of Roman law.

entries.label: Caesar is praetor
entries.note: 62 BC: Caesar is praetor. He supports the tribune Metellus Nepos and temporarily resigns after the latter has fled. Bona Dea scandal leads him to divorce Pompeia.

entries.label: Kingdom of the Vandals and Alans
Fidenae, an important trade post on the Tiber, was captured from the Veii
Death of Julia and Aurelia
entries.note: 54 BC: Death of Julia and her infant child. Death of Caesar’s mother Aurelia.

entries.label: Visit of Caracalla to sanctuary of Asclepius, Pergamum
Debasement of imperial currency and inflation
Death of Cornelia
entries.note: 69 BC: Death of Caesar's aunt Julia and wife Cornelia, both of whom are given public funerals.

entries.label: Caesar deified
entries.note: 44 BC: Assassination of Caesar a few days before he planned to set out for a series of campaigns against the Dacians and Parthians. Caesar deified.

entries.label: Widespread building programs in Asia Minor
Diocletian splits the Empire into two halves
entries.note: AD285 – Diocletian splits the empire into two halves and appoints Maximian emperor of the Western portion while Diocletian rules the East.

entries.label: Constitutio Antoniniana
entries.note: AD 212 - Constitutio Antoniniana extends Roman citizenship to all free residents of the empire.

entries.label: Diocletian appoints Constantius I and Galerius as caesars
Catiline conspiracies
entries.note: Second Catilinarian conspiracy: A conspiracy led by the senator Catiline to overthrow the Republic was exposed before the Senate. The five conspirators present were summarily executed in the Mamertine Prison.

entries.label: Diocletian issues the Edict on Maximum Prices
Volcanic winter
entries.note: The volcanic winter of 536 was the most severe and protracted episode of climatic cooling in the Northern Hemisphere in the last 2,000 years. The volcanic winter was caused by at least three simultaneous eruptions of uncertain origin, with several possible locations proposed in various continents. Most contemporary accounts of the volcanic winter are from authors in Constantinople, the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, although the impact of the cooler temperatures extended beyond Europe.

entries.label: Pompey clears Mediterranean of pirates
entries.note: 67 BC: Lex Gabinia: Pompey given extraordinary command to clear the Mediterranean of pirates, and succeeds in a brief, but highly organised campaign. Caesar spoke in favour of the law. | 64 BC: Caesar placed in charge of one of the extraordinary courts required to deal with Cato’s investigations into debts to the Republic left unpaid by Sulla’s supporters. 63 BC: Caesar appointed judge in prosecution of Rabirius.

entries.label: Diocletian and Maximian abdicate
entries.note: AD305 – Diocletian and Maximian abdicate. Constantius and Galerius becomes Augusti. Maximinus is appointed Caesar in the east and Severus in the west.

entries.label: Obstruction of Bibulus
entries.note: 59 BC: Determined obstruction by Caesar's colleague Bibulus and supporters including Cato produces repeated disorders. Caesar forces through his legislation, but leaves himself vulnerable to future prosecution.

entries.label: Constantine I proclaimed emperor
entries.note: AD306 – Constantius dies at Eboracum (York). His son Constantine I proclaimed emperor. Maxentius, son of Maximian, proclaims himself emperor in Rome.

entries.label: Republic of Ancona (from 1000 - 1198 Ancona gains gradual autonomy)
Caesar refuses Sulla’s order to divorce Cornelia
entries.note: 81 BC: Caesar refuses Sulla’s order to divorce Cornelia and goes on the run. He is subsequently pardoned following appeals from his mother’s relatives.

entries.label: Plague of Justinian
entries.note: The first recorded epidemic of Bubonic Plague ravaged the Byzantine Empire during the sixth century, and was named the Plague of Justinian after emperor Justinian I, who was infected but survived through extensive treatment. The epidemic is estimated to have killed approximately 50 million people in the Roman Empire alone.

entries.label: Caesar undergoes military service in Asia
entries.note: 80–78 BC: Caesar undergoes military service in Asia and wins the corona civica at Mytilene.

entries.label: Caesar's judicial appointments
entries.note: 77 BC: Caesar appears in the courts at Rome, unsuccessfully prosecuting Cnaeus Cornelius Dolabella. 76 BC: Caesar unsuccessfully prosecutes Caius Antonius.

entries.label: Donation of Pepin
entries.note: AD756 - The Donation of Pepin in 756 provided a legal basis for the creation of the Papal States, thus extending the temporal rule of the popes beyond the duchy of Rome.

entries.label: Caesar captured by pirates
entries.note: 75 BC: Caesar travels to Rhodes to study and is captured and ransomed by pirates.

entries.label: Caesar in Asia
entries.note: 74 BC: On his own initiative Caesar goes to Asia, raises local troops and defeats an invasion or raid led by one of King Mithridates’ commanders.

entries.label: Prisoner in the Vatican
entries.note: A prisoner in the Vatican or prisoner of the Vatican described the situation of the pope with respect to Italy during the period from the capture of Rome by the armed forces of the Kingdom of Italy on 20 September 1870 until the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929.

entries.label: Lateran Treaty
entries.note: The Lateran Treaty was one component of the Lateran Pacts of 1929, agreements between the Kingdom of Italy under King Victor Emmanuel III (with his Prime Minister Benito Mussolini) and the Holy See under Pope Pius XI to settle the long-standing Roman Question. The treaty and associated pacts were named after the Lateran Palace where they were signed on 11 February 1929, and the Italian parliament ratified them on 7 June 1929. The treaty recognised Vatican City as an independent state under the sovereignty of the Holy See. The Italian government also agreed to give the Roman Catholic Church financial compensation for the loss of the Papal States.

entries.label: Seige of Athens
entries.note: 86BC, Lucius Cornelius Sulla laid siege to Athens, and conquered the city, causing much destruction. It was during the siege that he laid waste to the Academy

entries.label: Caesar bridges the Rhine for the first time and leads an expedition to Britain
entries.note: 55 BC: Caesar bridges the Rhine for the first time and leads an expedition to Britain. 54 BC: Caesar bridges the Rhine a second time.

entries.label: Julius Caesar in Britain
entries.note: Augustus planned invasions in 34, 27 and 25 BC but circumstances were never favourable.

entries.label: Second and larger invasion of Britain
County of Apulia and Calabria (Duchy of Apulia and Calabria after 1059)
The last of the Cilician pirates were wiped out by Pompey
Sicilia
entries.note: 241 BC – Sicilia (Sicily) taken over from the Carthaginians and annexed at the end of the First Punic War.

entries.label: Macedonia
entries.note: 147 BC – Macedonia; mainland Greece. It was annexed after a rebellion by the Achaean League.

entries.label: Asia
entries.note: 129 BC – Asia; formerly the Kingdom of Pergamon in western Anatolia (modern Turkey) by its last king, Attalus III, in 133 BC.

entries.label: Creta et Cyrenae
entries.note: 67 BC – Creta et Cyrenae; Cyrenaica was bequeathed to Rome in 78 BC. However, it was not organised as a province. It was incorporated into the province of Creta et Cyrenae when Crete was annexed in 67 BC.

entries.label: Africa Nova
entries.note: 46 BC - Africa Nova (eastern Numidia - Algeria), Julius Caesar annexed eastern Numidia and the new province called Africa Nova (new Africa) to distinguish it from the older province of Africa, which become known as Africa Vetus (Old Africa).

entries.label: Aegyptus
entries.note: 30 BC - Aegyptus; Taken over by Augustus after his defeat of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII of Egypt in 30 BC. It was the first imperial province in that it was Augustus' own domain as the Egyptians recognised him as their new pharaoh. Its proper initial name was Alexandrea et Aegyptus. It was governed by Augustus' praefectus Alexandreae et Aegypti.

entries.label: Galatia
entries.note: 25BC – Galatia (central Anatolia, Turkey), formerly a client kingdom, it was annexed by Augustus when Amyntas, its last king died. (imperial propraetorial province)

entries.label: Moesia
entries.note: 6 AD? - Moesia (on the east and south bank of the River Danube part of modern Serbia, the north of the Republic of Macedonia, northern Bulgaria), Conquered in 28 BC, originally it was a military district under the province of Macedonia. The first mention of a provincial governor was for 6 AD, at the beginning of the Batonian war. In 85 Moesia was divided into Moesia Superior and Moesia Inferior (imperial proconsular provinces).

entries.label: Cappadocia
entries.note: 18 AD – Cappadocia (central Anatolia - Turkey). Imperial propraetorial (later proconsular) province.

entries.label: Mauretania Tingitana
entries.note: 42 AD – Mauretania Tingitana (northern Morocco), after the death of Ptolemy, the last king of Mauretania in 40 AD his kingdom was annexed. It was begun by Caligula and was completed by Claudius with the defeat of the rebels. In 42 AD Claudius divided it into two provinces (imperial procuratorial province).

entries.label: Alpes Maritimae
entries.note: 63 AD? - Alpes Maritimae (on the French Alps), created as a protectorate by Augustus, it probably became a province under Nero when Alpes Cottiae became a province (imperial procuratorial province).

entries.label: Arabia
entries.note: 106 AD – Arabia, formerly the Kingdom of Nabataea, it was annexed without resistance by Trajan (imperial propraetorial province).

entries.label: Mesopotamia
entries.note: 116 AD - Mesopotamia (Iraq) seized from the Parthians and annexed by Trajan, who invaded the Parthian Empire in late 115. Given back to the Parthians by Hadrian in 118. In 198 Septimius Severus conquered a small area in the north and named it Mesopotamia. It was attacked twice by the Persians (imperial praefectorial province).

entries.label: Numidia
entries.note: 193 AD - Numidia, was separated from Africa proconsularis by Septimius Severus (imperial propraetorial province).

entries.label: Dacia Aureliana
entries.note: 271 AD - Dacia Aureliana (most of Bulgaria and Serbia) created by Aurelian in the territory of the former Moesia Superior after his evacuation of Dacia Trajana beyond the River Danube.

entries.label: Lusitania
entries.note: 27 BC - Lusitania (Portugal and Extremadura in Spain), created with the reorganisation of the provinces in Hispania by Augustus (imperial proconsular province). | 27 BC – Achaia (southern and central Greece), Augustus separated it from Macedonia (senatorial propraetorial province).

entries.label: Raetia
entries.note: 15 BC – Raetia (imperial procuratorial province).

entries.label: Mauretania Caesariensis
entries.note: 42 AD - Mauretania Caesariensis, (western and central Algeria), after the death of Ptolemy, the last king of Mauretania in 40 his kingdom was annexed. It was begun by Caligula and was completed by Claudius with the defeat of the rebels. In 42 AD Claudiusdivided it into two provinces( imperial procuratorial province).

entries.label: Commagene
entries.note: 72 AD – Commagene, its client king was deposed and Commagene was annexed to Syria.

entries.label: Dacia
entries.note: 107 AD – Dacia "Trajana" (the Romanian regions of south-eastern Transylvania, the Banat, and Oltenia), conquered by Trajan in his Dacian Wars (imperial proconsular province). Divided into Dacia Superior and Dacia Inferior in 158 by Antoninus Pius. Divided into three provinces (Tres Daciae) in 166 by Marcus Aurelius: Porolissensis, Apulensis and Malvensis (imperial procuratorial provinces). Abandoned by Aurelian in 271.

entries.label: Assyria
entries.note: 116 AD - Assyria, Trajan suppressed a revolt by Assyrians in Mesopotamia and created the province. Hadrian relinquished it in 118.

entries.label: Syria Coele and Syria Phoenice
entries.note: 194 AD - Syria Coele and Syria Phoenice, Septimius Severus divided Syria into these two units in the north and the south respectively. Imperial provinces (proconsular and propraetorial respectively).

entries.label: Forum Romanum
entries.note: The Roman Forum (Latin: Forum Romanum, Italian: Foro Romano) Rectangular forum (plaza) surrounded by the ruins of several important ancient government buildings at the center of the city of Rome. Citizens of the ancient city referred to this space, originally a marketplace, as the Forum Magnum, or simply the Forum. It was for centuries the center of Roman public life: the site of triumphal processions and elections; the venue for public speeches, criminal trials, and gladiatorial matches; and the nucleus of commercial affairs. Here statues and monuments commemorated the city's great men. Located in the small valley between the Palatine and Capitoline Hills, the Forum today is a sprawling ruin of architectural fragments and intermittent archaeological excavations attracting 4.5 million sightseers yearly. Many of the oldest and most important structures of the ancient city were located on or near the Forum. The Roman kingdom's earliest shrines and temples were located on the southeastern edge. These included the ancient former royal residence, the Regia (8th century BC), and the Temple of Vesta (7th century BC), as well as the surrounding complex of the Vestal Virgins, all of which were rebuilt after the rise of imperial Rome. Other archaic shrines to the northwest, such as the Umbilicus Urbis and the Vulcanal (Shrine of Vulcan), developed into the Republic's formal Comitium (assembly area). This is where the Senate—as well as Republican government itself—began. The Senate House, government offices, tribunals, temples, memorials and statues gradually cluttered the area. Over time the archaic Comitium was replaced by the larger adjacent Forum and the focus of judicial activity moved to the new Basilica Aemilia (179 BC). Some 130 years later, Julius Caesar built the Basilica Julia, along with the new Curia Julia, refocusing both the judicial offices and the Senate itself. This new Forum, in what proved to be its final form, then served as a revitalized city square where the people of Rome could gather for commercial, political, judicial and religious pursuits in ever greater numbers. Eventually much economic and judicial business would transfer away from the Forum Romanum to the larger and more extravagant structures (Trajan's Forum and the Basilica Ulpia) to the north. The reign of Constantine the Great saw the construction of the last major expansion of the Forum complex—the Basilica of Maxentius (312 AD). This returned the political center to the Forum until the fall of the Western Roman Empire almost two centuries later.

entries.label: Corsica et Sardinia
entries.note: 237 BC – Corsica et Sardinia; these two islands were taken over from the Carthaginians and annexed soon after the Mercenary War, in 238 BC and 237 BC respectively.

entries.label: Hispania Citerior and Hispania Ulterior
entries.note: 197 BC – Hispania Citerior; along the east coast of the (Iberian Peninsula); 197 BC - Hispania Ulterior; along the southern coast of the (Iberian Peninsula); part of the territories taken over from the Carthaginians .

entries.label: Africa
entries.note: 146 BC – Africa; modern day Tunisia and western Libya; home territory of Carthage; annexed after the destruction of Carthage in the Third Punic War.

entries.label: Gallia Narbonensis
entries.note: 120 BC – Gallia Narbonensis (southern France); prior to its annexation it was called Gallia Transalpina (Gallia the other side of the Alps) to distinguish it from Gallia Cisalpina (Gaul this side of the Alps, in northern Italy). It was annexed following attacks on the allied Greek city of Massalia (Marseille).

entries.label: Pontus et Bithynia
entries.note: 63 BC – Pontus et Bithynia; the Kingdom of Bithynia (in North-western Anatolia - Turkey) was bequeathed to Rome by its last king, Nicomedes IV in 74 BC. It was organised as a Roman province at the end of the Third Mithridatic War (73-63 BC) by Pompey who incorporated the eastern part of the defeated Kingdom of Pontus into it in 63 BC.

entries.label: Aquitania
entries.note: 27 BC or 16-13 BC – Aquitania (south-western France) province created in the territories in Gaul conquered by Julius Caesar; there is uncertainty as to whether it was created with Augustus’ first visit and the first census on Gaul or during Augustus’ visit in 16-13 (imperial proconsular province). | 27 BC - Illyricum, Augustus conquered Illyria and southern Pannonia in 35-33 BC. Created as a senatorial province in 27 BC. Northern Pannonia was conquered during the Pannonian War (14-10 BC). Subdivided into Dalmatia (a new name for Illyria) and Pannonia, which were officially called Upper and Lower Illyricum respectively in 9 BC, towards the end of the Batonian War - initially a senatorial province; it became an imperial propraetorial province in 11 BC, during the Pannonian war. It was dissolved and the new provinces of Dalmatia and Pannonia were created during the reign of Vespasian (79-79). In 107 Pannonia was divided into Pannonia Superior and Pannonia Inferior - imperial provinces (proconsular and propraetorial respectively).

entries.label: Germania Magna
entries.note: 12 BC – Germania Magna, lost after three Roman legions were routed in 9 AD.

entries.label: Judaea
entries.note: 6 AD – Judaea, imperial procuratorial province (renamed Syria Palaestina by Hadrian, and upgraded to proconsular province).

entries.label: Britannia
entries.note: 43 AD – Britannia. Claudius initiated the invasion of Britannia. Up to 60 AD the Romans controlled the area south a line from the River Humber to the Severn Estuary. Wales was finally subdued in 78. In 78–84 Agricola conquered the north of England and Scotland. Scotland was then abandoned (imperial proconsular province). In 197 Septimius Severus divided Britannia into Britannia Superior and Britannia Inferior. Imperial provinces (proconsular and propraetorial respectively).

entries.label: Noricum
entries.note: 41/53 AD – Noricum (central Austria, north-eastern Slovenia and part of Bavaria), it was incorporated into the Empire in 16 BC. It was called a province, but it remained a client kingdom under the control of an imperial procurator. It was turned into a proper province during the reign of Claudius (41–54) (imperial propraetorial province).

entries.label: Lycia et Pamphylia
entries.note: 74 AD – Lycia et Pamphylia, in 43 AD the emperor Claudius had annexed Lycia. Pamphylia had been a part of the province of Galatia. Vespasian (reigned AD 69 - 79) merged Lycia and Pamphylia.

entries.label: Pannonia Superior and Pannonia Inferior
entries.note: 107 – Pannonia divided into Pannonia Superior and Pannonia Inferior, imperial provinces (proconsular and propraetorial respectively)

entries.label: Britannia Superior and Britannia Inferior
entries.note: 197 (formalized c. 212) – Britannia divided into Britannia Superior and Britannia Inferior, imperial provinces (proconsular and propraetorial respectively)

entries.label: Gallia Lugdunensis

completed: 19 BC
entries.note: Legend holds that in 19 BC thirsty Roman soldiers were guided by a young girl to a source of pure water thirteen kilometers from the city of Rome. (This scene is presented on the present fountain's façade.) The discovery of the source led Augustus to commission the construction of a 22km aqueduct leading into the city, which was named Aqua Virgo, or Virgin Waters, in honor of the legendary young girl. The aqueduct served the hot Baths of Agrippa, and Rome, for over four hundred years. The fountain at the junction of three roads (tre vie) marks the terminal point of the "modern" Acqua Vergine, the revived Aqua Virgo.

Imperial Library of Constantinople
entries.note: The Imperial Library of Constantinople, in the capital city of the Byzantine Empire, was the last of the great libraries of the ancient world. Long after the destruction of the Great Library of Alexandria and the other ancient libraries, it preserved the knowledge of the ancient Greeks and Romans for almost 1,000 years. A series of unintentional fires over the years and wartime damage, including the raids of the Fourth Crusade in 1204, impacted the building itself and its contents. The library continued in substantial form until the city of Constantinople was conquered by the Ottoman Empire in 1453 when the library's considerable surviving contents were destroyed or lost. The library was founded by Constantius II (reigned 337-361 AD) who established a Scriptorium so that the surviving works of Greek literature could be copied and so preserved. The Emperor Valens in 372 employed four Greek and three Latin calligraphers. The majority of Greek classics known today are known through Byzantine copies originating from the Imperial Library of Constantinople.

entries.label: Temple of Hercules Victor
entries.note: The Temple of Hercules Victor or Hercules Olivarius (Hercules as protector of the olive trade), is a circular peristyle building dating from the 2nd century BC. It consists of a colonnade of Corinthian columns arranged in a concentric ring around the cylindrical cella, resting on a tuff foundation. These elements originally supported an architrave and roof which have disappeared. It is the earliest surviving marble building in Rome.

entries.label: Khosrau I
entries.note: Khosrau I (b. 501, Persia; d. 579; r. 531–579) (Also called Chosroes I and Kasra in classical sources, most commonly known in Persian as Anooshiravan or Anushirvan or Anushirwan, meaning the undiminishing soul), also known as Anushirawan the Just. Khosrau I was the twenty-second Sasanian Emperor (Persian: Shahanshah, Great King) of Persia, and the most famous and celebrated of the Sasanian kings. He laid the foundations of many cities and opulent palaces, and oversaw the repair of trade roads as well as the building of numerous bridges and dams. During Khosrau I's ambitious reign, art and science flourished in Persia and the Sassanid Empire reached its peak of glory and prosperity. Khosrau is one of the most popular emperors in Iranian culture and literature and, outside of Iran, his name became, like that of Caesar in the history of Rome, a designation of the Sasanian kings. He introduced a rational system of taxation, based upon a survey of landed possessions, which his father had begun, and tried in every way to increase the welfare and the revenues of his empire. His army was in discipline decidedly superior to the Byzantines, and apparently was well paid. He was also interested in literature and philosophical discussions. Under his reign chess was introduced from India, and the famous book of Kalilah and Dimnah was translated. He thus became renowned as a wise king. | AD531 - Becomes Shahanshah, (Great King) of Persia.

Late Bronze Age collapse
entries.note: The half century between c. 1200 and 1150 BC saw the cultural collapse of the Mycenaean kingdoms, the Kassites in Babylonia, the Hittite Empire in Anatolia and the Levant, and the New Kingdom of Egypt, as well as the destruction of Ugarit and the Amorite states in the Levant, the fragmentation of the Luwian states of western Anatolia, and a period of chaos in Canaan. The deterioration of these governments interrupted trade routes and led to severely reduced literacy in much of this area. Only a few powerful states survived the Bronze Age collapse, particularly Assyria (albeit temporarily weakened), the New Kingdom of Egypt (also weakened), the Phoenician city-states and Elam.

The first league was formed in the 5th century BC. The second Achaean League existed between 280 BC and 146 BC. The league was named after the region of Achaea.

entries.label: Delian League
entries.note: The Delian League, founded in 478 BC, was an association of Greek city-states, members numbering between 150 to 173, under the leadership of Athens, whose purpose was to continue fighting the Persian Empire after the Greek victory in the Battle of Plataea at the end of the Second Persian invasion of Greece. The League's modern name derives from its official meeting place, the island of Delos, where congresses were held in the temple and where the treasury stood until, in a symbolic gesture, Pericles moved it to Athens in 454 BC. Shortly after its inception, Athens began to use the League's navy for its own purposes. This behavior frequently led to conflict between Athens and the less powerful members of the League. By 431 BC, Athens' heavy-handed control of the Delian League prompted the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War; the League was dissolved upon the war's conclusion in 404 BC under the direction of Lysander, the Spartan commander. | 461 BC: Triumph of radical democracy at Athens under Pericles; Pericles transforms Delian League into Athenian Empire.

entries.label: Aegean civilizations
entries.note: Aegean civilization is a general term for the Bronze Age civilizations of Greece around the Aegean Sea. There are three distinct but communicating and interacting geographic regions covered by this term: Crete, the Cyclades and the Greek mainland. Crete is associated with the Minoan civilization from the Early Bronze Age. The Cyclades converge with the mainland during the Early Helladic ("Minyan") period and with Crete in the Middle Minoan period. From ca. 1450 BC (Late Helladic, Late Minoan), the Greek Mycenaean civilization spreads to Crete.

entries.note: Troy was an ancient city located in modern-day Turkey. The entries on Troy have been included in this section on Greece due to the pivotal role it plays in the history and mythology of the Greeks, primarily through the great epic poetry of Homer, principally The Iliad.

Plague in Athens
entries.note: 430 BC - An outbreak of a plague hits Athens and the disease ravages the densely packed city. The plague wipes out over 30,000 citizens, sailors and soldiers as well as Pericles' two sons. Roughly one quarter of the Athenian population dies. The fear of plague is so widespread that the Spartan invasion of Attica is abandoned, their troops being unwilling to risk contact with the diseased enemy.

Hellenic League
entries.note: The League of Corinth, also referred to sometimes as the Hellenic League (from Greek Ἑλληνικός Hellenikos, "pertaining to Greece and Greeks"), was a federation of Greek states created by Philip II of Macedon during the winter of 338 BC/337 BC after the Battle of Chaeronea, to facilitate his use of military forces in his war against Persia. The name 'League of Corinth' was invented by modern historians due to the first council of the League being in Corinth. It was the first time in history that most of the Greek states (with the notable exception of Sparta) managed to become part of a single political entity. | Seleucus I Nicator Satrap 320–315, 312-305 BCE; King 305–281 BCE

entries.note: Pericles "surrounded by glory" (c. 495 – 429 BC) Arguably the most prominent and influential Greek statesman, orator and general of Athens during the Golden Age— specifically the time between the Persian and Peloponnesian wars.

Draco (fl. 7th century BC)
entries.note: Draco (Greek: Δράκων, Drakōn; fl. c. 7th century BC) The first recorded legislator of Athens in Ancient Greece. He replaced the prevailing system of oral law and blood feud by a written code to be enforced only by a court. Draco's written law became known for its harshness, with the adjective "draconian" referring to similarly unforgiving rules or laws.

The Great Temple of Apollo (Sicily: Selinunte)
entries.note: The Great Temple of Apollo, (Temple "G") (Sicily: Selinunte) c. 520 BC - 450 BC Doric peripteral octastyle temple with 18 columns at the sides, in the eastern group at Selinunte, with Temples "E" and "F". It is the largest temple at this site and was never completed. It is now in a state of total ruin. An ambitious building of distinctive plan, having a stylobate rising in two levels and aisles of sufficient width to suggest that either a second row of columns was intended, or that the builders of Sicily, unlike their mainland Greek counterparts, used the trussed roof. The colonnaded inner porch has side, as well as front columns, so that the temple might be termed "pseudo-dipteral". There was a double row of columns within the cella, rising in two stages, of very much more delicate proportions than the exterior colonnade. Dimensions:50.10 m × 110.36 m

entries.label: Temple of Apollo (Delos)
entries.note: The Delian Temple of Apollo (Delos) 470 BC - c. 300 BC Doric peripteral hexastyle building with 13 columns on the sides. . With other temple buildings inside the sanctuary at Delos. Its completion was delayed. The whole site is in a ruinous state and little of the temple remains except the outer part of the crepidoma. Dimensions:approx. 13 m × 30 m

entries.label: Alcibiades expelled from Sparta
entries.note: 412 BC - Alcibiades is expelled from Sparta, conspires to come back to Athens.

entries.label: Selinunte Temple “C” (Sicily: Selinunte)
entries.note: Selinunte Temple “C” (Sicily: Selinunte) c. 550 BC One of a group of Doric temples on the Acropolis or "western group" at Selinunte. (distant view) It has similarities to the Temple of Apollo at Syracuse. It is a peripteral hexastyle temple with 17 columns at the sides and an additional row of columns at the eastern end. Like other temples at this location it had a second room, only accessible from the naos, which was narrow and had no internal columns. The aisles are correspondingly wider. Metopes from this temple showing Archaic sculpture of the Labours of Hercules are in the National Museum,Palermo. Dimensions:23.93 m × 63.76 m

entries.label: Temple of Hera (Sicily: Selinunte)
entries.note: The Temple of Hera, (Temple "E") (Sicily: Selinunte) 5th century BC The best preserved Doric temple at Selinunte, it is in the eastern group with Temple "F" and Temple "G". It is a peripteral hexastyle temple with 15 columns at each side, wide aisles and a broad flight of steps to the stylobate. . It has a long narrow naos and inner chamber like other temples at Selinunte but has inner porches at both ends in the Greek manner. Dimensions:25.32 m × 67.74 m

entries.label: Temple of Apollo Epicurius (Bassae)
entries.note: The Temple of Apollo Epicurius (Bassae) c. 450 BC - 425 BC The architect, Ictinus, introduced the use of all three orders within a single building and orientated the building north south instead of east west. While the ends appear a regular hexastyle temple, it is very long for its width, about 2.3:1 The interior had many unusual features including Ionic capitals of unique design, a central Corinthian column and an asymmetrically placed statue of Apollo, lit by a side door facing the morning sun. Dimensions:14.6 m × 38.3 m

entries.label: Alcibiades reenters Athens in triumph
entries.note: 408 BC - Alcibiades reenters Athens in triumph, Lysander, a Spartan commander, has fleet built at Ephesus.

entries.label: Civil war in Elis and Megara
Temple of Hera (Olympia)
entries.note: Temple of Hera (Olympia) c. 590 BC Doric peripteral hexastyle building with 16 columns at each side, being long for its breadth in the Archaic style of this date. The building was originally of wood and clay brick construction on a stone base, with the wooden external columns and internal hypostyle columns being replaced with stone piecemeal, so columns are greatly varied. Dimensions:18.75 m × 50.01 m

entries.label: Temple of Apollo (Corinth)
entries.note: The Temple of Apollo (Corinth) c. 540 BC Doric peripteral hexastyle temple with 15 columns at each side with two inner chambers on a crepidoma of 3 steps. It was like the Temple of Hera at Olympia, but built entirely of stone. The columns were monolithic with seven of the original 38 surviving. The broad capitals were carved as separate pieces and coated with marble stucco. Dimensions:21.36 m × 53.30 m

entries.label: Temple of Athena (Italy: Paestum)
entries.note: The Temple of Athena (Italy: Paestum) c. 510 BC Also called the Temple of Demeter, a Doric peripteral hexastyle building with thirteen columns at the side, having proportions that were to be established as the Doric ideal in such buildings as the Temple of Poseidon at Sunion. The columns have pronounced entasis and the capitals are large and wide. This temple had a number of Ionic features, including the columns of its inner porch and the moulding that ran between the architrave and typically Doric frieze of triglyphs and metopes. Dimensions:14.54m 32.88m

entries.label: Temple of Zeus (Olympia)
entries.note: The Temple of Zeus (Olympia) c. 460 BC Doric, architect: Libon of Elis. A refined peripteral hexastyle temple with 13 columns along each side, in the Classical manner. It had pedimental sculpture of "outstanding magnificence". The local limestone was covered with stucco, while the sculpture, tiles and gutters were marble with bronze acroteria. From 448 BC it housed a colossal chryselephantine statue of Zeus 12 metres (40 feet) high by Pheidias. Dimensions:27.43 m × 64 m

entries.label: Phidias, completes statue of Zeus at Elis, One of 7 wonders of the world
Philip V
entries.note: The Temple of the Olympian Zeus (Athens) 174 BC - AD 132 A huge Corinthian temple, architect: Cossutius. Built as a gift to Athens by Antiochus Epiphanes and constructed in 3 stages. It was dipteral octastyle and was long for its width in the style off the much earlier Archaic period. It had 20 columns on each side and a triple row at the porticos, 104 columns, (diameter: 1.9 metres diameter, height: 17 metres high)(6 ft 4 ins; 56 ft). Some of the columns were shipped to Rome before the temple was complete and used for the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus where they had a profound effect on Roman architecture. It was completed and dedicated by Hadrian, more than 300 years after it began. Only 15 columns remain. Dimensions:44.35 m × 110.5 m

entries.label: Formal pederasty is introduced, first in Crete
Temple of Artemis (Corfu)
entries.note: Temple of Artemis (Corfu) c. 580 BC Doric peripteral pseudodipteral temple, which may be the earliest known to incorporate all the major elements of the Doric order. It is the earliest known Doric temple to have been built entirely in stone. Dimensions:23.46 m × 49.00 m

entries.label: Temple of Hera (Samos)
entries.note: The Temple of Hera (Samos) c. 540 BC Ionic temple, architects: Rhoikos and Theodoros of Samos, of dipteral plan, having two rows of 8 columns at the eastern end and two rows of 9 at the western and 24 columns at each side.. It was built on the site of the earliest very large Ionic temple, destroyed by fire. It was of similar plan, and retained the bases of the earlier temple's columns within its foundations. Dimensions:52.45 m × 108.6 m

entries.label: Temple of Apollo (Delphi)
entries.note: The Temple of Apollo (Delphi) c. 510 BC Doric temple on the side of Mount Parnassus, had its legendary origins with the mythical hero architects Trophonius and Agamedes. This, the third temple on the site (330 BC), is by Spintharus, Xenodoros and Agathon. with sculpture by Praias and Androsthenes, retained a hexastyleform with 15 columns at the sides from an earlier building, and was constructed of porous limestone. Little of the temple remains beyond its foundations. Dimensions:23.82 m × 60.32 m

entries.label: Temple on the Ilissus (Athens)
entries.note: The Temple on the Ilissus (Athens) 449 BC A small Ionic temple, architect: Callicrates, beside the Ilissus River which ran through Athens. It was amphi-prostyle tetrastyle. It differed from the small temples and treasuries by builders from Asia Minor in having a frieze around the entablature. Dimensions: approx. 6 m × 12.8 m

entries.label: Hermai statues are mutilated in Athens

entries.note: The Temple of Dionysus (Turkey: Teos) 193 BC Ionic temple, architect: Hermogenes of Priene, was peripteral hexastyle with 11 columns at the sides. The columns were set on plinths and there was a frieze of Dyonisiac scenes. Dimensions:18.5 m × 35 m
