Peace broken, King Decebalus loses Second Dacian War, the south-west part of Dacia becomes a Roman province
Galerius affirms his Dacian (Thracian) identity
entries.note: 313 - According to Lactantius' literary chronicle De mortibus Persecutorum, Galerius affirms his Dacian (Thracian) identity by avowing himself the enemy of the Roman name once made emperor, even proposing that the empire should be called the "Dacian Empire". He exhibited anti-Roman attitude as soon as he had attained the highest power, treating the Roman citizens with ruthless cruelty, like the conquerors treated the conquered, all in the name of the same treatment that the victorious Trajan had applied to the conquered Dacians, forefathers of Galerius, two centuries before.

entries.label: Menumorut dies and is succeeded by his son-in-law, Zoltán of Hungary
Benjamin of Tudela of the Kingdom of Navarre is one of the first writers to use the word Vlachs for a Romance-speaking population
The Unio Trium Nationum pact is signed as a reaction to the Transylvanian peasant revolt at Bobâlna
An Acts of the Apostles book is printed in Romanian, though written with the Cyrillic alphabet
George II Rákóczi invades Poland only to be defeated
The Habsburg Empire invades Wallachia during the Austro-Turkish War
Transylvanian petition
entries.note: 1791 - Romanian-speaking Transylvanians petition to Emperor Leopold II for recognition as the fourth nation of Transylvania and for religious equality. Their demands are rejected and their old marginalised status is reinforced.

entries.label: Treaty of Adrianople
entries.note: 1829 - Following the Treaty of Adrianople, without overturning Ottoman suzerainty, places Wallachia and Moldavia under Russian empire military rule until Turkey pays an indemnity. Wallachia gains the rayas of Turnu, Giurgiu and Brăila, Russia annexes the Danube estuary.

entries.label: At the end of the Balkan Wars, Romania acquires the southern part of the Dobruja from Bulgaria
Dacian-born Maximinus II (Galerius' nephew) becomes Roman Emperor
800 Cremation cemeteries of the "Nușfalău-Someșeni group" were discovered in northwestern Transylvania, with their 8th- and 9th-century tumuli.
The "Western part" of Troesmis is supposed to have been rebuilt and used again during the reign of the Eastern Roman Emperor John I Tzimiskes based on archaeological discoveries
A papal legate delivers a royal crown to Kaloyan of Bulgaria and crowned him "King of the Bulgarians and Vlachs"
The Battle of Breadfield
entries.note: 1479 - The Battle of Breadfield The most tremendous conflict fought in Transylvania up to that time in the Ottoman–Hungarian Wars, taking place during the reign of King Matthias Corvinus. The Hungarian army defeated a highly outnumbered Ottoman army and the Ottoman casualties were extremely high. The battle was the most significant victory for the Hungarians against the Ottomans, and as a result, the Ottomans did not attack southern Hungary and Transylvania for many years thereafter.

entries.label: Neacșu's letter is one of the oldest surviving documents written in the Romanian language
Prince Kemény proclaims the secession of Transylvania from the Ottomans
entries.note: 1661 Prince Kemény proclaims the secession of Transylvania from the Ottomans and appeals to help from the Habsburg monarchy. He was not aware of the secret agreement between the Habsburg Empire and Ottomans and the move will end his reign. Transylvania becomes a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire.

entries.label: The Revolt of Horea, Cloșca and Crișan
The first Legislative Assembly in Wallachia is established
Transylvanian Memorandum
entries.note: 1892 - The Transylvanian Memorandum is signed by the leaders of the Romanians to the Austro-Hungarian Emperor Franz Joseph, asking for equal ethnic rights with the Hungarians, and demanding an end to persecutions and Magyarization attempts. The memorandum was forwarded to the Hungarian Parliament and the results was that the Romanian leaders are sentenced to long terms in prison.

entries.label: A new constitution is ratified
entries.note: 1948 A new constitution is ratified on April 13. Two months later, on June 11 all banks and major enterprises are nationalized. During the year, also in the years to come, many pre-war politicians, businessmen, priests and even ordinary people are thrown in prisons. On August 30, following the model of Soviet NKVD, the Romanian secret police is formed. In 1949, forced collectivization begins, in which the agriculture is organized under the socialist model, comes into force. Romania joins Comecon. The construction of Danube-Black Sea Canal starts. The canal was the most known labour camp in the history of Romania;

entries.label: Bucharest urban planning program
entries.note: 1983 - As part of the urban planning programme, significant portions of the historic centre of Bucharest are demolished in order to accommodate standardized apartment blocks and government buildings, including the grandiose Centrul Civic and the palatial House of the People, the second largest government building in the world.

entries.label: Written on bronze tablets, the Roman laws of Troesmis attest the joint rule of Roman emperors Marcus Aurelius and Commodus
Licinius I, born to peasant family which had fled from Dacia Traiana, becomes Eastern Roman Emperor
Țara Făgărașului is mentioned in documents as Terra Blacorum
Basarab I wins the Battle of Posada against Charles I Robert of Hungary
Tranquillo Andronico remarks that Vlachs now name themselves Romanians
Battle of Vienna
entries.note: 1683 - Battle of Vienna The defeat of Ottoman armies in Battle of Vienna means the end of Ottoman rule over Transylvania. The Roman Catholic Church becomes official church in Transylvania in a move directed by the Habsburgs to weaken the noblemen estates, which were both Roman Catholic and Protestant.

entries.label: The first library in Transylvania is inaugurated
The Romanian Orthodox Church gains autocephaly
entries.note: 1885 Patriarch Joachim IV signs the recognition of the autocephalous status of the Romanian Orthodox Church that granted it equal rights with those of the other orthodox churches.

entries.label: Mass deportations
entries.note: 1951 - During the night of June 18 the third-largest mass deportation in modern Romanian history takes place. Some 45,000 people are taken from their homes and deported to the Bărăgan plain.

entries.label: Nicolae Ceaușescu and his wife are executed
entries.note: 1989 On December 16, protests break out in Timișoara. Five days later Nicolae Ceaușescu organises a mass meeting in Bucharest. The jeers and whistles soon erupt into a riot, as the crowd takes to the streets, placing the capital in turmoil. Nicolae Ceaușescu and his wife leave Bucharest putting an end to four decades of Communist rule in Romania. On December 25, after a short trial, Nicolae Ceaușescu and his wife are executed.

entries.label: Roman emperor Constantine I the Great is awarded the title Carpicus Maximus after winning a battle against the Carps
Abodrites send envoys to Emperor Louis the Pious in complaining "about vicious aggression by the Bulgars"
entries.note: 824 - The Fourth Section of the Royal Frankish Annals mentions the Abodrites who lived in "Dacia on the Danube as neighbors of the Bulgars". They sent envoys to Emperor Louis the Pious in 824, complaining "about vicious aggression by the Bulgars" and seeking the emperor's assistance against them, according to the Royal Frankish Annals. The Abodrites inhabited the lands along either the Timiș or the Tisza rivers.

entries.label: Andrew II of Hungary grants provisional autonomy to colonial Germans residing in the present-day area of Sibiu
The Diet of Torda in Transylvania declares freedom of religion
The Habsburgs consolidate control over Transylvania
Romanian independence is recognised by the Central Powers
First evidence of Diet in Transylvania
Andrew Lackfi, Count of the Székelys defeat on a large Tatar army ending the devastations of the Mongols in Transylvania
The Orăștie Palia is the oldest translation of the Pentateuch written in the Romanian language
Bucharest becomes capital of Wallachia (former capital was Târgoviște)
Caragea's plague claims 60,000 deaths in Wallachia
The Stock Exchange opens in Bucharest
According to legend and the 17th century Cantacuzino Annals, Radu Negru founds Wallachia
Wallachian prince Michael the Brave briefly imposes his rule over the Principality of Transylvania and Moldavia
Ion Caragea adopts the first modern code of law in Wallachia
The first telephone in Romania is installed
The Soviet Union Army leave Romania after fourteen years of occupation
Gabriel Bethlen becomes Prince of Transylvania
entries.note: 1613 Gabriel Bethlen becomes Prince of Transylvania succeeding to Gabriel Báthory. Under Bethlen's rule, the principality experiences a golden age. He promoted agriculture, trade, and industry, sank new mines, sent students abroad to Protestant universities, and prohibited landlords from denying an education to children of serfs.

entries.label: Union of Transylvania's Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic Churches
entries.note: 1699 - The Emperor Leopold I decrees Transylvania's Eastern Orthodox Church to be one with the Roman Catholic Church, by joining the newly created Romanian Greek-Catholic Church.

entries.label: The Principality of Transylvania is decreed to be independent of Hungary
entries.note: 1849 - After the failure of the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, the March Constitution of Austria decreed that the Principality of Transylvania be a separate crown land entirely independent of Hungary.

entries.label: Nicolae Ceaușescu is elected General Secretary of the Romanian Communist Party and becomes the state leader
Peace of Nikolsburg ends the war between Transylvania and Habsburgs
The first railway line in Romania opens
King Carol I Bridge is inaugurated
Romania refuse to participate in the invasion of Czechoslovakia
The University of Iași is established
Construction of Port of Constanța begins
Richard Nixon's visits Romania - the first by a US president to a Communist country
Romania switches from Cyrillic script to the Latin script
Romania becomes a founding member of League of Nations
The Transylvanian Association for the Literature and Culture of the Romanians is founded
entries.note: 1861 - The Transylvanian Association for the Literature and Culture of the Romanians is founded in Sibiu, as the first cultural association of the Romanian-speaking Transylvanians.

entries.label: Alexandru Ioan Cuza promulgates the Agrarian Reform
entries.note: 1863 - Alexandru Ioan Cuza promulgates the Agrarian Reform in which the majority of the land is transferred into the property of those who worked it. As there was not enough land, the Secularization of monastery estates in Romania, in which large estates owned by the Romanian Orthodox Church are transferred under state ownership and then to private property, takes place. This was an important turning point in the history of Romania, as it marked the almost disappearance of the Boyar class, leaving the country to look towards capitalism and industrialization.

entries.label: Peace treties between Romania and Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia
The Parliament of Romania is formed
entries.note: 1864 - The Parliament of Romania is formed. A tuition-free, compulsory public education for primary schools is introduced in Romania for the first time. Also a Criminal Code and a Civil Code, both based on the Napoleonic Code, are introduced.

entries.label: Nadia Comăneci scores the first 10.0 in gymnastics at the Montreal Olympics
Romania becomes the first European country to abolish the death penalty
entries.note: 1865 - Romania becomes the first European country to abolish the death penalty. This, however, did not last, it is now abolished in Romania since 1990.

entries.label: Territorial losses
entries.note: 1940 On June 27, following an ultimatum issued by the Soviet Union, Romania loses Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina. On August 30, under the Second Vienna Award, Romania loses the northern part of Transylvania to Hungary. Only one week later the Kadrilater/Southern Dobruja is lost to Bulgaria.

entries.label: Ion Mihai Pacepa defects to the U.S. becoming the highest ranking defector from the Eastern Bloc
Alexandru Ioan Cuza is forced to abdicate by the "Monstrous coalition"
Romania joins Operation Barbarossa
entries.note: 1941 - Romania joins Operation Barbarossa, attacking the Soviet Union hoping to recover the lost territories of Bessarabia and Bukovina. Later, Romania annexes Soviet lands immediately east of the Dniester.

entries.label: The Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867
entries.note: 1867 After the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867, the separate status of Transylvania ceased, it was incorporated again into the Kingdom of Hungary (Transleithania) as part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

entries.label: Grand Duchy of Moscow (AD1282 to AD1547)
Ivan the Terrible
entries.note: Ivan IV Vasilyevich (25 August 1530 – 28 March [O.S. 18 March] 1584) Commonly known as Ivan the Terrible. Grand Prince of Moscow from 1533 to 1547 and Tsar of All the Russias from 1547 until his death. His long reign saw the conquest of the Khanates of Kazan, Astrakhan, and Siberia, transforming Russia into a multiethnic and multiconfessional state spanning almost one billion acres, approximately 4,046,856 sq km. Ivan managed countless changes in the progression from a medieval state to an empire and emerging regional power, and became the first ruler to be crowned as Tsar of All the Russians.

entries.label: 8 Monarchs
entries.note: House of Godunov Irina (disputed) - 1598 to 1598 Boris I - 1598 to 1605 Feodor II - 1605 to 1605 Pseudo-Rurikovich usurpers False Dmitry I - 1605 to 1606 False Dmitry II - 1607 to 1610 False Dmitry III (Sidorka) - 1611 to 1612 House of Shuysky Vasiliy IV - 1606 to 1610 (deposed) House of Vasa Vladislav I - 1610 to 1612 (resigned his claim - 1634)

entries.label: Ivan V
entries.note: Sophia was regent from 1682 to 1689

entries.label: Russia sells Alaska to the United States for $7.2 million
Last known population of Wooly Mammoths surviving on Wrangle Island, Russia
entries.note: Woolly mammoths survived on Wrangle Island untill c. 2500–2000 BC, the most recent survival of all known mammoth populations. Mammoths generally died and disappeared from mainland Eurasia and North America around 10,000 years ago; however, about 500–1,000 mammoths isolated on Wrangel Island continued to survive for another 6,000 years.

entries.label: Peter the Great founds the city of Saint Petersburg
Saint Petersburg becomes the capital of the Russian Empire
Pale of Settlement
entries.note: Catherine the Great establishes the Pale of Settlement, an area in European Russia into which Russian Jews were transported. | 1917 - The Russian Revolution occurs. The Tsarist government is overthrown. The communist Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin take control in the October Revolution.

entries.label: Church Schism (Raskol) after the Reforms of Patriarch Nikon
entries.note: Nikon’s reforms split the Russian Orthodox Church and create the Old Believers.

entries.label: Abolition of the Patriarchate and Creation of the Holy Synod
Partitions of Poland
entries.note: Russia gains large territories through the dismemberment of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

entries.label: Treaty of Pereyaslav
entries.note: An alliance between the Tsardom of Russia and the Cossacks of Ukraine, leading to war with Poland.

entries.label: Battle of Poltava
entries.note: Decisive Russian victory over Sweden in the Great Northern War, marking Russia’s rise as a European power.

entries.label: Karelo-Finnish SSR
entries.note: The Karelo-Finnish SSR was also succeeded by the Karelian ASSR.

entries.label: Partially recognised or de facto state
Post-Soviet States
entries.note: The post-Soviet states, also referred to as the former Soviet Union (FSU) or the former Soviet republics, are the independent sovereign states that emerged/re-emerged out of the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. Prior to their independence, they existed as Union Republics — top-level constituents of the Soviet Union.

entries.label: Andronovo culture ( c. 2000 BC – 1150 BC)
entries.note: The Andronovo culture is a collection of similar local Late Bronze Age cultures that flourished c. 2000–1150 BC, spanning from the southern Urals to the upper Yenisei River in central Siberia.

entries.label: Yermak Timofeyevich defeats the Khanate of Sibir
Greek Crimea (establishment of Greek colonies on the Crimea)
Crown of the Kingdom of Poland
Pantikapaion (ealiest Greek colony on the Crimea) is founded (c.late 6th / early 5th century BC)
Government of the Ukrainian People's Republic in exile
Taurica (1st millenium BC)
entries.note: The Tauri or Taurians, also Scythotauri, Tauri Scythae, Tauroscythae were an ancient people settled on the southern coast of the Crimea peninsula, inhabiting the Crimean Mountains in the 1st millennium BC and the narrow strip of land between the mountains and the Black Sea.

entries.label: Zarubintsy culture (3rd century BC - 1st century AD)
Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria (under Hapsburg rule)
Corded Ware culture (c. 3000 BC – c. 2350 BC)
La Tène culture c. 450 BC - 1st century BC
Margraviate of Austria - Established as a frontier march of the Holy Roman Empire
The Privilegium Maius are forged
entries.note: 1359 - Rudolf the Founder ordered the creation of the Privilegium Maius, a set of forged documents, some purportedly issued by Julius Caesar, which raised Austria to an archduchy and granted it additional rights including the privilegium de non evocando, the right to issue judgments which could not be appealed to the Holy Roman Emperor.

entries.label: Archduchy of Austria 1453 AD - 1804 AD Elevated to an archduchy, becoming a significant power in Central Europe.
Mesolithic c. 8,000 BC - c. 5,000 BC - Transition between hunter-gatherer and agricultural societies.
La Tène A (La Tène I) 450–380 BC
La Tène B (La Tène I) 380–250 BC
La Tène C (La Tène II) 250–150 BC
La Tène D (La Tène III) 150–1 BC
Migration Period c. 300 AD - c. 800 AD Period of significant migrations and settlements by various tribes
March of Pannonia - Frontier region established by Charlemagne
Vienna was raised to a free imperial city
Forced conversion of the Jews in Austria
entries.note: 1420 - Albert the Magnanimous ordered the imprisonment and forcible conversion of the Jews in Austria.

entries.label: German Confederation
entries.note: 1850 - Prussia and Austria signed the Punctuation of Olmütz, under which the former agreed to the dissolution of the Prussian-led Erfurt Union and the revival of the German Confederation under Austrian leadership.

entries.label: Bell Beaker culture (c. 2800 – 2300 (to c. 1900 BC in Britain))
Roman Provinces of Noricum, Pannonia and Raetia
Battle of Mohi: Austrian forces defeated a small Golden Horde raiding party
Federal State of Austria - authoritarian regime preceding annexation by Nazi Germany
Celtic Kingdom of Noricum (c. 200 BC - 50 AD) A Celtic kingdom that became a Roman client state
Battle of the Leitha River
entries.note: 1246 - Battle of the Leitha River: The Kingdom of Hungary defeated an Austrian invasion near the banks of the Leitha. Frederick the Quarrelsome was killed.

entries.label: The citizens of Freiburg im Breisgau purchased their independence from the count of Freiburg and submitted to Habsburg protection. The city was added to Further Austria
Austrian Emperor Leopold I expels 4,000 Jews from Vienna
Francis takes the title Emperor of Austria
Treaty of St Germain defines Austria's boundaries
The term Ostarrîchi was first used, possibly in reference to a small fief within the Eastern March
Vienna was granted the staple right, the right to require merchants passing through to offer their goods for sale
Treaty of Neuberg
entries.note: 1379 - Albert with the Braid and Leopold the Just signed the Treaty of Neuberg at Neuberg Abbey, dividing their father's possessions. Albert and his descendants were to rule Austria, Leopold and his descendants Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, Tyrol, Further Austria and Friuli.

entries.label: Sigismund, Archduke of Austria annexes the County of Bregenz and takes the title count of Bregenz
Austrian explorers Julius von Payer and Karl Weyprecht discover the archipelago of Franz Joseph Land in the Arctic Sea
Henry II, Holy Roman Emperor, then duke of Bavaria and King of the Romans, added the land between the Kamp and Morava rivers and some territory southwest of Vienna to the territory of Austria
Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, invited Bohemia to invade and conquer Austria as punishment for the aggression and impertinence of Frederick the Quarrelsome
Albert VI supported an urban revolt in Frederick III's capital Vienna, enabling him to take possession of what is now Lower Austria
Turkey and Austria sign the Treaty of Zsitva-Torok
Turkey and Austria sign peace treaty - Austria cedes Belgrade to Turk
Foundation of the Phonogrammarchiv of the Austrian Academy of Science
entries.note: 1899 - Foundation of the Phonogrammarchiv of the Austrian Academy of Science, the world's first research sound archive (added to UNESCO's Memory of the World 1999).

entries.label: Investiture Controversy: Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor, king of Germany, invaded Austria in pursuit of the fugitive bishop Altmann of Passau
Frederick the Quarrelsome created two administrative divisions of Austria: Upper Austria, above the Enns, and Lower Austria below
The Imperial Free City of Trieste seceded from the Patriarchate of Aquileia and became part of Leopold the Just's domains in exchange for his protection
Sweden, Poland, Brandenburg, and Austria sign the Treaty of Oliva, one of the peace treaties ending the Second Northern War
Universal and direct suffrage (limited to males over 24) is introduced
Battle of Mailberg
entries.note: 1082 - Battle of Mailberg: A Bohemian army invading in support of the claim of Vratislaus II of Bohemia decisively defeated the Austrians at Mailberg.

entries.label: Wenceslaus I, king of Bohemia, invades Austria
Battle of Sempach
entries.note: 1386 - Battle of Sempach A Swiss force decisively defeated an invasion by Leopold the Just at Sempach. Leopold was killed, along with a number of his vassals.

entries.label: Siege of Vienna
entries.note: 1529 - Siege of Vienna Some hundred thousand Ottoman soldiers led by the sultan Suleiman the Magnificent laid siege to the Austrian capital Vienna. Following the failure of a massive assault on the city and several weeks of bad weather, Ottoman forces eventually withdraw from Vienna.

entries.label: Mentally ill Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II signs the Treaty of Lieben, giving up Austria, Hungary and Moravia
Barrier Treaty: Austria cedes area to Netherlands
Battle of Kressenbrunn
entries.note: 1260 - Battle of Kressenbrunn Austrian and Bohemian forces repulsed a Hungarian attack over the Morava near modern Engelhartstetten. Many Hungarian soldiers drowned in the river.

entries.label: Battle of Näfels: Swiss forces decisively defeated an Austrian invasion of Glarus
Austria and the Ottoman Empire signed the Treaty of Constantinople
entries.note: 1533 - Austria and the Ottoman Empire signed the Treaty of Constantinople, ending their conflict. Ferdinand recognized John Zápolya as king of Hungary in exchange for Ottoman recognition of his conquests in the west of the kingdom, signaling its de facto division into the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom, a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire, and Royal Hungary.

entries.label: Austria joins Triple Alliance
entries.note: 1718 - Austria joins Triple Alliance of Britain, France and the Dutch Republic forming the Quadruple Alliance, to fight against Spain.

entries.label: Franz Ferdinand, Archduke of Austria and his wife Sophie are assassinated by Bosnian-Serb assassin Gavrilo Princip in Sarajevo
The Hungarian king Matthias Corvinus takes the title duke of Austria
Battle of Trencsén: Austria defeats Hungarian rebellion army
Peace of Pressburg
entries.note: 1491 - Maximilian and Vladislaus II of Hungary, the king of Hungary, signed the Peace of Pressburg in what is now Bratislava. Vladislaus renounced Hungary's conquests in Austria and promised the throne to Maximilian in the event of his death without heirs. In return, Maximilian recognized Vladislaus's rule in Hungary.

entries.label: Austria and the Ottoman Empire sign the Peace of Vásvár
The first military academy in the world, the Theresian Military Academy, is founded in Austria
Switzerland replaces Austria as the representative of Liechtenstein's interests abroad
Liechtenstein celebrates "200 years of sovereignty" since the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806
Liechtenstein becomes a member of the German Confederation
Liechtenstein adopts the Swiss franc as its currency
Women gain the right to vote in national elections - the last country in Europe to do so
Lordship of Schellenberg and County of Vaduz acquired by Austria
Liechtenstein acquires its present name and becomes an independent principality of the Holy Roman Empire
Liechtenstein enters a customs union with Switzerland
The Lordship of Schellenberg becomes a de facto dependency of the County of Vaduz
Hans-Adam I, Prince of Liechtenstein, purchases the Lordship and County for 115,000 guilders
World War I - Liechtenstein remains neutral
Liechtenstein joins the European Free Trade Association
World War II - Liechtenstein remains neutral
Officials establish that the country is bigger than previously thought after re-measuring its borders
The Holy Roman Empire grants Monaco to the Genoese in return for cracking down on pirates
A member of the exiled Grimaldi family from Genoa - Francois - seizes the fortress of the incumbent Genoese rulers of Monaco
The King of France, Charles VIII and the Duke of Savoy recognize the sovereignty of Monaco
End of construction of Fontvieille (2.94 acres taken from the sea)
Monaco annexes the towns of Menton and Roquebrune, increasing its territory by almost ten times
The Grimaldi family allies itself with Spain and Monaco comes under Spanish protection
French Revolution - the Grimaldis are deposed and unification with France follows
The Principality of Monaco becomes a constitutional monarchy
Celebration of the 700th Anniversary of the Grimaldi Reign
Monaco is refounded as a colony of Genoa
The Grimaldis lose control of Monaco
The Grimaldi family purchase Monaco from the Crown of Aragon and become the official and undisputed rulers of "the Rock of Monaco"
Honoré II begins to style himself "Prince" of Monaco
All forms of direct taxation are abolished
Princess Grace dies following a car accident near Monte-Carlo
Charles I reconquers the Rock - many consider him to be the true founder of the Principality
After a siege of more than 100 days, the Genoese are repelled by the garrison of Lucien I
Treaty of Péronne
entries.note: 1641 After 10 years of negotiation and thanks to the influence of Richelieu, Honoré II and Louis XIII sign the Treaty of Péronne which recognizes the sovereign right of Monaco and grants the Prince and his descendants an equality of rank with the highest French nobles. The French Kingdom thus ensures a protective friendship with the Principality of Monaco.

entries.label: Monaco is returned to the Grimaldis
The First Monaco stamp is issued
Creation of the Museum of Prehistoric Anthropology
Prince Rainier marries Hollywood actress Grace Kelly
Louis XII, King of France, recognizes the independence of Monaco
The Spanish garrison is evicted from Monaco and they are replaced by a French garrison
Monaco's independence is restored under the Franco-Monegasque treaty
Prince Rainier suspends Monaco's National Council
Monaco loses the towns of Menton and Roquebrune to France
The Spélugues Plateau is named Monte-Carlo in honor of Prince Charles III
Adoption of the colors Red and White for the Flag of Monaco
c. 5,500 BC - Agriculture in Switzerland begins
Celtic tribes settle in the area of modern-day Switzerland - c. 1,500 BC
The Frankish Empire conquers the Burgundian kingdom, integrating it into their realm
c. 3,800 BC - Bronze Age pile dwellings begin to be constructed
Federal Charter of 1291
entries.note: Federal Charter of 1291 The three Waldstätte of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden signed the Federal Charter of 1291 establishing the Old Swiss Confederacy, a confederation for mutual defense and the adjudication of disputes.

entries.label: Revision of the constitution
entries.note: 1874 - The constitution was revised to establish free public education and the optional referendum, and to make it easier for Swiss citizens to move between cantons.

entries.label: Switzerland joins the Council of Europe
The Alemanni capture the Agri Decumates, a Roman frontier region, and expand into present-day Alsace and northern Switzerland
The Treaty of Verdun assigns Upper Burgundy (western Switzerland) to Lotharingia
The Rütlischwur oath
entries.note: 1307 - The leaders of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden swear the Rütlischwur, an oath of unity and common defense, on the Rütli above Lake Lucerne.

entries.label: Battle of Sempach
entries.note: 1386 - Battle of Sempach. Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zürich decisively defeat a Habsburg army. The victory begins to change the Confederation from a loose pact into a unified entity and allows expansion into former Habsburg lands.

entries.label: Free State of the Three Leagues
Women gain the right to vote in federal elections
The Alemanni are conquered by the Frankish leader Clovis I and incorporated into the Frankish realm
Battle of Morgarten - Swiss infantry ambush and destroy much of a Habsburg heavy cavalry army near Lake Ägeri
The first Schweizerisches Gesangsfest, a singing festival, is held in Zürich
Switzerland is a founding member of the League of Nations
Lucerne signs a mutual protection treaty with the three Confederates
A referendum approves the secession of the French-speaking canton of Jura from the mostly German-speaking canton of Bern
Creation of the League of God's House in the Canton of Graubünden to resist the Bishopric of Chur and the Habsburgs
The Peace of Westphalia ends the Thirty Years War - European powers recognise the Swiss Confederation as an independent state
Banks offer numbered bank accounts, giving account holder anonymity
The Grey League is created
entries.note: 1395 - Creation of the Grey League in Graubünden as the abbot of Disentis Abbey, the Baron of Rhäzüns and the Baron of Sax-Misox sign an eternal alliance.

entries.label: Early modern (Ancien Régime)
entries.note: The long nineteenth century is a term for the 125-year period beginning with the onset of the French Revolution in 1789, and ending with the outbreak of World War I in 1914. It was coined by Soviet writer Ilya Ehrenburg and later popularized by British historian Eric Hobsbawm.

entries.label: End of the Ancien Regime with the French Revolution
Neolithic in France include artifacts from:
Seine-Oise-Marne culture or "SOM culture" (c. 3100 – c. 2400 BC)
La Tène culture c. 450 BC - 1st century BC
Corded Ware culture (c. 3000 BC – c. 2350 BC)
La Tène A (La Tène I) 450–380 BC
La Tène B (La Tène I) 380–250 BC
La Tène C (La Tène II) 250–150 BC
La Tène D (La Tène III) 150–1 BC
Merovingians (428 - 751)
entries.note: During the final century of the Merovingian rule, the dynasty was increasingly pushed into a ceremonial role. The Merovingian rule ended in March 752 AD when Pope Zachary formally deposed Childeric III. Zachary's successor, Pope Stephen II, confirmed and anointed Pepin the Short, in 754 beginning the Carolingian monarchy.

entries.label: Carolingians
entries.note: Robertians

entries.label: House of Capet (987–1328)
entries.note: AD1328 - The Capetian dynasty dies out in France; Philip of Valois is elected as king of France, despite the claims of King Edward III of England to the French throne.

entries.label: House of Valois (1328–1498)
entries.note: House of Valois-Orléans (1498–1515)

entries.label: Robert II
entries.note: Attended the Cathedral school at Rheims in the 980s along with Fulbert of Chartres.

entries.label: Années folles
entries.note: The Années folles ( "crazy years" in French) was the decade of the 1920s in France. It was coined to describe the social, artistic, and cultural collaborations of the period. The same period is also referred to as the Roaring Twenties or the Jazz Age in the United States. In Germany, it is sometimes referred to as the Golden Twenties because of the economic boom that followed the hyperinflation in 1923 until the Wall Street crash of 1929.

entries.label: Charles de Gaulle becomes the first president of the Fifth Republic
Clovis
entries.note: Clovis (c. 466 – c. 511) The first king of the Franks to unite all of the Frankish tribes under one ruler, changing the form of leadership from a group of royal chieftains to rule by a single king and ensuring that the kingship was passed down to his heirs. Considered the founder of the Merovingian dynasty, which ruled the Franks for the next two centuries.

entries.label: Pepin the Short
entries.note: AD751 - Pepin the Short, with papal approval, deposes the last Merovingian king of the Franks; Carolingians become the new Frankish dynasty.

entries.label: Atlantic Bronze Age (c. 1300 BC – c. 700 BC)
Louis XVII
entries.note: Louis XVII - claimant

entries.label: Charles de Gaulle's famous "Vive le Québec libre" speech provokes a diplomatic crisis in Canada–France relations
Pope Stephen II crowns Pepin I king of Franks
Peter Abelard
entries.note: Marie of France, Countess of Champagne (1145 – March 11, 1198) The elder daughter of Louis VII of France and his first wife, Eleanor of Aquitaine. Marie was also a patron of literature, including Andreas Capellanus, who served in her court, and Chrétien de Troyes. She was literate in French and Latin and maintained her own library. A deep affection existed between Marie and her half-brother Richard I of England, and his celebrated poem J'a nuns hons pris, lamenting his captivity in Austria, was dedicated to her.

entries.label: Bell Beaker culture (c. 2800 – 2300 (to c. 1900 BC in Britain))
Nationalization of major industries including Renault and utilities
Charles Martel
entries.note: Charles Martel (c. 688 – 22 October 741) Frankish statesman and military leader who, as Duke and Prince of the Franks and Mayor of the Palace, was de facto ruler of Francia from 718 until his death in 741. The illegitimate son of the Frankish statesman Pepin of Herstal and a noblewoman named Alpaida, Martel successfully asserted his claims to power as successor to his father as the power behind the throne in Frankish politics. Continuing and building on his father's work, he restored centralized government in Francia and began the series of military campaigns that re-established the Franks as the undisputed masters of all Gaul. In foreign wars, Martel subjugated Bavaria, Alemannia, and Frisia, vanquished the pagan Saxons, and halted the Islamic advance into Western Europe at the Battle of Tours. Martel is considered to be the founding figure of the European Middle Ages. Skilled as an administrator and warrior, he is often credited with a seminal role in the development of feudalism and knighthood. Martel was a great patron of Saint Boniface and made the first attempt at reconciliation between the Papacy and the Franks. The Pope wished him to become the defender of the Holy See and offered him the Roman consulship. Martel refused the offer. Although Martel never assumed the title of king, he divided Francia, like a king, between his sons Carloman and Pepin. The latter became the first of the Carolingians, the family of Charles Martel, to become king. Martel's grandson, Charlemagne, extended the Frankish realms to include much of the West, and became the first Emperor since the fall of Rome.

entries.label: François Rabelais (birth date unsure between 1483 and 1494)
Exposition Universelle held in Paris, showcasing modern achievements
Battle of Châlons: Hunnic invasion of Gaul halted
entries.note: 451 - Battle of Châlons Romans, Visigoths under Theodoric I and their allies (including the Franks) definitively stop further Hunnic invasion in Gaul. Theodoric I died during the battle, he was succeeded by his son Thorismund who also had a decisive role during the battle.

entries.label: Fulbert of Chartres (birth date unsure - between 952 and 970)

Louis IX announces that the County of Poitiers would go to his brother Alphonse – offending Isabella of Angoulême, whose son would have inherited the territory had the English won the Battle of Bouvines
War of Devolution
entries.note: The War of Devolution took place from May 1667 to May 1668. In the course of the war, France occupied large parts of the Spanish Netherlands and Franche-Comté, both then provinces of the Holy Roman Empire ruled by Spain. Its name derives from an obscure law known as the Jus Devolutionis, used by Louis XIV to claim that these territories had "devolved" to him by right of marriage to Maria Theresa of Spain.

entries.label: France and England signed the Treaty of Utrecht
entries.note: 1713 - France and England signed the Treaty of Utrecht, under which Philip V of Spain renounced for himself and his descendants any right to the French throne. Similarly, possible heirs to the French crown renounced all rights to the rulership of Spain.

entries.label: Great Flood of Paris inundates the city
Launch of the Concorde project in partnership with the UK
Honorius gives land in Gallia Aquitania to his Visigoth federates in which to settle, forming the nucleus of the future Visigothic Kingdom under king Wallia and then his son and heir Theodoric I
Charles recognizes Chilperic II as king of the Franks in exchange for his appointment as mayor of the palace with extensive powers
Saintonge War: Henry III of England arrives with an army in support of Isabella's claim to Poitiers
Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle - France obtains Lille and other territories of Flanders from Spain
Reign of Terror
entries.note: The Reign of Terror was a period of the French Revolution when, following the creation of the First Republic, a series of massacres and numerous public executions took place in response to the Federalist revolts, revolutionary fervour, anticlerical sentiment, and accusations of treason by the Committee of Public Safety. While terror was never formally instituted as a legal policy by the Convention, it was more often employed as a concept. The Terror concluded with the fall of Robespierre and his alleged allies in July 1794, in what is known as the Thermidorian Reaction. By then, 16,594 official death sentences had been dispensed throughout France since June 1793, of which 2,639 were in Paris alone. An additional 10,000 to 12,000 people had been executed without trial, and 10,000 had died in prison.

entries.label: Paris hosts the Summer Olympic Games
Launch of Minitel, a pioneering online information service
entries.note: The Minitel, officially known as TELETEL, was an interactive videotex online service accessible through telephone lines. It was the world's first and most successful mass-market online service prior to the World Wide Web. It was developed in Cesson-Sévigné, Brittany, by government-owned France Télécom.

entries.label: Roman territory of Septimania is ceded to the Visigothic Kingdom
Battle of Toulouse: An Aquitainian force brakes an Umayyad siege of Toulouse
Charlemagne is crowned Imperator Augustus by Pope Leo III
Charles the Bald is crowned Holy Roman Emperor by Pope John VIII
The Treaty of Rastatt ends hostilities between France and Austria
Creation of the franc Poincaré, stabilizing the French currency
Battle of Soissons: A Frankish army under Clovis I defeated Syagrius and conquered the Domain of Soissons
Charles Martel dies and his realm is divided between his two sons, Pepin the Short and Carloman, acting as Mayors of the Palace.
Battle of Andernach
entries.note: 876 - Battle of Andernach After Louis the German's death, Charles the Bald is badly defeated at Andernach by Louis' successor, Carloman of Bavaria, in an attempt to conquer his late brother's kingdom.

entries.label: Charles III signed the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte with Rollo, the king of the Vikings, allowing their settlement in what would become the Duchy of Normandy
Louis VII becomes duke of Aquitaine by marriage to the duchess Eleanor
Battle of Bouvines
entries.note: 1214 - Battle of Bouvines The French army defeated a combined English–Flemish force, enabling the kingdom to consolidate its control over Anjou, Brittany, Maine, Normandy and the Touraine.

entries.label: Louis IX is canonized by Pope Boniface VIII - the only French monarch to be declared a saint
Treaties of Nijmegen - France obtains the Franche-Comté and some cities in Flanders and Hainaut (from Spain)
Forced abdication of Napoleon and subsequent exile to Elba
Treaty of Paris
entries.note: 1951 - Treaty of Paris Establishment of the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) between France, West Germany, Italy, and the Benelux countries, producing diplomatic and economic stability in Europe between former enemy states. The ECSC is credited as one of the major "ancestors" of the European Union.

entries.label: Kingdom of Soissons
entries.note: The Kingdom or Domain of Soissons is the historiographical name for de facto independent Roman remnant of the Diocese of Gaul, which existed during late antiquity as a rump state of the Western Roman Empire until its conquest by the Franks in AD 486. Its capital was at Noviodunum, today the town of Soissons in France.

entries.label: The Duchy of Gascony is created as a buffer state against the Vascones and the Visigothic Kingdom
Carloman renounces his position as Mayor of the Palace and withdraws to monastic life, his realm is given to his brother, Pepin the Short.
Charles the Fat dies and with no legitimate or recognized heir, the Empire falls apart never to be reunited again
Robert II annexes the Duchy of Burgundy
The marriage of Louis VII and Eleanor is annulled
Bruges Matins
entries.note: 1302 - Bruges Matins The exiled citizens of Bruges, in Flanders, returned to their hometown and killed every Frenchman.

entries.label: The Great Ordinance is passed
entries.note: 1357 - The Great Ordinance The States-General pass Étienne Marcel's Great Ordinance in an attempt to impose limits on the monarchy, in particular in fiscal and monetary matters.

entries.label: Charles VII issues the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges
entries.note: 1438 - Charles VII issues the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges, requiring Church councils to be held every 10 years, and confirming the right of the Gallican Church to appoint ecclesiastical officials.

entries.label: Treaty of The Hague
entries.note: 1720 - Treaty of The Hague: France and its allies signed a treaty with Spain, thus ending the War of the Quadruple Alliance.

entries.label: Hundred Days
entries.note: 1815 - Hundred Days Napoleon escapes from Elba. Napoleon greeted by the 5th Regiment at Grenoble after his escape from Elba. Battle of Waterloo: Napoleon is defeated by Seventh Coalition armies, definitively ending the First French Empire and the Napoleonic Wars, and marks the start of almost half a century of peace throughout Europe.

entries.label: The Dreyfus affair
entries.note: The Dreyfus affair was a political scandal that divided the Third French Republic from 1894 until its resolution in 1906. The scandal began in December 1894 when Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a 35-year-old Alsatian French artillery officer of Jewish descent, was wrongfully convicted of treason for communicating French military secrets to the German Embassy in Paris. He was sentenced to life imprisonment and sent overseas to the penal colony on Devil's Island in French Guiana, where he spent the following five years imprisoned in very harsh conditions. The Dreyfus affair came to symbolise modern injustice in the Francophone world; it remains one of the most notable examples of a miscarriage of justice and of antisemitism. The affair divided France into pro-republican, anticlerical Dreyfusards and pro-army, mostly Catholic anti-Dreyfusards, embittering French politics and encouraging radicalisation. The press played a crucial role in exposing information and in shaping and expressing public opinion on both sides of the conflict.

entries.label: The first armistice at Compiègne is signed between France and Germany with France regaining Alsace-Lorraine
Gallia Narbonensis
entries.note: Known informally as Gallia Transalpina as Rome gained it first foothold in Gaul until being named Gallia Narbonensis upon attaining Provincial status.

entries.label: Synod of Rouen: A Catholic synod is held in Rouen which again condemns simony
Battle of Tours
entries.note: 732 - Battle of Tours Frankish and Burgundian soldiers under the Mayor of the Palace Charles Martel inflicted a significant defeat on the invading armies of the Umayyad Caliphate.

entries.label: Childeric III is dethroned as the last king of the Merovingian dynasty - Pepin the Short is later crowned king of the Franks, thus starting the rule of the Carolingian dynasty.
Charles III is overthrown by a noble revolt and replaced by Robert I, Odo's brother
Italian Wars
entries.note: The Italian Wars were a series of conflicts fought between 1494 and 1559, mostly in the Italian Peninsula, but later expanding into Flanders, the Rhineland and Mediterranean Sea. The primary belligerents were the Valois kings of France, on one side, and their opponents in the Holy Roman Empire and Spain on the other. At different points, various Italian states participated in the war, some on both sides, with limited involvement from England, Switzerland, and the Ottoman Empire. Results: - Spain sovereign over the kingdoms of Sicily, Naples (including the Presidi), Sardinia and the Duchy of Milan - Lorraine cedes Three Bishoprics to France - France gains Calais from England - Independent Savoyard state re-established - Florence annexes Siena

entries.label: Truce of Ratisbon - France obtains further territories in the north-west from Spain
Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette are executed by guillotine
May 68
entries.note: May 68 was a period of widespread protests, strikes, and civil unrest in France that began in May 1968 and became one of the most significant social uprisings in modern European history. Initially sparked by student demonstrations against university conditions and government repression, the movement quickly escalated into a nationwide general strike involving millions of workers, bringing the country to the brink of revolution. The events have profoundly shaped French politics, labor relations, and cultural life, leaving a lasting legacy of radical thought and activism.

entries.label: Chlothar the Great issues the Edict of Paris
entries.note: 614 Chlothar the Great issued the Edict of Paris. Among its provisions, the edict banned Jews from holding royal office and granted the nobility the exclusive power to appoint royal officers.

entries.label: Battle of Soissons
entries.note: 718 Battle of Soissons: Charles defeated the armies of Chilperic II and Aquitaine at Soissons. Chilperic II fled to Aquitaine.

entries.label: Charlemagne and Carloman I are proclaimed Kings of the Franks after their father's death. Each brother obtaines half of their father's kingdom.
Henry II ends the Italian Wars by signing the Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis and renouncing all his Italian claims
Treaty of Vienna
entries.note: 1738 - Treaty of Vienna: The signing of the treaty ended the War of the Polish Succession. France gained the Duchy of Lorraine and Bar.

entries.label: Treaty of Versailles
entries.note: 1768 - Treaty of Versailles: In order to pay its debts and being no longer able to suppress struggle for independence, the Republic of Genoa ceded Corsica to France. Corsica remained French ever since.

entries.label: Coup of 18 Brumaire: Napoleon overthrows the French Directory, replacing it with the French Consulate
Battle of Vouillé
entries.note: 507 - Battle of Vouillé Clovis defeated a Visigoth army under Alaric II, and conquered Gallia Aquitania, thus forming the basis of modern-day France.

entries.label: Childebert I dies. His brother Chlothar I inherites his territory, thus becoming sole King of the Franks and reuniting Clovis' kingdom
687 Battle of Tertry
entries.note: 687 Battle of Tertry Austrasian forces loyal to Pepin of Herstal defeated the invading army of Theuderic III at modern Tertry, Somme. Pepin of Herstal accepted Theuderic's unification of the Frankish kingdoms on the condition that he replace Berchar as his mayor of the palace.

entries.label: Carloman I dies - Charlemagne annexes his kingdom
Treaty of Verdun
entries.note: 843 - Treaty of Verdun An alliance between Louis the German and Charles the Bald, and their victories over Lothair I, compelled the elder brother to negotiate the division of the Frankish Empire. It was divided in three parts; West Francia for Charles the Bald, Middle Francia for Lothair I and East Francia for Louis the German, hence laying the foundations of modern France and Germany.

entries.label: Battle of Soissons: Robert is killed and Charles is captured by Rudolph, the duke of Burgundy
An English army under King Henry V lands in the north of France
Battle of Pavia: Francis is defeated by Imperial forces under Charles V and captured
Louis XIII makes Cardinal Richelieu his chief minister
Yew Tree Ball
entries.note: 1745 - Yew Tree Ball Masked ball given by the Louis XV in the Grand Gallery of the Chateau of Versailles, on the occasion of the marriage of Louis, Dauphin of France with Maria Teresa, Infanta of Spain. Fifteen thousand people attended including Jeanne Antoinette Poisson who met with the King for a second time.

entries.label: War of the First through Sixth Coalitions
Charles de Gaulle holds his Appeal of 18 June
The Euro replaces the French franc
Battle of Vézeronce
entries.note: 524 - Battle of Vézeronce The united armies of Clovis' sons inflicted a serious defeat on the Burgundian king Godomar. Chlodomer, the king of Orléans, was killed in battle.

entries.label: Charlemagne becomes king of the Lombards
Battle of Roncevaux Pass: A combined Basque-Banu Qasi force defeats a Frankish pacifying expedition at Roncevaux Pass
Battle of Agincourt
entries.note: The Battle of Agincourt was an English victory in the Hundred Years' War. It took place on 25 October 1415 (Saint Crispin's Day) near Azincourt, in northern France. The unexpected victory of the vastly outnumbered English troops against the numerically superior French army boosted English morale and prestige, crippled France, and started a new period of English dominance in the war that would last for 14 years until England was defeated by France in 1429 during the Siege of Orléans.

entries.label: Battle of Castillon
entries.note: 1453 - Battle of Castillon In what is considered the last battle of the Hundred Years' War, the French inflict a decisive victory on the English army, eventually gaining back all English-held territories of France.

entries.label: French Wars of Religion
entries.note: The French Wars of Religion were a series of civil wars between French Catholics and Protestants (called Huguenots) from 1562 to 1598. Between two and four million people died from violence, famine or disease directly caused by the conflict, and it severely damaged the power of the French monarchy. One of its most notorious episodes was the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572. The fighting ended with a compromise in 1598, when Henry of Navarre, who had converted to Catholicism in 1593, was proclaimed King Henry IV of France and issued the Edict of Nantes, which granted substantial rights and freedoms to the Huguenots. However, Catholics continued to disapprove of Protestants and of Henry, and his assassination in 1610 triggered a fresh round of Huguenot rebellions in the 1620s.

entries.label: Battle of Fontenoy
entries.note: 1745 - War of the Austrian Succession: French forces defeat an Anglo-Dutch-Hanoverian army at the Battle of Fontenoy; Louis XV, and his son, the Dauphin, were present at the battle.

entries.label: The Treaty of Campo Formio is signed between France and Austria
entries.note: 1797 - War of the First Coalition - The Treaty of Campo Formio is signed between France and Austria following decisive French military victories. The treaty marks the collapse of the First Coalition, composed of European powers which tried to contain Revolutionary France.

entries.label: Tallest building in the world until 1930
entries.note: During its construction, the Eiffel Tower surpassed the Washington Monument to become the tallest human-made structure in the world, a title it held for 41 years until the Chrysler Building in New York City was finished in 1930.

entries.label: Fifth Council of Orléans: A synod presided over by Sacerdos of Lyon in Orléans condemns Nestorianism and simony
Umayyad invasion of Gaul: The Umayyad Caliphate conquers Narbonne
The Spanish March is created by Charlemagne as a buffer zone between the Frankish kingdom and Al-Andalus
The army of John the Fearless, duke of Burgundy, captures Paris. The dauphin, the future Charles VII, flees
Massacre of Vassy begins The French Wars of Religion
Napoleon is declared Emperor by the Senate and crowns himself in Notre-Dame de Paris
The Entente Cordiale is signed
entries.note: The Entente Cordiale ( 'Cordial Agreement') comprised a series of agreements signed on 8 April 1904 between the United Kingdom and the French Republic which saw a significant improvement in Anglo-French relations.

entries.label: Battle of Roncevaux Pass
entries.note: 778 - Battle of Roncevaux Pass A Basque force attacked and decimated Charlemagne's army in the Roncevaux Pass

entries.label: The treaty of Heiligen is signed between Charlemagne and the Danish king establishing the boundary between Denmark and the Frankish Empire
John the Fearless is assassinated by companions of the dauphin
entries.note: 1419 - John the Fearless was assassinated by companions of the dauphin. He was succeeded by his son Philip the Good, who would ally himself with the English against the French crown.

entries.label: St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of French Protestants
The Fronde
entries.note: The Fronde was a series of civil wars in the Kingdom of France between 1648 and 1653, occurring in the midst of the Franco-Spanish War, which had begun in 1635. The government of the young King Louis XIV confronted the combined opposition of the princes, the nobility, the noble regional court assemblies (parlements), as well as much of the French population, and managed to subdue them all. The dispute started when the government of France issued seven fiscal edicts, six of which were to increase taxation. The parlements resisted, questioned the constitutionality of the king's actions, and sought to check his powers.

entries.label: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle ends the War of the Austrian Succession
Pastry War
entries.note: The Pastry War, also known as the first French intervention in Mexico or the first Franco-Mexican war (1838–1839), began in November 1838 with the naval blockade of some Mexican ports and the capture of the fortress of San Juan de Ulúa in the port of Veracruz by French forces sent by King Louis Philippe I. It ended in March 1839 with a British-brokered peace. The intervention followed many claims by French nationals of losses due to unrest in Mexico. This was the first of two French invasions of Mexico; a second, larger intervention would take place in the 1860s.

entries.label: The 1905 French law on the separation of Church and State ends government funding of religious groups
Battle of the River Garonne: An Umayyad army wipes out an Aquitainian force on the Garonne
Siege of Paris: Some three hundred Viking ships arrived at Paris
The Burgundians compel Charles VI to sign the Treaty of Troyes, under which the throne was to pass to Henry V of England
Henry IV issues the Edict of Nantes to end the French Wars of Religion
Napoleon dissolves the Holy Roman Empire
entries.note: 1806 - Napoleon dissolves the Holy Roman Empire, and created the Confederation of the Rhine, a union of French client states composed of 16 states in present-day Germany.

entries.label: First Tour de France cycling race is held
Battle of the Boarn: A Frankish army led by Charles defeats and annexes the Frisian Kingdom and kills its king, Bubo.
Siege of Paris: The army of Charles the Fat arrives in Paris. He allows the Viking fleet to sail to Burgundy, then in revolt.
Francis I issues an edict incorporating Brittany into the kingdom of France
Treaty of Paris ends the Seven Years' War
Napoleon is exiled on Saint Helena
Opening of the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées and premiere of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring
Battle of Nîmes: Charles destroys the Umayyad Septimanian cities of Nîmes, Agde, Béziers and what is now Villeneuve-lès-Maguelone
Concordat of 1801
entries.note: 1801 - The Concordat of 1801 was signed between Napoleon and Pope Pius VII, solidifying the Roman Catholic Church as the majority church of France, returning most of its civil status, and restoring much power to the papacy.

entries.label: Women gain the right to vote in municipal elections in some colonies (though not yet in France)
Battle of Avignon: Charles breaches and burns the Umayyad-held city of Avignon
Battle of Thimeon: Louis the Younger destroys a Viking camp near modern Charleroi
Construction
entries.note: 1130: Sens Cathedral, the first French Gothic cathedral, begun (consecrated 1171)

entries.label: Rouen
entries.note: 1145: Rouen Cathedral begun. (consecrated 1237)

entries.label: Senlis
entries.note: 1153: Senlis Cathedral begun. (consecrated 1191)

entries.label: Poitiers
entries.note: 1162: Poitiers Cathedral begun. (consecrated 1379)

entries.label: Strasbourg
entries.note: Strasbourg Cathedral or the Cathedral of Our Lady of Strasbourg is a Roman Catholic cathedral in Strasbourg, Alsace, France. (begun 1015, completed 1439) Although considerable parts of it are still in Romanesque architecture, it is widely considered to be among the finest examples of high, or late, Gothic architecture. Erwin von Steinbach is credited for major contributions from 1277 to his death in 1318. At 142 metres (466 feet), it was the world's tallest building from 1647 to 1874 (227 years), when it was surpassed by St. Nikolai's Church, Hamburg. Today it is the sixth-tallest church in the world and the highest still-standing structure built entirely in the Middle Ages. Described by Victor Hugo as a "gigantic and delicate marvel", and by Goethe as a "sublimely towering, wide-spreading tree of God", the cathedral is visible far across the plains of Alsace and can be seen from as far off as the Vosges Mountains or the Black Forest on the other side of the Rhine.

entries.label: Coutances
entries.note: 1210: Coutances Cathedral, Normandy, begun. (completed 1274)

entries.label: Beauvais
entries.note: 1225: Beauvais Cathedral begun, but after tower falls in 1272 it is left unfinished

entries.label: Tours
entries.note: The choir and transept were rebuilt between 1240 and the beginning of the 14th century

entries.label: Palais des Papes
entries.note: 1252: Palais des Papes in Avignon begun. (major enlargement and modification between 1334 and 1364)

entries.label: Saint-Domingue expedition
entries.note: 1802 - Saint-Domingue expedition French Army General Charles Leclerc and the first 5,000 of 20,000 troops arrive at Cap-François (now Cap-Haïtien) to suppress Toussaint L'Ouverture and the rebellion of the black population in Haiti.

entries.label: February Revolution
entries.note: The French Revolution of 1848, also known as the February Revolution, was a period of civil unrest in France, in February 1848, that led to the collapse of the July Monarchy and the foundation of the French Second Republic. It sparked the wave of revolutions of 1848. The revolution took place in Paris, and was preceded by the French government's crackdown on the campagne des banquets. Starting on 22 February as a large-scale protest against the government of François Guizot, it later developed into a violent uprising against the monarchy. After intense urban fighting, large crowds managed to take control of the capital, leading to the abdication of King Louis Philippe on 24 February and the subsequent proclamation of the Second Republic.

entries.label: Popular Front government introduces paid vacations and the 40-hour workweek
Battle of Narbonne: Charles besieges but fails to capture the Umayyad-held city of Narbonne
Saint-Denis
entries.note: 1135: Basilica of Saint-Denis reconstruction in new style begun by Abbot Suger, The Gothic ambulatory was finished in 1144.

entries.label: Laon
entries.note: 1155: Laon Cathedral begun. Reconstructed with three traverses and completed in 1220

entries.label: Notre Dame de Paris
entries.note: 1163: Notre Dame de Paris begun. Choir completed in 1172, Cathedral consecrated in 1182.

entries.label: Chartres
entries.note: 1194: Chartres Cathedral begun to replace earlier church destroyed by fire. Consecrated 1260. Flamboyant north spire added after earlier spire destroyed by lightning.

entries.label: Toul
entries.note: 1210: Toul Cathedral reconstruction from Romanesque began. Flamboyant facade was added in the 15th century.

entries.label: Notre-Dame de Paris (additions)
entries.note: 1220 to 1270: Notre-Dame de Paris; Addition of transepts and rose windows, modified buttresses

entries.label: Notre-Dame de l'Épine
entries.note: 1405–1527: Notre-Dame de l'Épine (begun 1405–1406, completed 1527)

entries.label: Notre-Dame de Louviers
entries.note: 1493–1510: The north façade, south façade, and south porch of the Church of Notre-Dame de Louviers

entries.label: Louisiana Purchase
entries.note: 1803 - Louisiana Purchase France sells Louisiana to the United States of America, renouncing its last territorial possessions on continental North America.

entries.label: France becomes the fourth country to develop and test nuclear weapons
Battle of the River Berre: Charles intercepts and destroys an Umayyad army sent to relieve his siege of Narbonne near the Étang de Berre
Noyon
entries.note: 1150: Noyon Cathedral begun. (completed 1231)

entries.label: Lyon
entries.note: 1170: Lyon Cathedral begun. (completed 14th century)

entries.label: Bourges
entries.note: 1183: Bourges Cathedral begun, nave was finished by 1255; consecrated in 1324.

entries.label: Reims
entries.note: 1211: Reims Cathedral begun. (completed 1345)

entries.label: Amiens
entries.note: 1220: Amiens Cathedral begun. (completed 1288). Rose window was added 1366–1341

entries.label: Basilica of Saint-Denis enlarged
entries.note: 1231: Basilica of Saint-Denis enlarged with new nave, transept, and rose windows (completed 1264)

entries.label: Church of Saint-Maclou, Rouen.
entries.note: 1435–1521: Church of Saint-Maclou, Rouen.

entries.label: Beauvais Cathedral south transept constructed
entries.note: 1500–1508: Beauvais Cathedral south transept constructed

entries.label: Charles divides his lands between his two elder sons Carloman and Pepin the Short, the former ruling as king in the east and the latter in the west
Angers
entries.note: 1150 c. Angers Cathedral rebuilding from Romanesque to Angevin Gothic beginning mid-12th century, completed 1250

entries.label: Lisieux
entries.note: 1170: Lisieux Cathedral in Normandy reconstruction begins from Romanesque to Gothic style. Work continued until 13th century.

entries.label: Le Mans
entries.note: 1217: Le Mans Cathedral begun. (consecrated 1254)

entries.label: Sainte-Chapelle
entries.note: 1238: Sainte-Chapelle on the Ile de la Cité in Paris begun. (completed 1248).

entries.label: Chartres Cathedral north tower
entries.note: 1507–13: Chartres Cathedral north tower is destroyed by lightning, and rebuilt in the Flamboyant style

entries.label: French invasion of Russia
entries.note: The French invasion of Russia, also known as the Russian campaign, the Second Polish War, and in Russia as the Patriotic War of 1812, was initiated by Napoleon with the aim of compelling the Russian Empire to comply with the continental blockade of the United Kingdom. Widely studied, Napoleon's incursion into Russia stands as a focal point in military history, recognized as among the most devastating military endeavors globally. In a span of fewer than six months, the campaign exacted a staggering toll, claiming the lives of nearly a million soldiers and civilians. While exact figures remain elusive, Napoleon's initial force upon entering Russia exceeded 450,000 men, accompanied by over 150,000 horses, approximately 25,000 wagons and nearly 1,400 artillery pieces. However, the surviving count dwindled to a mere 120,000 men (excluding early deserters); signifying a staggering loss of approximately 380,000 lives throughout the campaign, half of which resulted from diseases. This catastrophic outcome shattered Napoleon's once-untarnished reputation of invincibility.

entries.label: Frederick II
entries.note: Frederick II (26 December 1194 – 13 December 1250) One of the most powerful Holy Roman Emperors of the Middle Ages and head of the House of Hohenstaufen. His political and cultural ambitions, based in Sicily and stretching through Italy to Germany, and even to Jerusalem, were enormous; however, his enemies, especially the popes, prevailed, and his dynasty collapsed soon after his death. Historian Donald Detwiler,wrote of him: "A man of extraordinary culture, energy, and ability – called by a contemporary chronicler stupor mundi (the wonder of the world), by Nietzsche the first European, and by many historians the first modern ruler – Frederick established in Sicily and southern Italy something very much like a modern, centrally governed kingdom with an efficient bureaucracy." Viewing himself as a direct successor to the Roman Emperors of Antiquity, he was Emperor of the Romans from his papal coronation in 1220 until his death; he was also a claimant to the title of King of the Romans from 1212 and unopposed holder of that monarchy from 1215. As such, he was King of Germany, of Italy, and of Burgundy. At the age of three, he was crowned King of Sicily as a co-ruler with his mother, Constance of Hauteville, the daughter of Roger II of Sicily. His other royal title was King of Jerusalem by virtue of marriage and his connection with the Sixth Crusade. He was frequently at war with the Papacy, hemmed in between Frederick's lands in northern Italy and his Kingdom of Sicily (the Regno) to the south, and thus he was excommunicated four times and often vilified in pro-papal chronicles of the time and since. Pope Gregory IX went so far as to call him the Antichrist. Speaking six languages (Latin, Sicilian, German, French, Greek and Arabic), Frederick was an avid patron of science and the arts. He played a major role in promoting literature through the Sicilian School of poetry. His Sicilian royal court in Palermo, from around 1220 to his death, saw the first use of a literary form of an Italo-Romance language, Sicilian. The poetry that emanated from the school had a significant influence on literature and on what was to become the modern Italian language. The school and its poetry were saluted by Dante and his peers and predate by at least a century the use of the Tuscan idiom as the elite literary language of Italy.

entries.note: The Zollverein, or German Customs Union, was a coalition of German states formed to manage tariffs and economic policies within their territories. By 1866, the Zollverein included most of the German states. The Zollverein was not part of the German Confederation. The foundation of the Zollverein was the first instance in history in which independent states consummated a full economic union without the simultaneous creation of a political federation or union.

Events of the reign of Charlemagne
entries.note: Events of the reign of Charlemagne 770 Charlemagne married Desiderata of the Lombards, a daughter of Desiderius, the king of the Kingdom of the Lombards. 771 Charlemagne repudiated his marriage to Desiderata. 772 Saxon Wars: Charlemagne invaded the territory of the Saxons and destroyed their sacred symbol Irminsul near Paderborn. 773 Siege of Pavia (773–74): Charlemagne laid siege to the Lombard capital Pavia. 774 Siege of Pavia (773–74): Desiderius opened the gates of Pavia and surrendered to Charlemagne. 774 Charlemagne was crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy king of the Lombards at Pavia. 776 Charlemagne established the March of Friuli on the territory of the old Duchy of Friuli. 781 Charlemagne appointed his son Pepin of Italy king of Italy. 782 Massacre of Verden: Charlemagne had some forty-five hundred Saxon captives murdered at modern Verden an der Aller. 785 Saxon Wars: The Saxon leader Widukind converted to Christianity and pledged fealty to Charlemagne. 785 Charlemagne issued the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae, a legal code which, among other clauses, prescribed the death penalty for any Saxons who refused to convert to Christianity. 789 Charlemagne issued the Admonitio generalis, reforming the Christian liturgy in his empire and calling for the establishment of schools. 799 Siege of Trsat: Eric of Friuli, the duke of Friuli and an officer of Charlemagne, was killed during a failed siege of Trsat, in Croatia. 800 Leo crowned Charlemagne Holy Roman Emperor. 802 Charlemagne issued the Capitularia missorum specialia, defining the office of the missus dominicus, a salaried emissary to the kingdom. 803 Charlemagne issued the Lex Saxonum, allowing Saxon customs which were not contradictory to Christianity and granting some rights and protections to the church in the Saxon lands. 804 Charlemagne organized the Duchy of Saxony on the territories of the conquered Saxons.

entries.label: Events of the reign of Louis the Pious
entries.note: Events of the reign of Louis the Pious 817 Louis the Pious appointed his son Pepin I of Aquitaine king of Aquitaine, his son Louis the German king of Bavaria, and his son Lothair I co-Holy Roman Emperor with the promise of receiving his other domains. 819 Louis the Pious issued the Notitia de servitio monasteriorum, which listed monasteries in his kingdom and the services they owed the crown. 829 Louis the Pious promised the inheritance of Alamannia to his son Charles the Bald. 830 A rebellion of Pepin I of Aquitaine, Louis the German and Lothair I, instigated in part by Wala of Corbie, the abbot of Corbie Abbey, captured their father Louis the Pious at Compiègne and forced their stepmother, Charles the Bald's mother Judith of Bavaria (died 843), into a nunnery. 830 Pepin I of Aquitaine and Louis the German declared their loyalty to their father Louis the Pious against Lothair I in exchange for the promise of a greater portion of his inheritance. Wala was deposed as abbot of Corbie Abbey and Judith returned to her husband's court. 832 Louis the Pious declared Charles the Bald king of Aquitaine and promised Lothair I the rest of his kingdom in the face of an uprising by Pepin I of Aquitaine and Louis the German. 833 Lothair I joined the rebellion of his brothers Pepin I of Aquitaine and Louis the German against his father Louis the Pious. 833 Louis the Pious met his sons Pepin I of Aquitaine, Louis the German and Lothair I and their armies, as well as the pope, Pope Gregory IV, at the Field of Lies near Colmar. 833 Ebbo, archbishop of the archdiocese of Reims, presided over a synod in Soissons which deposed Louis the Pious as Holy Roman Emperor. 834 Louis the Pious was restored as Holy Roman Emperor with the support of the Frankish nobility. 835 Synod of Thionville: Ebbo publicly recanted his charges against Louis the Pious at a synod at Thionville. 836 Louis the Pious appointed Lothair I king only of Italy; all else was divided between Pepin I of Aquitaine, Louis the German and Charles the Bald. 837 Louis the Pious crowned Charles the Bald king of Alamannia and Burgundy, granting him some lands which were before promised to Louis the German. Louis the German rose in revolt; Louis the Pious responded by promising all his lands save Bavaria to Charles the Bald. 838 Pepin I of Aquitaine died. Louis the Pious appointed Charles the Bald king of Aquitaine. 840 Louis the Pious and Lothair I agreed to a division of the empire after the former's death, with Charles the Bald inheriting the western part and Lothair I inheriting the eastern, including Italy. 840 Defeated by the forces of Louis the Pious and Lothair I, the Aquitainian nobility accepted Charles the Bald as king of Aquitaine. 840 Louis the Pious and Lothair I defeated the armies of Louis the German.

entries.note: Operation Paperclip was a secret United States intelligence program in which more than 1,600 German scientists, engineers, and technicians were taken from former Nazi Germany to the US for government employment after the end of World War II in Europe, between 1945 and 1959; several were confirmed to be former members of the Nazi Party, including the SS or the SA.

The Imperial Diet issues the Golden Bull of 1356
entries.note: 1356 - The Imperial Diet issued the Golden Bull of 1356, which fixed the offices of the seven prince-electors and established that the Holy Roman Emperor could be elected by a simple majority vote.

Napoleonic Wars: Prussia declares war on France
Germany and Austria-Hungary form the Dual Alliance

Childeric II, his wife Bilichild and a son are killed by a conspiracy of nobles
