entries.label: Pactum Lotharii is signed
entries.note: 840 Lothair I and Pietro Tradonico, doge of the Republic of Venice, signed the Pactum Lotharii, reiterating earlier agreements between the Franks and the Byzantine Empire.

entries.label: Frankish-Moravian War
entries.note: 882 Frankish-Moravian War Svatopluk I of Moravia, the king of Great Moravia, intervened in Pannonia on the side of Aribo.

entries.label: Battle of Riade: A Hungarian force camped on the Unstrut is put to flight by a German army
Schmalkaldic War
entries.note: 1546 Schmalkaldic War A war began between the Schmalkaldic League of Lutheran principalities and a coalition led by the Holy Roman Empire. Ended in an imperial victory.

entries.label: France and Prussia sign the second Treaty of Tilsit
entries.note: 1807 - France and Prussia signed the second of the Treaties of Tilsit, in which the latter ceded half of its territory to Russia and French client states.

entries.label: Treaty of Rapallo
entries.note: 1922 - Germany and Russia signed the Treaty of Rapallo, in which each renounced all territorial and financial claims against the other and pledged to normalize relations.

entries.label: West Germany wins the 1990 FIFA World Cup
Council of Clermont
entries.note: 535 Council of Clermont A synod was held in modern Clermont-Ferrand which limited the rights of Catholic bishops to appeal to the state and which condemned marriage between Christians and Jews and between relatives.

entries.label: Dagobert I establishes the Duchy of Thuringia on the former territory of the Thuringii
Council of Paderborn
entries.note: 785 Council of Paderborn A council held at Paderborn outlawed idolatry and called for the death penalty for anyone who had caused another to be executed for witchcraft.

entries.label: Battle of Fontenoy
entries.note: 841 Battle of Fontenoy The forces of Charles the Bald and Louis the German dealt a decisive defeat to Lothair I and Pepin the Younger.

entries.label: Battle of Leuven
entries.note: 891 - Battle of Leuven An East Frankish force repells a Viking invasion at modern Leuven.

entries.label: Otto the Great creates the Billung March and the Marca Geronis.
Battle of Bouvines
entries.note: 1214 - Battle of Bouvines The French army defeated a combined English–Flemish force, enabling the kingdom to consolidate its control over Anjou, Brittany, Maine, Normandy and the Touraine.

entries.label: The Victual Brothers are hired by the Duchy of Mecklenburg to assist in its fight against Denmark
Moritzbastei is constructed as a bastion
Johann Gottlieb Fichte publishsd his 'Addresses to the German Nation', arguing for German nationalism and unity
France invades the valley of the Ruhr
Charibert II is killed on the orders of Dagobert I
Pepin of Herstal becomes mayor of the palace of Austrasia
Concilium Germanicum
entries.note: 742 Concilium Germanicum A synod called by Carloman and presided over by Saint Boniface settled some issues of Catholic ritual and organization. The Rule of Saint Benedict became mandatory in Frankish monasteries.

entries.label: Saxon Wars
entries.note: The Saxon Wars were the campaigns and insurrections of the thirty-three years from 772, when Charlemagne first entered Saxony with the intent to conquer, to 804, when the last rebellion of tribesmen was defeated. In all, 18 campaigns were fought, primarily in what is now northern Germany. They resulted in the incorporation of Saxony into the Frankish realm and their forcible conversion from Germanic paganism to Christianity.

entries.label: Battle of Andernach
entries.note: 939 Battle of Andernach A rebellion of Franconia and Lotharingia against Otto the Great is decisively defeated at Andernach. The dukes of Franconia and Lotharingia Eberhard of Franconia and Gilbert were killed. Otto the Great prevented succession in both duchies and dissolved the former.

entries.label: St. Nicholas' Church is constructed in Berlin
The Peace of Augsburg is signed, granting princes of the Holy Roman Empire the right to determine the state religion within their territories
The Landtag of Bavaria is established
Italy joins the Triple Alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary
The Free Democratic Party (FDP) is established
The Frankish army on the Po, suffering from dysentery, surrender to the Byzantines
The nobility of Austrasia join a revolt led by Pepin of Landen
Council of Cannstatt: Carloman executes the Alemanni nobility, numbering in the thousands, in modern Stuttgart.
Battle of Lechfeld: Otto the Great repells a Hungarian invasion
Lübeck and Hamburg form an alliance
Battle of Grunwald: The Teutonic Order is decisively defeated by the combined forces of Poland and Lithuania at Grunwald
The Treaty of London is signed
entries.note: 1839 - Belgium, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Austria, France, Russia and the German Confederation signed the Treaty of London, recognizing Belgium's independence and guaranteeing its neutrality.

entries.label: Reinsurance Treaty is signed
entries.note: 1887 - Germany and Russia signed the secret Reinsurance Treaty, in which each promised benevolent neutrality in the event the other should go to war.

entries.label: Beer Hall Putsch
entries.note: 1923 - Beer Hall Putsch Nazi Party chairman Adolf Hitler led some six hundred Sturmabteilung (SA) to the Bürgerbräukeller in Munich, where they held Bavarian state officials Gustav Ritter von Kahr, Hans Ritter von Seisser and Otto von Lossow at gunpoint to demand they support a Nazi coup.

entries.label: Treaty of Paris is signed
entries.note: 1951 - The Inner Six European nations including West Germany signed the Treaty of Paris establishing the European Coal and Steel Community, a single market in coal and steel governed by supranational institutions.

entries.label: The Maastricht Treaty establishing the European Union (EU) is signed by twelve European countries including Germany
Frankish forces under Theudebert I drive Byzantine and Ostrogothic armies from their encampments on the Po
Pepin of Herstal takes the title Duke of the Franks
Carloman retires to live as a monk in Rome. His son Drogo succeeds him as mayor of the palace.
Oaths of Strasbourg
entries.note: 842 - Louis the German and Charles the Bald took the Oaths of Strasbourg, in which each pledged to aid the other against Lothair I. Their soldiers pledged not to obey an order counter to this oath.

entries.label: Battle on the Raxa: A German army defeats an Obotrite rebellion in the Billung March
Freie Stadt Mainz is founded in Mainz
Educator Friedrich Fröbel coins the term kindergarten
Germany joins the League of Nations
The Euro is introduced - the Deutsche Mark loses its status as legal tender in Germany
Pepin of Landen becomes mayor of the palace of Austrasia
Charles Martel is acclaimed mayor of the palace of Austrasia
Upon the death of Gero, the Marca Geronis is divided into five marches: Northern, Saxon Eastern, Meissen, Zeitz and Merseburg
The Prussian three-class franchise is introduced
entries.note: 1850 - The Prussian three-class franchise, according to which all males over the age of 24 were allowed to vote for their representatives in the lower house of the Prussian parliament, with votes weighted by amount of taxes paid, was introduced.

entries.label: Enabling Act of 1933
entries.note: The Enabling Act of 1933, which granted the cabinet the power to make laws, was passed and signed in the presence of armed members of the SA and Schutzstaffel (SS).

entries.label: Uprising of 1953 in East Germany
entries.note: Uprising of 1953 in East Germany 100,000 protestors gathered at dawn, demanding the reinstatement of old work quotas and, later, the resignation of the East German government. At noon German police trapped many of the demonstrators in an open square; Soviet tanks fired on the crowd, killing hundreds and ending the protest.

entries.label: German Stem Duchies
entries.note: The German stem duchies (Stammesherzogtümer) were the major tribal-based political units of East Francia (later the Holy Roman Empire) in the early medieval period. These duchies represented the major ethnic or "stem" (Stamm) groups of the German people. The Duchies were: Saxony (c. 804 – 1296) Bavaria (c. 555 – 1180+) Swabia (c. 915 – 1268) Franconia (c. 882 – 1034) Lotharingia (843 – c. 1033)

entries.label: The Peace of Westphalia
entries.note: 1648 Thirty Years' War The Peace of Westphalia was concluded, ending the war and granting Switzerland and the Netherlands independence from the Holy Roman Empire.

entries.label: Neanderthal remains are discovered in Neandertal
Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II issues the Edict of Restitution
entries.note: 1629 - Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II issued the Edict of Restitution, which demanded that lands expropriated since and in contradiction to the terms of the Peace of Augsburg be restored to the Catholic Church.

entries.label: The General German Workers' Association is formed
President Paul von Hindenburg issues the Reichstag Fire Decree, suspending most civil liberties
Sack of Magdeburg
entries.note: 1631 Sack of Magdeburg Forces under the command of the Holy Roman Empire and the Catholic League breached the walls of the Protestant city of Magdeburg and murdered some twenty thousand of its thirty thousand inhabitants.

entries.note: Avebury is a Neolithic henge monument containing three stone circles, around the village of Avebury in Wiltshire, in southwest England. One of the best known prehistoric sites in Britain, it contains the largest stone circle in Europe.

Gauls
entries.note: Gallia Lugdunensis (French: Gaule Lyonnaise) was a province of the Roman Empire in what is now the modern country of France, part of the Celtic territory of Gaul formerly known as Celtica. It is named after its capital Lugdunum (today's Lyon), possibly Roman Europe's major city west of Italy, and a major imperial mint. The date of the creation of Gallia Lugdunensis is under discussion, whether between 27 and 25 BC or between 16 and 13 BC, during Augustus' visits to Gaul.

c. 400 BC Iron Age settlements emerge in Wales, two of the earliest being Castell Odo, a small hillfort near the tip of the Llŷn Peninsula and Lodge Wood Camp, above the later Roman fort at Caerleon
Sub-Roman Britain
entries.note: Sub-Roman Britain is the period of late antiquity on the island of Great Britain between the end of Roman rule and the Anglo-Saxon settlement. The term was originally used to describe archaeological remains found in fifth and sixth century sites that hinted at the decay of locally made wares from a previous higher standard under the Roman Empire. It is now used to described the period that commenced with the evacuation of Roman troops to Gaul by Constantine III in 407 AD and to have concluded with the Battle of Deorham in 577 AD.

entries.label: Kingdom of Mann and the Isles
entries.note: The Kingdom of the Isles was a Norse-Gaelic kingdom comprising the Isle of Man, the Hebrides and the islands of the Clyde from the 9th to the 13th centuries AD. The islands were known to the Norsemen as the Suðreyjar, or "Southern Isles" as distinct from the Norðreyjar or Northern Isles of Orkney and Shetland. In Scottish Gaelic, the kingdom is known as Rìoghachd nan Eilean. The territory is sometimes called the Kingdom of Mann and the Isles, although only some of the later rulers claimed that title. The historical record is incomplete, and the kingdom was not a continuous entity throughout the entire period. At times the rulers were independent of external control, although for much of the period they had overlords in Norway, Ireland, England, Scotland or Orkney. At times there also appear to have been competing claims for all or parts of the territory.

James VI of Scotland crowned James I of England
entries.note: 1603 - James VI of Scotland crowned James I of England. James was the son of Mary Queen of Scots and Lord Darnley. He was the first king to rule over Scotland and England.

entries.label: Prince Charles is invested as the Prince of Wales
entries.note: 1969 - Prince Charles is invested as the Prince of Wales at Caernarfon Castle; the televised event attracts a world-wide audience of 500 million people, the largest TV audience ever gained for an event in Wales.

entries.label: Gnaeus Julius Agricola
entries.note: Gnaeus Julius Agricola (13 June 40 – 23 August 93) Roman Italo-Gallic general responsible for much of the Roman conquest of Britain. Written by his son-in-law Tacitus, the De vita et moribus Iulii Agricolae is the primary source for most of what is known about him, along with detailed archaeological evidence from northern Britain. He supported Vespasian during the Year of the Four Emperors (69), and was given a military command in Britain when the latter became emperor. When his command ended in 73, he was made patrician in Rome and appointed governor of Gallia Aquitania. He was made consul and governor of Britannia in 77. While there, he completed the conquest of what is now Wales and northern England, and led his army to the far north of Scotland, establishing forts across much of the Lowlands. He was recalled from Britain in 85 after an unusually lengthy service. After his return, he retired from military and public life.

entries.label: Æthelfrith unites Bernicia and Deira to form the kingdom of Northumbria
Vikings sack the Island of Lindisfarne
entries.note: Possibly the holiest site of Anglo-Saxon England, Lindisfarne is situated off the Northumberland coast in the north east of England.

entries.label: Norman conquest of England - William the Conqueror, duke of Normandy, lands with an army at Pevensey
Richard is captured by Duke Leopold of Austria whilst returning from the Crusades
Battle of Bosworth Field
entries.note: The Battle of Bosworth Field (or Battle of Bosworth) was the last significant battle of the Wars of the Roses, the civil war between the Houses of Lancaster and York that raged across England in the latter half of the 15th century. Fought on 22 August 1485, the battle was won by the Lancastrians. Their leader Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, by his victory became the first English monarch of the Tudor dynasty as well as the third and last Welsh-born King of England. His opponent, Richard III, the last king of the House of York, was killed in the battle. Historians consider Bosworth Field to mark the end of the Plantagenet dynasty, making it a defining moment of English and Welsh history

entries.label: Sophie of Hanover
entries.note: Sophia of the Palatinate (commonly referred to as Sophia of Hanover) 14 October 1630 – 8 June 1714 Electress of Hanover from 1692 to 1698. She was also an heiress to the crowns of England (later in union with the Kingdom of Scotland known as Great Britain) and Ireland. She was declared heiress presumptive to Queen Anne by the Act of Settlement 1701, which was passed by the English parliament, and therefore only applied to the Kingdom of England (which included Wales) and the Kingdom of Ireland. A few years later, the Kingdom of Scotland agreed to accept the Hanoverian succession for the new single throne of a new country, the Kingdom of Great Britain that Scotland and England had agreed to unite as, and which came into being under the Acts of Union, 1707. Sophia, a granddaughter of James VI and I, died less than two months before she would have become queen; her claim to the thrones passed on to her eldest son, George Louis, Elector of Hanover, who ascended them as George I on 1 August 1714 (Old Style).

entries.label: Anglo-Saxon Heptarchy
entries.note: The Heptarchy (from the Greek ἑπτά hepta, "seven" and ἄρχω arkho, "to rule") is a collective name applied to the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of south, east, and central England during late antiquity and the early Middle Ages, conventionally identified as seven: East Anglia, Essex, Kent, Mercia, Northumbria, Sussex, and Wessex. The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms eventually unified into the Kingdom of England. The term has been in use since the 16th century, but the initial idea that there were seven Anglo-Saxon kingdoms is attributed to the English historian Henry of Huntingdon in the 12th century and was first used in his Historia Anglorum. By convention, the Heptarchy lasted from the end of Roman rule in Britain in the 5th century, until most of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms came under the overlordship of Egbert of Wessex in 829: a period of European history often referred to as the Early Middle Ages or, more controversially, as the Dark Ages.

Danes triumph at the Battle of Ashingdon

entries.label: Battle of Stamford Bridge
entries.note: 1066 - On 25th September at the Battle of Stamford Bridge near York, Harold defeats an invading army led by Harald Hardrada, King of Norway. Just 3 days later, William the Conqueror lands his Norman invasion fleet on England’s south coast.

entries.label: Thomas Becket
entries.note: Thomas Becket, also known as Saint Thomas of Canterbury, Thomas of London and later Thomas à Becket (21 December 1119 or 1120 – 29 December 1170) Archbishop of Canterbury from 1162 until his murder in 1170. He is venerated as a saint and martyr by the Catholic Church and the Anglican Communion. He engaged in conflict with Henry II, King of England, over the rights and privileges of the Church and was murdered by followers of the king in Canterbury Cathedral. Soon after his death, he was canonised by Pope Alexander III.

entries.label: Richard is ransomed and returns to England
King Edward II retreats to Wales
entries.note: 1326 - King Edward II retreats to Wales with his forces after his regime collapses; he is captured by rebel forces north of Caerphilly, escorted back to England via Monmouth Castle and relinquishes his crown two months later.

entries.label: Battle of Stoke - the last battle of the Wars of the Roses
The Glorious Revolution replaces James II with William and Mary
Entente Cordiale signed between Britain and France
A Scottish Parliament sits for the first time in 272 years
entries.note: 1999 - A Scottish Parliament sits for the first time in 272 years. Donald Dewar of the Scottish Labour Party elected as First Minister and forms Scottish Executive in coalition with the Scottish Liberal Democrats.

entries.label: British Bronze Age
entries.note: There is no clear consensus on the date for the beginning of the Bronze Age in Great Britain and Ireland. Some sources give a date as late as 2000 BC, while others set 2200 BC as the demarcation between the Neolithic and the Bronze Age. The period from 2500 BC to 2000 BC has been called the "Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age", in recognition of the difficulty of exactly defining this boundary. Some archaeologists recognise a British Chalcolithic when copper was used between the 25th and 22nd centuries BC, but others do not because production and use was on a small scale.

entries.label: Æthelberht of Kent
entries.note: Æthelberht (c. 550 – 24 February 616) King of Kent from about 589 until his death. The eighth-century monk Bede, in his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, lists him as the third king to hold imperium over other Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. In the late ninth century Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, he is referred to as a bretwalda, or "Britain-ruler". He was the first English king to convert to Christianity.

entries.label: Óengus mac Fergusa becomes King of the Picts
Offa builds Offa’s Dyke to keep out the Welsh
entries.note: A great defensive earthwork with a ditch on the Welsh side, it runs for 140 miles from the mouth of the River Dee in the north to that of the Wye in the south.

entries.label: Kenneth mac Alpin, King of the Picts
Battle of Ethandun, defeat of Viking forces, results in Treaty of Wedmore and establishment of the Danelaw
Llywelyn ap Seisyll defeats Aeddan and takes control of Gwynedd and Powys
entries.note: 1018 - Llywelyn ap Seisyll, with distant claims to Gwynedd and Deheubarth, defeats Aeddan (who is killed along with his four sons) and takes control of the kingdoms of Gwynedd and Powys.

entries.label: The Anarchy
entries.note: After Henry I died of food poisoning, the Council considered a woman unfit to rule and so offered the throne to Stephen, a grandson of William I. Over a decade of civil war known as The Anarchy ensued when Matilda invaded from Anjou in 1139.

entries.label: Thomas Becket is murdered in Canterbury Cathedral
Scottish and English populate Ulster
entries.note: 1609 - The northern area of Ulster is mostly populated by Scottish and English.

entries.label: Restoration of the Monarchy
entries.note: 1660 Restoration of the Monarchy. Two and half years after his death, Oliver Cromwell, Lord Protector of England, is disinterred and executed on 30 January 1661. His head is impaled on a 25 foot pole on the roof of Westminster Hall.

entries.label: Act of Union joins England and Scotland
First national census

entries.label: Boy Scouts movement begins

entries.label: Festival of Britain
entries.note: 1951 - Festival of Britain. Just six years after World War II, the Festival of Britain opened on the 4th May, celebrating British industry, arts and science and inspiring the thought of a better Britain.

entries.label: Scotish independence referendum
entries.note: 2014 - Scotland has a referendum on national independence. Result is to remain part of the UK, by 55% to 45%.

entries.label: Beginning of Roman withdrawal from Britain
Kingdom of Dal Riada conquers the region of Scotland
Aberdeen founded
entries.note: AD580 - Aberdeen A settlement was established by c. 580 when records show the city's first church was built then. However, there is archaeological evidence of settlements in the area dating back to 6000BC.
