entries.label: The Stolen Generation
entries.note: From 1869, children of Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander descent are removed from their families by Australian and State government agencies. This practice lasted 100 years and is known as the Stolen Generation. | 1976 - The Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 (ALRA) is Australian federal government legislation that provides the basis upon which Aboriginal Australian people in the Northern Territory can claim rights to land based on traditional occupation. It was the first law by any Australian government that legally recognised the Aboriginal system of land ownership, and legislated the concept of inalienable freehold title, as such was a fundamental piece of social reform. 1985 The government grants the freehold title of a large area of land in central Australia, including prominent landmarks Uluru and Kata Tjuta, to the Mutitjulu people, who in turn give them a 99-year lease. 1992 The High Court delivers the Mabo Decision, which rules that indigenous native title does exist. This effectively extinguishes the concept of terra nullius. 1996 The High Court hands down the Wik Decision, which holds that indigenous native title can survive the granting of pastoral leases.

entries.label: Cook claims the eastern coast of Australia for the Britain. Australia was dubbed "terra nullius"
entries.note: 1770 English Lieutenant James Cook's expedition in HMS Endeavour charted the eastern coast, and claimed it for the British Crown. Australia was dubbed "terra nullius" i.e., according to the European legal precepts of the era, it was unclaimed by any sovereign nation.

entries.label: Aboriginal Reconciliation
entries.note: 1991 - Council for Aboriginal Reconciliation Act 1991 is passed; reconciliation in Australia policy established. 1999 - Both houses of the federal parliament pass a Motion of Reconciliation signifying both recognition of and regret at past mistreatment of indigenous Australians.

entries.label: Australian Colonial period
entries.note: 1 January 1901 Six colonies of the United Kingdom formed the Commonwealth of Australia. Parliament met in Melbourne until the federal capital could be built.

entries.label: Western Australia votes to secede
entries.note: 1933 - Western Australia votes at a rerefendum to secede from the Commonwealth, but the vote is ignored by both the Commonwealth and British governments.

entries.label: Territorial Evolution
entries.note: Territorial evolution of Australia The first colonies of the British Empire on the continent of Australia were the penal colony of New South Wales, founded in 1788, and the Swan River Colony (later renamed Western Australia), founded in 1829. Over the next few decades, the colonies of New Zealand, Queensland, South Australia, Van Diemen's Land (later renamed Tasmania), and Victoria were created from New South Wales, as well as an aborted Colony of North Australia. On 1 January 1901, these colonies, excepting New Zealand, became states in the Commonwealth of Australia. Since federation, the internal borders have remained mostly stable, except for the creation of some territories with limited self-government: the Northern Territory from South Australia, to govern the vast, sparsely populated centre of the country; the split of the Northern Territory into Central Australia and North Australia, and then the quick merger of those back into the Northern Territory; and the Australian Capital Territory, a federal district ceded from New South Wales. Outside of the continent, Queensland attempted an expansion into New Guinea, but British authorities rejected this; the claim would later be made a British protectorate and ceded to Australia. The League of Nations mandated northeast New Guinea to Australia after World War I, as well as Nauru, which was placed under joint Australian-British-New Zealand jurisdiction. These mandates (and, later, United Nations trust territories) became the independent nations of Nauru and Papua New Guinea in the mid-20th century. Australia has also obtained several small island territories, mainly from earlier British colonies, and has a large claim on Antarctica.

entries.label: Colony of New South Wales
entries.note: 25 April 1787 The Colony of New South Wales was created as a penal colony by the Kingdom of Great Britain in Australia east of 135° east. This was proclaimed in Australia by Governor Arthur Phillip on 7 February 1788. The commission included "all the islands adjacent in the Pacific Ocean" within the latitudes of 10°37' south and 43°39' south, which included most of New Zealand. | 16 July 1825 New South Wales was extended west to 129° east, so that it would include a trading post set up on Melville Island; and the borders of the "islands adjacent in the Pacific Ocean" were moved north to 39°12' south, now including only a small part of New Zealand.

entries.label: Arthur Phillip
entries.note: 1792 Governor Philip returned to England, accompanied by Bennelong, who became the first Australian-born person to sail to Europe.

entries.label: Colony of Queensland
entries.note: 6 June 1859 The portion of New South Wales north of 29° south, the Dumaresq and Macintyre Rivers, and several mountain ridges, and east of 141° east, was made the Colony of Queensland. | 13 March 1862 The portion of New South Wales north of South Australia and east of 138° east was transferred to Queensland.

entries.label: Province of South Australia
entries.note: 19 February 1836 The portion of New South Wales between 132° east and 141° east, and south of 26° south, was made the Province of South Australia. The actual landing and proclamation occurred on 28 December 1836. Its border with New South Wales south of the Murray River would be erroneously surveyed roughly 3.6 kilometres (2.2 mi) west of 141° east, and the resulting disputes with the colonies and, later, states that share that border would not be fully resolved until 1914. | 10 October 1861 The portion of New South Wales west of South Australia was transferred to South Australia by letters patent. The act of parliament was passed on 22 July 1861. 6 July 1863 The region of New South Wales north of South Australia was transferred to South Australia.

entries.label: Colony of Van Diemen's Land
entries.note: 3 Dec 1825 The southern islands of New South Wales were made the Colony of Van Diemen's Land. | 1 January 1856 Van Diemen's Land was renamed Tasmania, as a way to get away from its past as a penal colony.

entries.label: Colony of Victoria
entries.note: 1 July 1851 The portion of New South Wales south of the Murray River and a line from the headwaters of the river to Cape Howe was made the Colony of Victoria.

entries.label: Colony of Western Australia
entries.note: 2 May 1829 A colony commonly known as the Swan River Colony was founded in the remainder of Australia outside of New South Wales. Most documents calling for the colony's foundation make no mention of a name, apart from its location at the "Port on the Western Coast of New Holland, at the Mouth of the River called 'Swan River', with the adjacent Territory", and that a settlement should be formed "within the Territory of 'Western Australia'". However, the law calling for the creation of the colony does appear to specify that it should be called "Western Australia". | 6 February 1832 The legal instrument required to formally appoint James Stirling governor of the Colony of Western Australia was proclaimed, and this is commonly held as the date that the Swan River Colony was renamed Western Australia.

entries.label: Macquarie Island discovered
entries.note: 11 July 1810 Macquarie Island was discovered by Frederick Hasselborough, who claimed it for the United Kingdom and declared it part of New South Wales.

entries.label: Colony of North Australia
entries.note: 17 February 1846 The half of New South Wales north of 26° south was made the Colony of North Australia. 28 December 1847 Following a change in government in the United Kingdom, North Australia was merged back in to New South Wales. This is the date Queen Victoria revoked the letters patent establishing North Australia, but it was not proclaimed in Australia until 16 January 1849.

entries.label: Overland Telegraph Line opened
entries.note: 1872 The Overland Telegraph Line linking Darwin and Adelaide opened.

entries.label: Federal Capital Territory
entries.note: 1 January 1911 The Federal Capital Territory was split from New South Wales. While the acts creating it use the term "Territory for the Seat of Government", legislation and proclamations immediately began using the term "Federal Capital Territory." | 4 September 1915 A small peninsula along Jervis Bay was ceded to the Federal Capital Territory by New South Wales. | 29 July 1938 The Federal Capital Territory was renamed the Australian Capital Territory.

entries.label: Australian Capital Territory
entries.note: 31 December 1973 The peninsula along Jervis Bay belonging to the Australian Capital Territory was formally named the Jervis Bay Territory; at this time, it was still considered part of the ACT.

entries.label: Northern Territory
entries.note: 1 January 1911 The Northern Territory was split from South Australia. | 12 June 1931 The territories of Central Australia and North Australia were merged to become the Northern Territory.

entries.label: The First Fleet departs from Great Britain
entries.note: 1787 The First Fleet of 11 ships, led by Governor Arthur Phillip, departed from Great Britain for Australia to begin European colonisation.

entries.label: HMS Beagle sails into Darwin Harbour
entries.note: 1839 HMS Beagle sailed into Darwin Harbour during its surveying of the area. John Clements Wickham named the area Port Darwin in honour of their former shipmate Charles Darwin. The settlement became the town of Palmerston in 1869 and was renamed Darwin in 1911.

entries.label: Ned Kelly hanged at Melbourne Gaol
Central Australia Territory
entries.note: 1 February 1927 The Northern Territory was split at 20° south into the territories of Central Australia and North Australia.

entries.label: Jarvis Bay Territory
entries.note: 11 May 1989 Jervis Bay Territory was split from the Australian Capital Territory to become its own territory.

entries.label: The ship Supply reaches Botany Bay
Norfolk Island transferred
entries.note: 26 September 1844 Norfolk Island transferred from New South Wales to Van Diemen's Land.

entries.label: Macquarie Island transferred
entries.note: 17 June 1890 Macquarie Island was transferred from New South Wales to Tasmania; while Tasmania immediately requested it then be transferred to New Zealand, this was not done.

entries.label: Phillip reaches Port Jackson and Sydney Cove
Colony of Norfolk Island
entries.note: 1 November 1856 Norfolk Island was split from Tasmania, becoming its own colony.

entries.label: Constitution developed
entries.note: 1890 - The Australian Federation Conference called a constitutional convention. 1891 - A National Australasian Convention met and agreed on adopting the name "the Commonwealth of Australia," also drafting a constitution. The first attempt at a federal constitution was drafted. The Convention adopts the constitution, although it had no legal status. 1893 - The Corowa Conference (the "people's convention") called on the colonial parliaments to pass enabling acts, allowing the election of delegates to a new constitutional convention aimed at drafting a proposal and putting it to a referendum in each colony. 1895 - The premiers, except for those of Queensland and Western Australia, agreed to implement the Corowa proposals. 1896 - The Bathurst Conference (the second "people's convention") met to discuss the 1891 draft constitution. 1897 - In two sessions, the Second National Australasian Convention met (with representatives from all colonies except Queensland present). They agreed to adopt a constitution based on 1891 draft, and then revised and amended it later that year. Catherine Helen Spence became the first female political candidate for political office, standing for election as a representative for South Australia. 1898 - The Convention agreed on a final draft to be put to the people. 1900 - The constitution was passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom as a schedule to the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act, and was given royal assent.

entries.label: Australian Antarctic Territory
entries.note: 13 June 1933 The United Kingdom transferred the portion of its claim to Antarctica between 45° east and 136° east, and 142° east and 160° east, to Australia, where it became the Australian Antarctic Territory.

entries.label: 26 January 1788 - Phillip proclaimed British sovereignty over New South Wales
entries.note: 26 January 1788 Early in the morning, Captain Phillip took a party ashore at Sydney Cove, raised the British colours and formally proclaimed British sovereignty over New South Wales. In a ceremony at sunset Phillip and the officers drank to the health of the king and the royal family, and success to the new colony. This day is now celebrated as Australia Day.

entries.label: Islands off Qld coast annexed
entries.note: 30 May 1872 All islands lying within 60 miles (97 km) of Queensland were annexed to the colony by letters patent. This was done primarily to incorporate the Torres Strait Islands, which were starting to be claimed by New South Wales. It is unknown which specific islands may have already been considered part of Queensland, and the map included with the letters patent contained errors, such as including Melville Island in Queensland.

entries.label: Territory of Norfolk Island
entries.note: 1 July 1914 Norfolk Island was transferred from the United Kingdom, becoming the Territory of Norfolk Island.

entries.label: Territory of Christmas Island
entries.note: 1 October 1958 Christmas Island was transferred from the United Kingdom, becoming the Territory of Christmas Island.

entries.label: First religious service held
entries.note: 1788 Rev. Richard Johnson held the colony's first religious service ‘on the grass’. Rev. Johnson celebrated Holy Communion for the first time in the colony, according to the rites of the church of England. The Communion took place in the tent of Lt. Ralph Clark. Lt. Henry Ball, commander of the Supply on its way to Norfolk Island, discovered an island that he named after Admiral Lord Howe.

entries.label: Penal colony founded at Moreton Bay (Brisbane)
Torres Strait Islands annexed
entries.note: 21 July 1879 The Torres Strait Islands were specifically annexed to Queensland.

entries.label: Territory of Ashmore and Cartier Islands
entries.note: 10 May 1934 The Ashmore and Cartier Islands were transferred from the United Kingdom and became the Territory of Ashmore and Cartier Islands. A British order-in-council dated 23 July 1931 had stated that the islands would be placed under the authority of the Commonwealth of Australia when Australia passed legislation to accept them. 29 July 1938 The Territory of Ashmore and Cartier Islands was annexed to the Northern Territory. 1 July 1978 The Ashmore and Cartier Islands were split from the Northern Territory, becoming the Territory of Ashmore and Cartier Islands.

entries.label: First criminal court held
entries.note: At the first criminal court, Samuel Barnsley was sentenced to 150 lashes for assault and Thomas Hill to confinement in irons on a small rocky island at the head of the cove for stealing bread.

entries.label: Blaxland, Lawson and Wentworth cross the Blue Mountains
Uluru first sighted
entries.note: Uluru was first sighted by Europeans, and named Ayers Rock.

entries.label: White Australia policy
entries.note: 1901 - The Immigration Restriction Act was introduced forming the basis of the White Australia policy

entries.label: Heard Island and McDonald Islands
entries.note: 26 December 1947 Heard Island and McDonald Islands were transferred from the United Kingdom. The receipt was confirmed in letters exchanged on 19 December 1950. 24 April 1953 Heard Island and McDonald Islands were formally declared the Territory of Heard Island and McDonald Islands.

entries.label: First execution
entries.note: Thomas Barratt was hanged for stealing in stores, the first execution.

entries.label: The name 'Australia' used by Matthew Flinders
Burke and Wills expedition
entries.note: 1860–61 – Robert O'Hara Burke and William Wills are the first to cross Australia from south to north, traveling from Melbourne to the Flinders River.

entries.label: Breaker Morant is executed
entries.note: 1902 Breaker Morant is executed for having shot Boers who had surrendered.

entries.label: Territory of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands
entries.note: 23 November 1955 The Cocos (Keeling) Islands were transferred by the United Kingdom from the Colony of Singapore, becoming the Territory of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.

entries.label: Norfolk Island settlement
entries.note: Lt. Philip Gidley King takes possession of Norfolk Island. British settlement founded.

entries.label: New Holland becomes Australia
entries.note: 1824 Permission was granted to change the name of the continent from "New Holland" to "Australia". Previously, in 1817, Governor Lachlan Macquarie had petitioned the British Admiralty to use the name "Australia" instead of "New Holland".

entries.label: Last convict ship arrives in Australia
Mandate of Nauru
entries.note: 17 December 1920 The League of Nations mandated the Mandate of Nauru, with New Zealand and the United Kingdom as co-trustees of Nauru. | The Mandate of Nauru was captured by Japan. | The Japanese garrison in the Mandate of Nauru surrendered. | 1 November 1947 The Mandate of Nauru was reconstituted as the United Nations Trust Territory of Nauru. | 31 January 1968 The Trust Territory of Nauru became independent as the Republic of Nauru.

entries.label: Hume and Hovell expedition encounters the Murray River
entries.note: 1824 The Hume and Hovell expedition travelled overland to Port Phillip Bay and encountered the Murray River.

entries.label: High Court is established
entries.note: 1903 The High Court of Australia is established with Samuel Griffith as the first Chief Justice.

entries.label: Coral Sea Islands Territory
entries.note: 30 September 1969 The Coral Sea Islands Territory was created from Queensland. 7 July 1997 Elizabeth Reef and Middleton Reef were transferred from New South Wales to the Coral Sea Islands Territory.

entries.label: The whole of Australia claimed as British territory
entries.note: The whole of Australia was claimed as British territory when Major Edmund Lockyer formally annexed the western portion in a ceremony at King George Sound. In 1829 Captain Charles Fremantle took possession of the western side of Australia for the British crown.

entries.label: First Test Cricket match
entries.note: 1877 - The first internationally recognised game of Test Cricket is played between Australia and England at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG).

entries.label: Territory of Papua
entries.note: aohara: 1 September 1906 British New Guinea was transferred from the United Kingdom, becoming the Territory of Papua. | 1 July 1949 The Territory of New Guinea and Territory of Papua were merged into the Territory of Papua and New Guinea, mainly for administrative purposes. The act makes it clear that the identities of New Guinea as a United Nations Trust Territory and Papua as a possession of the Crown remain intact.

entries.label: Territory of Papua and New Guinea
entries.note: 27 December 1971 The Territory of Papua and New Guinea was renamed Papua New Guinea.

entries.label: The Aboriginal man Arabanoo captured and held in confinement
entries.note: Because the Aboriginal Australians could not be coaxed into the settlement, one named Arabanoo was captured and held in confinement. Phillip hoped to learn his language and so to promote good relations between Aboriginal Australians and Europeans.

entries.label: Queensland claims New Guinea
entries.note: 4 April 1883 Queensland claimed southeast New Guinea as a dependency, though the British government rejected the claim. 6 November 1884 The British Empire declared southeast New Guinea as a protectorate, removing it from immediate Queensland control, though the colony still largely administered it.

entries.label: Territory of New Guinea
entries.note: 17 December 1920 The League of Nations mandated the former German New Guinea to Australia as the Territory of New Guinea. | 13 December 1946 The Territory of New Guinea was reconstituted as a United Nations trust territory.

entries.label: Papua New Guinea gains independence
entries.note: 11 September 1975 The Republic of the North Solomons declared the independence of the region surrounding Bougainville Island in Papua New Guinea. 16 September 1975 Papua New Guinea became independent as the Independent State of Papua New Guinea, rendering the dispute with the Republic of the North Solomons moot.

entries.label: Charles Sturt charts the Darling and Murray Rivers
New Parliament House opens in Canberra
The Black Line
entries.note: The Black Line A huge six-week military offensive, is launched, using moving cordons to drive all Aboriginal Tasmanians from the colony's settled districts to the Tasman Peninsula.

entries.label: Right to vote
entries.note: 1855 - South Australias men 1857 - Victorian men 1858 - New South Wales men

entries.label: Harold Holt
entries.note: 1967 - Prime Minister Harold Holt disappears while swimming at Cheviot Beach, Victoria

entries.label: The Sydney Morning Herald) was published
entries.note: 1831 The Sydney Herald (later to become The Sydney Morning Herald) was first published.

entries.label: Sydney
entries.note: Oldest city in Australia

entries.label: Strzelecki climbs Mount Kosciuszko
entries.note: 1839 Paul Edmund Strzelecki became the first European to ascend and name Australia's highest peak, Mount Kosciuszko.

entries.label: Parramatta
entries.note: Second oldest settlement in Australia

entries.label: John Oxley charts the Lachlan and Macquarie Rivers
Kingston, Norfolk Island
entries.note: Norfolk Island was settled as part of the Colony of New South Wales. It is now a separate territory of Australia.

entries.label: Australia's first bank opened
entries.note: 1817 Australia's first bank, the Bank of New South Wales, opened in Macquarie Place, Sydney. (The bank became Westpac in 1982).

entries.label: Victorian gold rush starts
entries.note: 1851 - The Victorian gold rush started when gold was found at Summerhill Creek and Ballarat.

entries.label: Windsor
entries.note: Windsor, NSW Third-oldest place of British settlement on the Australian continent.

entries.label: Bathurst
entries.note: Oldest inland settlement in Australia

entries.label: Australia's first political party established
entries.note: 1835 - William Wentworth established Australian Patriotic Association, Australia's first political party, to demand democracy for New South Wales.

entries.label: Adelaide
entries.note: In 1840, the City of Adelaide becomes Australia's first municipal authority followed by Sydney City Council.

entries.label: Tharwa
entries.note: Oldest official settlement in the Australian Capital Territory.

entries.label: Hobart
entries.note: Second oldest city in Australia

entries.label: The Tolpuddle Martyrs are transported to Sydney and Hobart
Statute of Westminster adopted
entries.note: 1942 - The UK Statute of Westminster is formally adopted by Australia. The Statute formally grants Australia the right to pass laws that conflict with UK laws.

entries.label: Australia Act 1986
entries.note: 3 March 1986 The Australia Act 1986 made Australia completely independent of the United Kingdom. The Act removed the right of appeal from State courts to the British Privy Council, making the High Court the final court of appeal in Australia. The Act also removes all remaining rights of the UK parliament to pass law for Australia.

entries.label: Newcastle
entries.note: Third oldest city in Australia

entries.label: Prussian settlers arrive
entries.note: The largest group of non-British migrants in Australia at the time, arrive in South Australia.

entries.label: Tenterfield Oration
entries.note: The Tenterfield Oration was a speech given by Sir Henry Parkes, Premier of the Colony of New South Wales at the Tenterfield School of Arts in Tenterfield, in rural New South Wales, Australia, on 24 October 1889. In the Oration, Parkes called for the Federation of the six Australian colonies, which were at the time self-governing but under the distant central authority of the British Colonial Secretary. The speech is considered to be the start of the federation process in Australia, which led to the foundation of the Commonwealth of Australia 12 years later.

entries.label: Canberra
entries.note: In 1912, Walter Burley Griffin wins a design competition for the new city of Canberra.

entries.label: Sydney Opera House construction
entries.note: 1973 The Sydney Opera House formally opened by Elizabeth II.

entries.label: Launceston
entries.note: Fourth oldest city in Australia

entries.label: First parliamentary elections in New South Wales
entries.note: 1843 Australia's first parliamentary elections was held for the New South Wales Legislative Council (though voting rights are restricted to males of certain wealth or property).

entries.label: Banjo Paterson publishes "The Man from Snowy River"
Cowra breakout
entries.note: 1944 Cowra breakout, mass escape of Japanese prisoners of war occurs in NSW.

entries.label: Indigenous Australian suffrage
entries.note: The Commonwealth Electoral Act provided that all Indigenous Australians should have the right to enrol and vote at federal elections, removing remaining restrictions applying in QLD, WA and NT.

entries.label: The Cataraqui is wrecked off King Island
entries.note: 1845 The ship Cataraqui was wrecked off King Island in Bass Strait. It is Australia's worst civil maritime disaster, with 406 lives lost.

entries.label: Womens' Suffrage
entries.note: 1894 South Australia became the first Australian colony, and the second place in the world, to grant women the right to vote, as well the first Parliament in the world to allow women to stand for office with the Constitutional Amendment (Adult Suffrage) Act 1894.

entries.label: Battle of Beersheba
entries.note: 1917 - Battle of Beersheba: Australian 4th Light Horse Brigade launches last cavalry charge in modern warfare to capture Beersheba from the Ottoman Turks.

entries.label: Japanese air raids
entries.note: 1942 Japanese air raids – almost 100 attacks against sites in the Northern Territory, Western Australia and Queensland (to 1943). Bombing of Darwin sees largest attack on Australia by a foreign power.

entries.label: Voyager incident
entries.note: 82 sailors die when HMAS Voyager sinks after collision with the aircraft carrier HMAS Melbourne.

entries.label: Redcliff
entries.note: First European settlement in Queensland

entries.label: Portland
entries.note: Oldest European settlement in Victoria.

entries.label: Western Australia became a penal colony
The first national census is conducted
Daylight saving introduced
entries.note: Daylight saving is introduced to New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia and the Australian Capital Territory.

entries.label: Albany
entries.note: Oldest city in the West Coast of Australia

entries.label: Australian Colonies Government Act [1850]
entries.note: The Australian Colonies Government Act [1850] granted representative constitutions to New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Tasmania. These colonies set about writing constitutions which produced democratically progressive parliaments.

entries.label: Australian soldiers first fight under the Australian flag
Neville Bonner elected to Parliament
entries.note: 1971 - Neville Bonner becomes the first Aborigine to become an Australian Member of Parliament.

entries.label: Brisbane
entries.note: Fifth oldest city in Australia

entries.label: Melbourne
entries.note: John Batman and John Pascoe Fawkner establish a settlement at Port Phillip, now the city of Melbourne.

entries.label: Australia's first university, the University of Sydney founded
Penicillin developed
entries.note: 1940 A team of scientists, under Howard Florey, develops penicillin.

entries.label: Port Arthur
entries.note: Founded as a penal settlement.

entries.label: First paddle steamers on Murray River
entries.note: First paddle steamers on Murray River on the spring flood. From South Australia, the Lady Augusta captained by Francis Cadell, reached Swan Hill while Mary Ann captained by William Randell, made it as far as Moama (near Echuca).

entries.label: Signing of the Treaty of Versailles
entries.note: 1919 - Prime Minister Billy Hughes signs Treaty of Versailles: the first signing of an international treaty by Australia.

entries.label: Aboriginal Tent Embassy erected
entries.note: 1972 Aboriginal Tent Embassy erected in response to the Coalition government's approval of exploration licences and mining tenements on reserves.

entries.label: Bendigo Petition and Red Ribbon Rebellion at Bendigo
Transportation of convicts to Norfolk Island ceases
Edith Cowan becomes the first woman parliamentarian
National Gallery of Australia is opened
Sydney and Melbourne are linked by electric telegraph
The Smith Family charity is founded in Sydney
White Australian Policy is officially dismantled
Australian rules football codified
entries.note: Melbourne Football Club is founded.

entries.label: John McDouall Stuart reached the centre of the continent
entries.note: He later reaches Port Darwin in 1862.

entries.label: Last legally execution
entries.note: 1967 - Ronald Ryan becomes the last person legally executed in Australia.

entries.label: Female leaders elected
entries.note: 1989 - Rosemary Follett (Australian Labor Party) becomes the first Chief Minister of the Australian Capital Territory and the first woman to become head of government in an Australian state or territory. 1990 - Carmen Lawrence becomes the first female premier of an Australian state.

entries.label: Phar Lap wins the Melbourne Cup
Vietnam War demonstrations
entries.note: 1969 - More than 200,000 people participate in the largest demonstrations in Australian history, against the Vietnam War.

entries.label: John Macarthur
entries.note: John Macarthur (1767 – 11 April 1834) British Army officer, racketeer, entrepreneur, grazier, usurper, politician, and highly influential figure in the early British colonisation of New South Wales. Macarthur is recognised as the pioneer of the Australian Merino wool industry. He was instrumental in agitating for, and organising, a rebellion against the colonial government in what is often described as the Rum Rebellion.

entries.label: Transportation of convicts to Western Australia ceases
Aboriginal Australians to be included in the population count
entries.note: 1967 The constitution is changed to allow Aboriginal Australians to be included in the population count and for the federal government to legislate for them.

entries.label: Railway network
entries.note: 1883 - The opening of the Sydney–Melbourne railway. 1883 - The first direct Inter-colonial passenger trains began running between Adelaide and Melbourne. 1889 - The completion of the railway network between Adelaide, Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney. 1917 - Transcontinental railway linking Adelaide to Perth is completed.

entries.label: Douglas Mawson charts the Antarctic coastline
entries.note: 1931 - Sir Douglas Mawson charts 4,000 miles of Antarctic coastline and claims 42% of the continent for Australia.

entries.label: H. V. McKay
entries.note: Hugh Victor McKay CBE (21 August 1865 – 21 May 1926) Australian industrialist who is known for heading the company that developed the Sunshine Harvester, arguably the first commercially viable combine harvester. He subsequently established the Sunshine Harvester Works, which became one of Australia's largest manufacturers of agricultural equipment.

entries.label: Battle of Kokoda Trail
entries.note: Battle of Kokoda Trail: Australian soldiers halt Japanese march on Port Moresby.

entries.label: Patrick White wins the Nobel Prize in Literature
Bert Hinkler
entries.note: Herbert John Louis Hinkler AFC, DSM (8 December 1892 – 7 January 1933), better known as Bert Hinkler, was a pioneer Australian aviator (dubbed "Australian Lone Eagle") and inventor. He designed and built early aircraft before being the first person to fly solo from England to Australia, and the first person to fly solo across the Southern Atlantic Ocean. He married in 1932 at the age of 39, and died less than a year later after crashing into remote countryside near Florence, Italy during a solo flight record attempt. | Bert Hinkler makes the first flight from Britain to Australia.

entries.label: Donald Bradman
entries.note: 1930 New South Wales batsman Don Bradman scores a world record first-class individual innings of 452 not out in a Sheffield Shield match against Queensland In the Third Test at Leeds against England, Don Bradman scored a Hundred before Tea, a Hundred before lunch, and a Hundred by the end of the day's play, 309 in Total. He went on to make 334. Altogether in his 52 Test career, Bradman scored 29 Hundreds, 12 Double Hundreds and 2 Triple Hundreds. This is therefore the fastest Triple Hundred in Test History.

entries.label: Charles Kingsford Smith
entries.note: Charles Kingsford Smith makes the first flight from the U.S. to Australia.

entries.label: Australian citizenship
entries.note: 1949 - The Nationality and Citizenship Act is passed. Rather than being identified as subjects of Britain, the Act established Australian citizenship for people who met eligibility requirements.

entries.label: Gough Whitlam dismissed
entries.note: 1975 - A constitutional crisis occurs when Malcolm Fraser delays supply, threatening a government shutdown until Governor-General John Kerr dismisses Prime Minister Gough Whitlam on 11 November 1975. Kerr then appointed Malcolm Fraser, Leader of the Opposition, as caretaker Prime Minister.

entries.label: Disappearance of Azaria Chamberlain
entries.note: 1980 - Baby Azaria Chamberlain disappears from a campsite at Uluru (Ayers Rock), reportedly taken by a dingo.

entries.label: Heidelberg

entries.label: Eternity
entries.note: Arthur Malcolm Stace (9 February 1885 – 30 July 1967), known as Mr Eternity, was an Australian soldier. He was an alcoholic from his teenage years until the early 1930s, when he converted to Christianity and began to spread his message by inscribing the word "Eternity" in copperplate writing with yellow chalk on footpaths and doorsteps in and around Sydney, from Martin Place to Parramatta, from 1932 to his death in 1967.
