NT in 1380 OT in 1382 (with help of Nicholas of Hereford) Translations into Middle English, 1st complete translation to English, included deuterocanonical books, preached against abuses, expressed anti-catholic views of the sacraments (Penance and Eucharist), the use of relics, and Clerical celibacy

entries.label: Martin Luther
entries.note: Martin Luther OSA (10 November 1483 – 18 February 1546) German monk, Catholic priest, professor of theology and seminal figure of the 16th-century movement in Christianity known later as the Protestant Reformation. He strongly disputed the claim that freedom from God's punishment for sin could be purchased with monetary values. He confronted indulgence salesman Johann Tetzel, a Dominican friar, with his Ninety-Five Theses in 1517. His refusal to retract all of his writings at the demand of Pope Leo X in 1520 and the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms in 1521 resulted in his excommunication by the Pope and condemnation as an outlaw by the Emperor. | AD1518 - Heidelberg Disputation, Martin Luther puts forth his Theology of the Cross. AD1519 - Leipzig Debate between Martin Luther and Johann Eck. AD1520 - Luther publishes three monumental works, To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church, and On the Freedom of a Christian. AD1522 - Luther's NT, German NT translation. | AD1528 - Luther affirms the real presence of Christ's body and blood in his Confession Concerning Christ's Supper. | AD1549 - original Book of Common Prayer of the Church of England by Thomas Cranmer.

entries.label: Edict of Fontainebleau
entries.note: AD1685 - Edict of Fontainebleau outlaws Protestantism in France.

entries.label: Revised Version Bible
entries.note: 1881-1894 Revised Version, called for by Church of England, used Greek based on Septuagint (B) and (S), Hebrew Masoretic Text used in OT; follows Greek order of words, greater accuracy than AV, includes Apocrypha; scholarship never disputed.

entries.label: The cult of Cybele is introduced to Rome from Pessinus
Marcionite missions are sent to Asia Minor, Syria, and Mesopotamia
Anti-Caecilianists appeal to Constantine; Council of Rome vindicates Caecilian
Tome of Leo
entries.note: Leo's Tome refers to a letter sent by Pope Leo I to the Council of Chalcedon explaining the position of the Papacy in matters of Christology. The text confessed that Christ had two natures, and was not of or from two natures.

entries.label: Mission of the nine saints to Ethiopia.
Replacement of the Great Dome of Hagia Sophia
Pantheon renamed Church of Santa Maria Rotonda
Alexius appeals to Pope Urban II and Western princes
Pope Boniface VIII seized at Anagni
entries.note: AD1303 - Pope Boniface VIII is seized by his enemies at Anagni and, although soon freed, dies later that same year.

entries.label: Martin Luther's ninety-five theses
entries.note: AD1517 - The Reformation begins with Martin Luther nailing his ninety-five theses to the door of the church in Wittenberg, Germany.

entries.label: Ukrainian Catholic Church forms
entries.note: AD1596 - Ukrainian Catholic Church forms when Ukrainian subjects of the king of Poland are reunited with Rome, largest Byzantine Catholic Church.

entries.label: Collegium
entries.note: A collegium (plural collegia, "joined together"; English "college") was any association in ancient Rome with a legal personality. There were four great religious colleges (quattuor amplissima collegia) of Roman priests, in descending order of importance: Pontifices Augures Quindecimviri Epulones

entries.label: Ordo Sacerdotum
entries.note: Ordo Sacerdotum A religious hierarchy implied by the seating arrangements of priests (sacerdotes) at sacrificial banquets. As "the most powerful", the rex sacrorum was positioned next to the gods, followed by the Flamen Dialis, then the Flamen Martialis, then the Flamen Quirinalisand lastly, the Pontifex Maximus. The ordo sacerdotum observed and preserved ritual distinctions between divine and human power. In the human world, the Pontifex Maximus was the most influential and powerful of all sacerdotes.

entries.label: Imperial rescripts concerning treatment of Christians
entries.note: c. AD 140–160 - imperial rescripts are issued concerning treatment of Christians in Macedonia and Achaea.

entries.label: Pope deported to Sardinia
entries.note: AD235 - Emperor Maximinus Thrax, ends Christian schism in Rome by deporting Pope Pontian and Antipope Hippolytus to Sardinia where they soon die.

entries.label: Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre founded
entries.note: The Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre, or The Holy Community of the All-Holy Sepulchre (founded AD 313), is the Orthodox monastic fraternity that for centuries has guarded and protected the Christian Holy places in the Holy Land. The Brotherhood also administers the Greek Orthodox Church of Jerusalem. The Greek Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem is the chief, president, governor, and hegumen of the Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre.

entries.label: Platonic Academy closed
entries.note: Justinian closes the Platonic Academy in 529; Often sited as the end of Antiquity

entries.label: Byzantine Iconoclasm
entries.note: The Byzantine Iconoclasm refers to two periods in the history of the Byzantine Empire when the use of religious images or icons was opposed by religious and imperial authorities within the Eastern Church and the temporal imperial hierarchy. The "First Iconoclasm", as it is sometimes called, lasted between about 726 and 787. The "Second Iconoclasm" was between 814 and 842. According to the traditional view, Byzantine Iconoclasm constituted a ban on religious images by Emperor Leo III (Pope Gregory II excommunicates him) and continued under his successors. It was accompanied by widespread destruction of images and persecution of supporters of the veneration of images. The Western church remained firmly in support of the use of images throughout the period, and the whole episode widened the growing divergence between the East and Western traditions in what was still a unified church, as well as facilitating the reduction or removal of Byzantine political control over parts of Italy.

entries.label: Cluniac Reforms
entries.note: The Cluniac Reforms were a series of changes within medieval monasticism of the Western Church focused on restoring the traditional monastic life, encouraging art, and caring for the poor. The movement was founded at Cluny in 910 by Duke William I (875-918), where it started within the Benedictine order. The reforms were largely carried out by Saint Odo (c. 878 – 942) and spread throughout France (Burgundy, Provence, Auvergne, Poitou), into England, and through much of Italy and Spain.

entries.label: Diet of Worms
entries.note: The Diet of Worms 1521 An imperial diet of the Holy Roman Empire held in Worms, Germany at the Heylshof Garden, (a "diet" being a formal deliberative assembly). It is most memorable for the Edict of Worms, which addressed Martin Luther and the effects of the Protestant Reformation. It was conducted from 28 January to 25 May 1521, with Emperor Charles V presiding. Luther refused to recant his works and was subsequently excommunicated. Other imperial diets at Worms were convened in the years 829, 926, 1076, 1122, 1495, and 1545. Unqualified mentions of a Diet of Worms usually refer to the 1521 assembly.

entries.label: Peace of Augsburg
entries.note: AD1555 - Peace of Augsburg gives religious freedom in Germany only to Lutheran Protestants.

entries.label: King James Bible
entries.note: AD1611 - King James Version (Authorised Version) is published, based primarily on Tyndale's work and Bishop's Bible of 1572, first printings included separate Apocrypha between the testaments.

entries.label: The Piazza of St Peter's is built in Rome
Sacrifice test in Bithynia
entries.note: AD 112–113 - Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia, corresponds with Trajan regarding Christians and makes the first report of the use of the sacrifice test.

entries.label: as Emperor
entries.note: AD 330 - Dedication of Constantinople, the “New Rome,” as the Christian capital. | AD 337 - Baptism of Constantine I by an Arian bishop.

entries.label: Council of Carthage; “Catholic” ascendency in North Africa
Attila delivers ultimatum to Court of Ravenna
Justinian purges the Roman administration of pagans
Christianity in China
entries.note: c. AD635 - The first documentation of Christianity entering China was written on an 8th-century stone tablet known as the Nestorian Stele. It records that Christians reached the Tang dynasty capital Xian in 635 and were allowed to establish places of worship and to propagate their faith. The leader of the Christian travelers was Alopen.

entries.label: Popular Crusade
entries.note: AD 1096–1097 - Massacres of Jews in Rhine Valley by Popular Crusade. AD 1096 - People’s Crusade under Peter the Hermit; Hugh of Vermandois and Godfrey of Bouillon arrive at Constantinople.

entries.label: Albigensian Crusade
entries.note: AD1208 - Pope Innocent III preaches Albigensian Crusade (1208–1229).

entries.label: Spanish Inquisition established
entries.note: AD1478 - Spanish Inquisition established by Pope Sixtus IV and King Ferdinand II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile.

entries.label: Excommunication of Martin Luther
entries.note: AD1521 - Papal bull Decet Romanum Pontificem, It Pleases the Roman Pontiff, excommunicates Luther.

entries.label: Collegium Pontificum
entries.note: The College of Pontiffs (Collegium Pontificum) A body of the ancient Roman state whose members were the highest-ranking priests of the state religion.

entries.label: Quindecimviri Sacris Faciundis
entries.note: The quindecimviri sacris faciundis were the fifteen (quindecim) members of a college (collegium) with priestly duties. Most notably they guarded the Sibylline Books, scriptures which they consulted and interpreted at the request of the Senate. This collegium also oversaw the worship of any foreign gods which were introduced to Rome.

entries.label: Apostolic Succession
entries.note: Apostolic Succession An early understanding of apostolic succession is represented by the traditional claims of various churches, as organised around important episcopal sees, to have been founded by specific apostles. On the basis of these traditions, the churches claim to have inherited specific authority, doctrines and/or practices on the authority of their founding apostle(s), which is understood to be continued by the bishops of the apostolic throne of the church that each founded and whose original leader he was.

entries.label: Hadrian’s Rescript concerning toleration of Christians
entries.note: AD 124 - Issuance of Hadrian’s Rescript to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, concerning toleration of Christians.

entries.label: Diocletian Persecution
entries.note: AD 303 - Diocletian issues three edicts of persecution of Christians, initiating the Great Persecution. AD 304 - Diocletian’s fourth edict of persecution is issued, ordering general sacrifice; apostasy of Pope Marcellinus. 306 Fifth edict of persecution is issued in the East; Maximinus II reorganizes pagan cults in the East; Constantius I orders toleration for Christians in Rome and Africa. 308 Sixth edict of persecution in the East.

entries.label: Outbreak of Priscillianism dispute in Spain
Attila the Hun is turned away from Rome by Pope Leo I
Filioque clause is added to Nicene Creed
Northern Crusades
entries.note: The Northern Crusades or Baltic Crusades were crusades undertaken by the Christian kings of Denmark and Sweden, the German Livonian and Teutonic military orders, and their allies against the pagan peoples of Northern Europe around the southern and eastern shores of the Baltic Sea. The official starting point for the Northern Crusades was Pope Celestine III's call in 1193; but the Christian kingdoms of Scandinavia and the Holy Roman Empire had begun moving to subjugate their pagan neighbors even earlier. Swedish and German Catholic campaigns against Russian Eastern Orthodox Christians are also sometimes considered part of the Northern Crusades.

entries.label: Tomás de Torquemada as Grand Inquisitor
Augsburg Confession
entries.note: AD1530 - Augsburg Confession, first doctrinal statement of the Lutheran Church.

entries.label: Baptist Church founded by John Smyth
entries.note: AD1609 - Baptist Church founded by John Smyth (c. 1570 – c. 28 August 1612), due to objections to infant baptism and demands for church-state separation.

entries.label: Persecutions in the East
entries.note: AD 311 - Rigorous persecutions by Maximinus in the East.

entries.label: Ban on pagan sacrifice
entries.note: AD341 – Constans and Constantius II issue a ban against pagan sacrifice.

entries.label: Dispute between Patriarch Flavian of Constantinople and Eutyches
entries.note: 446 Dispute between Patriarch Flavian of Constantinople and Eutyches; Dioscurus supports Eutyches; renewal of the Christological Controversy 448 Condemnation of Eutyches by Home Synod 449 Dioscurus proclaims the Monophysite Christology during the Latrocinium (“Robber Council”) of Ephesus

entries.label: Fulbert of Chartres
entries.note: Fulbert of Chartres (952-970 –10 April 1028) Bishop of the Cathedral of Chartres from 1006 till 1028. He was a teacher at the Cathedral school there, he was responsible for the advancement of the celebration of the Nativity of the Virgin feast day, and he was responsible for one of the many reconstructions of the Cathedral. Most of the information we have about him is found in the letters he wrote from 1004–1028, to both secular and religious figures of the day.

entries.label: County of Edessa (1098 to 1149)
entries.note: AD 1098 - Baldwin establishes the County of Edessa

entries.label: Latin Empire of Constantinople
entries.note: AD1204 – Crusaders sack Constantinople and establish the Latin Empire of Constantinople.

entries.label: Thirty-Nine Articles of Church of England
entries.note: The Thirty-Nine Articles of Religion are the historically defining statements of doctrines of the Church of England with respect to the controversies of the English Reformation. First established in 1563, the articles served to define the doctrine of the Church of England as it related to Calvinist doctrine and Roman Catholic practice. The full name for the articles is commonly abbreviated as the Thirty-Nine Articles or the XXXIX Articles.

entries.label: Formation of the World Council of Churches
Journeys of Paul
entries.note: Journeys of Paul 46–48 First Missionary Journey of Paul and Barnabas; churches founded in Cyprus, Galatia, and Pisidia. 49–52 Second missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas; churches are founded in cities of Asia and Bithynia; first missions to Greece (Philippi, Beroea, Athens, and Corinth). 53–56 Paul’s mission at Ephesus; organization of churches in the Maeander Valley, including Colossae and perhaps Laodicea ad Lycum. 56–57 Paul’s tour of inspection of Corinth, Philippi, Thessalonica, Troas, and the Aegean islands. 58 Departure of Paul from Miletus to Jerusalem; arrest and imprisonment of Paul at Jerusalem. 59–60 Paul’s journey to Rome. 60–62 Paul in Rome.

entries.label: Sporadic Christian persecutions
entries.note: c. AD 165–175 - Sporadic persecutions of Christians in the cities of western Asia Minor.

entries.label: Decian persecution
entries.note: AD 250–251 - Decian persecution begins as general orders for sacrifice are circulated throughout the empire and Christian leaders are arrested; Cyprian flees Carthage; Dionysius flees Alexandria; Pope Fabian is arrested and executed.

entries.label: Forced resignations
entries.note: AD298–302 - Christians are forced to resign from the Roman army and administration.

entries.label: Persecutions in the East
entries.note: AD 321–324 - Persecution of Christians by Licinius in the East.

entries.label: Pagan worship prohibited
entries.note: AD 356 - Constantius II prohibits public pagan worship on pain of death.

entries.label: Conflict between Valentinian II and Ambrose
Timothy “Wobble Cap” becomes patriarch of Alexandria
Monastery of Lindisfarne
entries.note: The monastery of Lindisfarne was founded by Irish monk Saint Aidan, who had been sent from Iona off the west coast of Scotland to Northumbria at the request of King Oswald. The priory was founded before the end of 634 and Aidan remained there until his death in 651.

entries.label: Hellenes of Laconia, Greece, resist the attempt of Tarasius, Patriarch of Constantinople, to convert them to Christianity
Bruno the Great
entries.note: Bruno the Great (or Bruno I), (May 925 – 11 October 965) Archbishop of Cologne, Germany, from 953 until his death, and Duke of Lotharingia from 954. He was the brother of Otto I, king of Germany and later Holy Roman Emperor. Bruno was the youngest son of Henry the Fowler and his second wife Matilda of Ringelheim. While he was still a child, it was decided that he should pursue an ecclesiastical career. In the early 940s he was educated in Trier by the leading scholar, Israel the Grammarian. In 951, Otto appointed Bruno as his archchaplain.

entries.label: Principality of Antioch (1098 to 1268)
entries.note: AD 1098 - Bohemond establishes Principality of Antioch.

entries.label: Thomas More executed
entries.note: AD1535 - Thomas More refused to accept King Henry VIII's claim to be the supreme head of the Church in England, and was executed.

entries.label: The Church of the East is created by St. Thomas
entries.note: The Church of the East, also known as the Nestorian Church, is a Christian church, part of the Syriac tradition of Eastern Christianity. It was the church of the Persian Sassanid Empire, and quickly spread widely through Asia. Between the 9th and 14th centuries it was the world's largest Christian church in terms of geographical extent, with dioceses stretching from the Mediterranean to China and India. Several modern churches claim continuity with the historical Church of the East.

entries.label: Valerian's Massacre
entries.note: AD258 - "Valerian's Massacre" Roman emperor issued edict to execute immediately all Christian Bishops, Presbyters, and Deacons, including Pope Sixtus II, Antipope Novatian, Cyprian of Carthage.

entries.label: Vision of Constantine
entries.note: AD312 - Vision of Constantine: while gazing into the sun he saw a cross with the words (hoc signo victor eres) by this sign conquer, see also Labarum, he was later called the 13th Apostle and Equal-to-apostles.

entries.label: Reign of Julian II “the Apostate”
entries.note: AD 360 - Julian II “the Apostate” is proclaimed Augustus by the Western army.

entries.label: Visigoths conquer Spain and advance Arian Christianity
Egbert
entries.note: Egbert (ca. 950 – 9 December 993) Archbishop of Trier from 977 until his death. After being trained in Egmond Abbey, founded and controlled by his family, and at the court of Bruno I, Archbishop of Cologne, he became the chancellor of Otto II in 976. The following year he was appointed to the archdiocese of Trier, still probably in his twenties. He accompanied Otto II on visits to Italy in 980 and 983. Egbert was a significant patron of science and the arts, who established one or more workshops of goldsmiths and enamellers at Trier, which produced works for other Ottonian centres and the Imperial court. Beginning with his tenure, Trier came to rival Mainz and Cologne as the artistic centre of the Ottonian world. These were the three most important episcopal sees in Germany, who at this period disputed the primacy of the emerging German (East Frankish) kingdom between them.

entries.label: Peter Damian
entries.note: Saint Peter Damian, Order of St. Benedict (O.S.B.) (c. 1007 – 21/22 February 1072 or 1073) A reforming monk in the circle of Pope Leo IX and a cardinal. In 1823, he was declared a Doctor of the Church. Dante placed him in one of the highest circles of Paradiso as a great predecessor of Saint Francis of Assisi.

entries.label: The Kingdom of Jerusalem (1099 to 1291)
entries.note: Four major vassals of the Kingdom of Jerusalem: - The Principality of Galilee - The County of Jaffa and Ascalon - The Lordship of Oultrejordain - The Lordship of Sidon

entries.label: Original Church of St. Peter
entries.note: 1506 - Pope Julius II begins demolition of the original Church of St. Peter. Bramante begins the design of the new St. Peter’s.

entries.label: Dissolution of the Monasteries
entries.note: AD1536-1540 - Dissolution of the Monasteries in England, Wales and Ireland.

entries.label: Our Lady of Kazan icon
entries.note: AD1579 - Discovery of the holiest Russian icon, Our Lady of Kazan.

entries.label: Pontifex Maximus
entries.note: The pontifex maximus was the most important member of the college. Until 104 BC, the pontifex maximus held the sole power in appointing members to the other priesthoods in the college.

entries.label: Fifteen Flamens
entries.note: The flamens were priests in charge of fifteen official cults of Roman religion, each assigned to a particular god.

entries.label: Barnabas the Apostle:
entries.note: Assyrian Church of the East Ancient Church of the East Chaldean Catholic Church Syro-Malabar Catholic Church Syro-Malankara Catholic Church Jacobite Syrian Christian Church Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church Mar Thoma Syrian Church

entries.label: Seven Churches of Asia
entries.note: 1. Ephesus (Revelation 2:1-7) - the church that had forsaken its first love 2. Smyrna (Revelation 2:8-11) - the church that would suffer persecution 3. Pergamum (Revelation 2:12-17) - the church that needed to repent 4. Thyatira (Revelation 2:18-29) - the church that had a false prophetess 5. Sardis (Revelation 3:1-6) - the church that had fallen asleep 6. Philadelphia (Revelation 3:7-13) - the church that had endured patiently 7. Laodicea (Revelation 3:14-22) - the church with the lukewarm faith

entries.label: Gallienus publishes an edict of toleration
entries.note: AD 260 - Gallienus publishes an edict of toleration of Christianity, ending the Valerianic persecution and starting “the Peace of the Church.”

entries.label: Edict of Milan
entries.note: Constantine issues Edict of Milan, ending persecution of Christians and establishing religious toleration throughout the Empire.

entries.label: Julian declares himself a pagan
entries.note: AD361 – Constantius dies of illness, naming Julian his successor. Julian openly declares himself a pagan. Julian restores worship of the pagan gods and enacts legislation to restore cults and cities, but his attempt at rejuvenating paganism in the empire fails.

entries.label: Outbreak of the Great Mutiny in North Africa
Bernward of Hildesheim
entries.note: Saint Bernward (c. 960 – 20 November 1022) The thirteenth Bishop of Hildesheim from 993 until his death in 1022.

entries.label: INNOCENT VIII
entries.note: In 1487, Innocent confirmed Tomas de Torquemada as Grand Inquisitor of Spain. He also urged a crusade against the Waldensians, offering plenary indulgence to all who should engage in it.[citation needed] In 1486, he became convinced that 13 of the 900 theses of Pico Mirandola were heretical and the book was interdicted. In Rome he built for summer use the Belvedere of the Vatican, on an unarticulated slope above the Vatican Palace, which his successor would turn into the Cortile del Belvedere. In season, he hunted at Castello della Magliana, which he enlarged. Invariably short of money, he institutionalized simony at the papal court, creating new titles of offices that were discreetly auctioned. After a shaky peace of 1486 with King Ferdinand I of Naples failed and Ferdinand repeatedly refused to pay the tariff for his investiture, Innocent excommunicated him in 1489 and invited King Charles VIII of France to come to Italy with an army and take possession of the Kingdom of Naples, a disastrous political event for the Italian peninsula as a whole. The immediate conflict was not ended until 1494, after Innocent VIII's death. An important event that coincided with Innocent's pontificate was the fall of Granada in January 1492, which was celebrated in the Vatican with great rejoicings. Innocent granted Ferdinand II of Aragon the epithet "Catholic Majesty." Authentic Image of Jesus of Nazareth Taken from an engraved emerald, made by order of the Roman Emperor Tiberius. It comes from the Treasure of Constantinople and was surrendered by the Sultan of Turkey to Pope Innocent VIII as ransom for his brother, held captive by the Christians.

entries.label: Apostles Andrew and Simon the Zealot:
Aurelian intervenes in church affairs
entries.note: AD 272 - Church of Antioch appeals to Aurelian against Paul of Samosata; first imperial intervention in church affairs.

entries.label: Edict of Thessalonica
entries.note: AD380 - Edict of Thessalonica issued by Theodosius I makes Nicene Christianity the State church of the Roman Empire. Later, (AD 380, November 24) Emperor Theodosius I is baptised. Dispute over the Altar of Victory begins.

entries.label: Imperial edict bars pagans from military and civil positions
Imperial laws are declared against heretics in North Africa
Monastery of Lindisfarne sacked by Vikings
Battle of Manzikert
entries.note: AD 1071 - Emperor Romanos IV is defeated by the Seljuk Turks at the Battle of Manzikert. The subsequent civil wars result in the loss of most of Asia Minor to the Turks. In the same year, the last Byzantine outpost in Italy, Bari, is conquered by the Normans.

entries.label: Crusaders arrive at Constantinople
entries.note: AD 1097 Robert of Normandy, Stephen of Blois, Raymond IV of Toulouse, and Bohemond arrive at Constantinople; Battle of Dorylaeum: Crusaders defeat Sultan Kilij Arslan I of Rum.

entries.label: Roderic Llançol i de Borja (Rodrigo Borgia)
Sistine Chapel ceiling
entries.note: 1508 - 1512 - Michelangelo commissioned by Pope Julius II to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling

entries.label: Marian Apparition - Our Lady of Guadalupe
entries.note: AD1531 - Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico. According to tradition, when the roses fell from it the icon of the Virgin of Guadalupe appeared imprinted on the cactus cloth. The sudden, extraordinary success of the evangelizing of ten million Indians in the decade of 1531–1541.

entries.label: Apostles Thomas and Bartholomew, and Thaddeus of Edessa:
Introduction of Baal of Emesa (sun god) at Rome
Persecution of Manicheans
entries.note: AD 297 - Diocletian issues an edict of persecution of Manicheans.

entries.label: Persecutions of Christians in Persian Empire
Theodosius closes the pagan temples and outlaws sacrifices
entries.note: AD 391 - Edict of Theodosius I closes the pagan temples and outlaws sacrifices.

entries.label: Events (1100 - 1124)
entries.note: AD 1100 - AD 1124 1100 Bohemond captured by Danishmend Turks 1100 Baldwin I summoned as King of Jerusalem (r. 1100–1118); Baldwin II Le Bourg crowned count of Edessa. 1101 Tancred assumes regency at Antioch; Crusade of 1101. 1103 Count Raymond IV besieges Tripoli; Release of Bohemond. 1108 Treaty of Devol; Bohemond recognizes Byzantine suzerainty over Antioch. 1109 Crusaders capture Tripoli - Creation of fourth Crusader state, County of Tripoli; Count Betram offers homage to King Baldwin I of Jerusalem. 1112–1119 Roger of Salerno serves as regent in Antioch. 1118 Accession of Baldwin II, king of Jerusalem (1118–1131); Accession of Joscelin I, count of Edessa 1119 Battle of Ager Sanguinis (“Field of Blood”); Emir Ilghazi defeats and slays Roger of Salerno 1124 Capture of Tyre by Crusaders and Venetians.

entries.label: Events (1150 - 1174)
entries.note: AD 1150 - AD 1174 1150 Nur-ad-Din captures and imprisons Count Joscelin II of Edessa. 1152 Assassins murder Count Raymond II of Tripoli; Accession of Count Raymond III (1152–1187) 1153 Reynald of Châtillon crowned prince of Antioch (r. 1153–1160); Surrender of Ascalon to King Baldwin III. 1154 Nur-ad-Din occupies Damascus 1158 Marriage of Baldwin III to Theodora, niece of Manuel I; Expedition of Emperor Manuel I against Antioch (1158–1159). 1160 Capture of Reynald of Châtillon; King Baldwin III assumes regency of Antioch. 1163 Accession of Amalric I, king of Jerusalem (1163–1174); Bohemond III (1163–1201), prince of Antioch, attains his majority 1163 First expedition of Amalric I against Fatimid Egypt. 1164 Intervention of Shirkuh, general of Nur-ad-Din, in Cairo. 1167 Second and third expeditions of Amalric I into Fatimid Egypt; Marriage of Amalric I to Maria Comnena. 1168 Fourth expedition of King Amalric I into Fatimid Egypt. 1169 Fifth expedition of Amalric into Egypt. 1171 Saladin restores Abbasid authority Sunni (Orthodox Muslim) in Egypt; End of Fatimid Caliphate. 1174 Accession of Baldwin IV, “Leper King” (1174–1183) 1174 Saladin unites Muslim Syria and Egypt. Crisis in the Crusader states over succession.

entries.label: Events (1200 - 1224)
entries.note: AD 1200 - AD 1224 1200 Sultan al-Adil secures Egypt and Syria. 1201 Crusaders conclude Treaty of Venice; Boniface III Marquis of Montferrat succeeds to command of Fourth Crusade. 1202 Doge Enrico Dandolo commits Venice to the Fourth Crusade; Fourth Crusade captures Zara. 1202 Treaty of Zara: Crusaders pledge to restore Alexius IV to Byzantine throne. 1203 Fourth Crusade restores Alexius IV at Constantinople; Rising tensions between Byzantines and Crusaders. 1205 Election of Thomas Morosini as patriarch of Constantinople; Latin emperor Baldwin I defeated and captured by Tsar Kalojan of Bulgaria. 1214 Battle of Bouvines: Philip II Augustus and Frederick II defeat Otto IV. 1215 Succession of Frederick II (r. 1215–1250) as king of Sicily; Unification of the Two Sicilies and the Holy Roman Empire by Frederick II. 1217 Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor, vows to go on crusade. 1218 Fifth Crusade besieges Damietta, Egypt; Sultan al-Kamil (1218–1238) succeeds to Ayyubid Egypt. 1219 Fall of Damietta to Fifth Crusade. 1220 Frederick II renews his Crusader vows. 1221 Defeat of the Fifth Crusade and surrender of Damietta to Sultan al- Kamil. 1224 Thessalonica occupied by Theodore, Byzantine despot of Epirus; Collapse of Frankish rule in northern Greece.

entries.label: Events (1250 - 1291)
entries.note: AD 1250 - AD 1291 1250 Battle of Mansurah: Mamluks check advance of Seventh Crusade; Retreat and surrender of Louis IX; Surrender of Damietta and ransoming of Crusaders at 800,000 livres tournois; Mamluks overthrow Ayyubid sultanate and institute military sultanate at Cairo; Louis IX at Acre rules Outremer (1250–1254). 1253 Mission of William Rubruquis to the Mongols sent by Louis IX. 1254–1261 War of St. Sabas between Venice and Genoa; Civil war in Outremer. 1256 Hulagu, Ilkhan of the Mongols, captures Alamut and destroys Assassin Order. 1258 Hulagu and Mongols sack Baghdad: End of Abbasid Caliphate. 1260 Battle of Ain Jalut: Mamluks defeats Mongols; Baybars (1260–1277) seizes the Mamluk sultanate 1260 Election of Kublai Khan as Great Khan of Mongols (1260–1294). 1261 Treaty of Nymphaeum: Michael VIII (1258–1282) concedes commercial privileges to Genoa 1266 Battle of Benevento: Charles of Anjou defeats Hohenstaufen rival Manfred; Angevin rule established in southern Italy and Sicily. 1267 Charles of Anjou imposes hegemony over Frankish Greece. 1268 Louis IX of France leads the Eighth Crusade (1268–1270). 1270 Siege of Tunis; Death of Louis IX and end of Eighth Crusade. 1271 Baybars captures Krak des Chevaliers. 1274 Council of Lyons; Michael VIII unifies Orthodox church under Rome. 1277 Charles of Anjou purchases right to Latin throne of Constantinople. 1286 Henry II (1285–1324) unites the thrones of Cyprus and Jerusalem.

entries.label: Raphael begins to paint his Stanze
St Basil's Cathedral is built in Moscow
Babylon or Seleucia-Ctesiphon, in present-day Iraq
“Christians for Christians” funerary monuments in northwest Phrygia
Christian riots destroy the Serapeum in Alexandria
Felix condemns the Henoticon; Mutual excommunicates of Acacius and Felix III
Capture of Jerusalem
entries.note: AD 1099 - Crusaders capture Jerusalem (July 15) Godfrey of Bouillon elected Advocate of Holy Sepulcher (r. 1099–1100).

entries.label: Events (1125 - 1149)
entries.note: AD 1127 - AD 1149 1127 Zengi appointed emir of Mosul (r. 1127–1146). 1130 Roger II (1127–1154) crowned king of Norman Sicily; Succession crisis at Antioch (1130–1131). 1131 Accession of Fulk of Anjou and Melisende to Kingdom of Jerusalem; Accession of Joscelin II, count of Edessa (r. 1131–1150). 1136 Marriage of Raymond of Poitiers and Princess Constance at Antioch; Raymond succeeds as prince of Antioch (1136–1149). 1137 Marriage of Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine (1137–1152). 1137–1138 First expedition of Emperor John II against Antioch. 1142–1143 Second expedition of John II against Antioch. 1143 Queen Melisende regent of Baldwin III (1143–1163). 1144 Zengi captures Edessa. 1145 Pope Eugenius III proclaims the Second Crusade. 1146 Nur-ad- Din retakes Edessa. 1146–1148 The Second Crusade; failure of King Louis VII to capture Damascus; Nur-ad-Din (1146–1174) unifies Muslim Syria. 1147 Departure of Conrad III of Germany and Louis VII of France on the Second Crusade; Outbreak of the Norman naval war (1147–1155); Henry the Lion, duke of Saxony, leads northern crusade. 1148 Defeat of Second Crusade at Damascus; departure of Louis VII and Conrad III. 1149 Nur-ad-Din defeats and slays Prince Raymond of Antioch.

entries.label: Events (1175 - 1199)
entries.note: AD 1176 - AD 1199 1176 Battle of Myriocephalon:Seljuk Turks defeat Manuel I; Battle of Legnano: Defeat of Frederick Barbarossa by Lombard League. 1176 Byzantine withdrawal from central Anatolia; emergence of a Turkish, Muslim civilization in Anatolia (1180–1300). 1177 Battle of Mount Gisard: Baldwin IV defeats Saladin. 1180 Marriage of Sybilla and Guy of Lusignan; Accession of John II (1180–1182) 1182 Reynald of Châtillon raids Muslim ports on Red Sea; Outbreak of anti- Latin riots in Constantinople 1185 Death of King Baldwin IV; Accession of Baldwin V (1185–1186); Guy and Sybilla clash with Humphrey IV of Toron and Isabel over regency. 1185 King William II of Sicily invades Byzantine Empire; Riots in Constantinople 1186 Succession of Sybilla and Guy of Lusignan (King Guy of Jerusalem (1186–1192)); Bulgarians revolt from Byzantine rule. 1187 Conrad of Montferrat defends Tyre (1187–1190). 1188 Dispute between Conrad of Montferrat and Guy Lusignan over kingship. 1189 Departure of Frederick I Barbarossa on Third Crusade; King Guy and Pisan fleet commence siege of Acre. 1190 Departure of King Richard I and Philip Augustus on Third Crusade; Death of Queen Sibylla of Jerusalem 1190 Marriage of Conrad of Montferrat to Isabelle, titular queen of Jerusalem. 1191 Richard I and Philip II clash over strategy and succession in Outremer; Richard I captures Acre; Battle of Arsuf: Victory of Richard I. 1192 Treaty between Richard I and Saladin; End of Third Crusade; King Guy Lusignan purchases Cyprus. 1192 Murder of Conrad Montferrat; Henry of Champagne marries Isabelle and succeeds as king of Jerusalem. 1193 Sultan al-Adil battles for Ayyubid Sultanate (1193–1200). 1194 Unification of Holy Roman Empire and Sicily under Henry VI (r. 1191–1197); Accession of Amalric II Lusignan as king of Cyprus. 1197 Death of Henry of Champagne; Marriage of Amalric II and Isabel: Unification of Acre and Cyprus (1197–1205). 1198 Accession of Philip of Swabia as king of Germany (1198–1208); Civil war in Hohenstaufen Empire (1198–1215). 1199 Tournament at Écry; Count Theobald III of Champagne assumes the cross.

entries.label: Events (1225 - 1249)
entries.note: AD 1225 - AD 1249 1225 Marriage of Frederick II to Yolande- Isabel, heiress of Jerusalem; Frederick renews his vows to go on crusade. 1226 King Louis VIII of France assumes direction of the Albigensian Crusade. 1227 Gregory IX excommunicates Frederick II for failure to honor crusade vows. 1228 Frederick II sails on Sixth Crusade (1228–1229). 1229 Treaty between Frederick II and Sultan al-Kamil; Jerusalem and Bethlehem returned to the Christians. 1230 Battle of Klokotnitsa: Tsar John Asen crushes army of Theodore of Epirus. 1232 Outbreak of civil war in Outremer; Barons under John of Ibelin oppose Hohenstaufen rule (1232–1243). 1239 Crusade of Theobald V of Champagne (1239–1240); Pope Gregory IX preaches a crusade against the Hohenstaufen (1239–1266). 1240 Crusade of Richard of Cornwall (1240–1241). 1243 Battle of Köse Dag: Mongols crush Seljuk army; Mongols impose lordship on Muslim Anatolia, Cilician Armenia, and Georgia 1243 End of Hohenstaufen rule in Outremer. 1244 Korezmian Turkomen mercenaries seize and sack Jerusalem; Battle of La Forbie (Gaza): Ayyubid-Korezmian army decisively defeats Franks 1244 King Louis IX of France vows to go on crusade. 1245 Council of Lyons: Pope Innocent IV deposes Frederick II; Welf nobility of Germany rebel against Frederick II 1245 Mission of Giovanni Plano Caprini to the Mongols (1245–1246). 1246 Nicene forces occupy Thessalonica; Accession of William II Prince of Achaea (1246–1278). 1248 Louis IX sails for Cyprus on Seventh Crusade (1248–1254); Mission of Friar Andrew of Longjameau to Mongols (1248–1251). 1249 Louis IX and Seventh Crusade capture Damietta.

entries.label: Michelangelo's dome completed
entries.note: AD1590 - Michelangelo's dome in St Peter's Basilica completed.

entries.label: Activities of Alexander of Abonouteichos and the creation of cult of Glycon (160–180)
Cyprian reasserts his authority over the African church
Pagan revolt in the West
entries.note: AD 392 - Revolt of Eugenius in the West begins, backed by the Western army and pagan Roman senators. Renewed antipagan and anti-heretical legislation is issued by Theodosius I. Theodore is made bishop of Mopsuestia.

entries.label: Revolt of Leontius and Illus in Asia Minor
Protection of pilgrim routes
entries.note: AD1001 - Byzantine emperor Basil II and Fatimid Caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah execute a treaty guaranteeing the protection of Christian pilgrimage routes in the Middle East.

entries.label: Bernard of Clairvaux preaches the 2nd Crusade
entries.note: AD 1146 - Bernard of Clairvaux preaches the 2nd Crusade at Vézelay.

entries.label: Sack of Constantinople
entries.note: AD 1204 - Fourth Crusade captures and sacks Constantinople; Election of Count Baldwin IX of Flanders as Latin emperor (1204–1205). - Venetians and Crusaders partition the Byzantine Empire; Boniface of Montferrat founds kingdom of Thessalonica - Geoffrey Villehardouin and William Champlitte conquer Achaea (Peloponnesus). - Otto de le Roche conquers Athens and Thebes; Splinter empires founded in Epirus and at Trebizond.

entries.label: Emperor Frederick II recovers Jerusalem
entries.note: AD 1229 Treaty between Frederick II and Sultan al-Kamil; Jerusalem and Bethlehem returned to the Christians.

entries.label: Mamluk capture of Acre: End of Outremer
Society of Jesus founded
entries.note: 1534 - St. Ignatius Loyola founds the Society of Jesus. Helped reconvert large areas of Poland, Hungary, and S. Germany and sent missionaries to the New World, India, and China.

entries.label: Cyprian writes On the Unity of the Catholic Church, the first defense of papal leadership
Pachomian foundation at Panopolis expands the monastic movement in Egypt
First papal visit north of the Alps
Louis the Pious issues the Constitutio Romana
entries.note: AD824 - Louis the Pious issues the Constitutio Romana, formalizing Carolingian control of papal elections.

entries.label: Church of the Holy Sepulchre destroyed and repaired
entries.note: AD1009 - Caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah destroys the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built over the tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem, and then rebuilds it to its current state.

entries.label: Saladin assumes power in Fatimid Cairo
Peace of Paris
entries.note: AD 1229 - Peace of Paris officially ends the Albigensian Crusade.

entries.label: Michael VIII occupies Constantinople and restores the Byzantine Empire
Marian Apparition - Our Lady of Lourdes
entries.note: AD1846 - Bernadette Soubirous received the first of 18 apparitions of Our Lady of Lourdes in Lourdes, France.

entries.label: Marian Apparition - Our Lady of Fatima
Spanish congregations appeal to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage
Church of the Holy Apostles
entries.note: AD330 - Old Church of the Holy Apostles, dedicated by Constantine.

entries.label: Edict of Toleration granted to Christians in Persia
Jerusalem Hospital rebuilt
entries.note: AD1023 - merchants from Amalfi and Salerno in Italy were given permission by the Caliph Ali az-Zahir of Egypt to rebuild the hospital in Jerusalem. The hospital, which was built on the site of the monastery of Saint John the Baptist, took in Christian pilgrims travelling to visit the Christian holy sites. It was served by Benedictine monks. This served as the foundation for the Knights Hospitaller.

entries.label: Capture of Tyre by Crusaders and Venetians.
Battle of Hattin
entries.note: AD 1187 - Battle of Hattin: Saladin annihilates Crusader army and captures King Guy; Saladin captures Jerusalem and overruns Outremer.

entries.label: Pauline Epistles
entries.note: c. 48–62 Composition of the Pauline Epistles (Romans, Philippians, Galatians, 1 and 2 Corinthians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon).

entries.label: Synoptic Gospels
entries.note: c. 80–100 Synoptic Gospels (Mark, Luke, and Matthew) take on their final form. | c. 100–120 Gospel of John takes on its final form; composition of the Johannine Epistles; Second Letter of Peter written.

entries.label: Gospel of John, Johannine Epistles; Peter II
Paul of Samosata serves as bishop of Antioch
Eusebius of Nicomedia ordains Ulfilas (Wulfila) as missionary to the Goths
Persian persecution of Christians
entries.note: AD 416 – 420 - Persecution of Christians as Yazdegerd revokes his earlier order.

entries.label: Donation of Constantine
entries.note: AD752? - Donation of Constantine Granted Western Roman Empire to the Pope, later proved a forgery.

entries.label: Church of the Holy Sepulcher dedicated
entries.note: AD 1149 - Dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulcher by Baldwin III.

entries.label: Death of Frederick I
entries.note: AD 1190 - 1190 Death of Frederick I in Asia Minor and dispersal of German Crusade.

entries.label: Franciscan property ownership
entries.note: AD1322/1323 - Pope John XXII rules that the Franciscan Order can own property and that those who maintain that Jesus and his apostles had owned no property are in error.

entries.label: Council of Antioch issues three condemnations of Paul of Samosata
Church of the Holy Sepulchre
entries.note: AD335 - Consecration of Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.

entries.label: Toleration of Christians in Persia
entries.note: AD 409 - Christians permitted to publicly worship and to build churches in Sasanian Empire.

entries.label: Peace of God first proclaimed
entries.note: AD 989 - Council of Charroux - Peace of God first proclaimed.

entries.label: Truce of God first proclaimed
entries.note: AD 1027 - Council of Touluges - Truce of God first proclaimed.

entries.label: Knights Templar
entries.note: 1119 - Hugues de Payens and his relative Godfrey de Saint-Omer found the order of The Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon. - Existed for approximately two centuries in the Middle Ages. - St Bernard of Clairvaux was the patron of the Order - Became a favoured charity throughout Christendom, grew rapidly in membership and power - Among the most skilled fighting units of the Crusades. - Non-combatant members managed a large economic infrastructure throughout Christendom - Built many fortifications across Europe and the Holy Land. - Existence tied closely to the Crusades; when the Holy Land was lost, support for the Order faded. - Rumours about the Templars created mistrust - Philip IV of France, deeply in debt to the Order, took advantage of this.

entries.label: Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius founded
entries.note: The Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius is the most important Russian monastery and the spiritual centre of the Russian Orthodox Church. The monastery was founded in 1345 by one of the most venerated Russian saints, Sergius of Radonezh, who built a wooden church in honour of the Holy Trinity on Makovets Hill. The monastery is situated in the town of Sergiyev Posad, about 70 km to the north-east from Moscow by the road leading to Yaroslavl, and currently is home to over 300 monks.

entries.label: Suppression of the Jesuits
entries.note: The Suppression of the Jesuits in the Portuguese Empire, France, the Two Sicilies, Malta, Parma and the Spanish Empire by 1767 was a result of a series of political moves in each polity rather than a theological controversy. Monarchies attempting to centralize and secularize political power viewed the Jesuits as being too international, to strongly allied to the papacy, and too autonomous of the monarchs in whose territory they operated. By the brief Dominus ac Redemptor (21 July 1773) Pope Clement XIV suppressed the Society of Jesus. The Jesuits took refuge in non-Catholic nations, particularly in Prussia and Russia, where the order was ignored or formally rejected.

entries.label: Letter to the Hebrews, Catholic Epistles
Saint Alban (b. uncertain - died between c. 209 – c. 313)
Retaliation against persecution of Christian Persians
entries.note: AD421–422 - Roman retaliation against Bahram's persecution of Christian Persians.

entries.label: Donation of Pepin
entries.note: AD756 - Donation of Pepin recognizes Papal States.

entries.label: Great Lavra Monastery at Mt. Athos
entries.note: The Monastery of Great Lavra (Greek: Μονή Μεγίστης Λαύρας) is the first monastery built on Mount Athos. It is located on the southeastern foot of the Mount at an elevation of 160 metres. The founding of the monastery in AD 963 by Athanasius the Athonite marks the beginning of the organized monastic life at Mount Athos.

entries.label: Anselm of Canterbury
entries.note: Saint Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033 – 21 April 1109) Benedictine monk, philosopher, and prelate of the Church, who held the office of Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093 to 1109. Called the founder of scholasticism, he has been a major influence in Western theology and is famous as the originator of the ontological argument for the existence of God and the satisfaction theory of atonement.

entries.label: Knights Templar endorsed
entries.note: 1129 - Knights Templar officially endorsed by Pope Honorius II at Council of Troyes

entries.label: Trinitarians
entries.note: Trinitarians (Order of the Most Blessed Trinity, sometimes called the Red Friars), founded 1193.

entries.label: Suppression of the Templars in France
entries.note: AD1307 - King Philip IV of France orders the arrest of many of the Knights Templar, beginning confiscation of their property and extraction of confessions under torture.

entries.label: Hussite Wars
entries.note: Minims (Hermits of St. Francis of Paola), founded 1436.

entries.label: Huldrych Zwingli
entries.note: Huldrych Zwingli (1 January 1484 – 11 October 1531) Leader of the Reformation in Switzerland. Born during a time of emerging Swiss patriotism and increasing criticism of the Swiss mercenary system, he attended the University of Vienna and the University of Basel, a scholarly centre of humanism. He continued his studies while he served as a pastor in Glarus and later in Einsiedeln, where he was influenced by the writings of Erasmus.

entries.label: Immaculate Conception defined as Catholic dogma
Canon
entries.note: The Apostolic Fathers is a term used to describe a group of Early Christian writings produced in the late 1st century and the first half of the 2nd century. These writings, though popular in Early Christianity, were ultimately not part of the New Testament once it reached its final form. Some of the writings found among the "Apostolic Fathers" seem to have been just as highly regarded as some of the writings (that remained) in the New Testament. List of Works The Epistle to Diognetus The First Epistle of Clement The Second Epistle of Clement (not actually written by Clement) The Didache The Epistle of Barnabas Seven Epistles of Ignatius (the longer forms of these Epistles, and those beyond the seven, are widely considered later emendations and forgeries) The Epistle of Polycarp The Martyrdom of Polycarp The Shepherd of Hermas Fragments of the writings of Papias, which have survived as quotations in later writers.

entries.label: Oldest Gospels fragments
entries.note: c. 130 - date of the oldest known papyri fragments of the Gospels and the works of Papias.

entries.label: Bede publishes his "History"
entries.note: The Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum (Latin for the Ecclesiastical History of the English People)

entries.label: Saint Methodius
entries.note: Saint Methodius (815–820 - 6 April 885) One of the six patron saints of Europe, together with Benedict of Nursia, Saint Cyril, Catherine of Siena, Bridget of Sweden and Edith Stein.

entries.label: Quedlinburg Abbey
entries.note: Quedlinburg Abbey A house of secular canonesses in Quedlinburg, Saxony-Anhalt, Germany. It was founded in 936 on the initiative of Saint Mathilda, the widow of Henry the Fowler, as his memorial. For many centuries it enjoyed great prestige and influence. Quedlinburg Abbey was an Imperial Estate and one of the forty-odd self-ruling Imperial Abbeys of the Holy Roman Empire.

entries.label: Investiture Controversy
entries.note: Investiture Controversy - Pope Gregory VII, with Henry IV, Holy Roman Emperor, proponent of Clerical celibacy, opponent of simony, concubinage.

entries.label: Templars exempted from local laws
entries.note: 1139 - Pope Innocent II exempted the Order from obedience to local laws.

entries.label: Mercedarians
entries.note: Mercedarians (Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mercy), founded 1218.

entries.label: Templars absolved
entries.note: 1308 - Pope Clement V absolves the Templars of all heresies.

entries.label: Donation of Constantine shown to be a forgery
entries.note: AD1440 - Lorenzo Valla publishes his work demonstrating that the Donation of Constantine is not what it purports to be.

entries.label: Thomas Cranmer
entries.note: Thomas Cranmer (2 July 1489 – 21 March 1556) Leader of the English Reformation and Archbishop of Canterbury during the reigns of Henry VIII, Edward VI and, for a short time, Mary I. He helped build the case for the annulment of Henry's marriage to Catherine of Aragon, which was one of the causes of the separation of the English Church from union with the Holy See. Along with Thomas Cromwell, he supported the principle of Royal Supremacy, in which the king was considered sovereign over the Church within his realm. During Cranmer's tenure as Archbishop of Canterbury, he was responsible for establishing the first doctrinal and liturgical structures of the reformed Church of England.

entries.label: Dechristianisation of France during the French Revolution
entries.note: AD1789-1801 - Dechristianisation of France during the French Revolution

entries.label: Lateran Palace given to Pope Miltiades
entries.note: AD313? Lateran Palace given to Pope Miltiades for residence by Constantine.

entries.label: Saint Illtud (uncertain - c. 470 – c. 535)
entries.note: Saint Gregory of Tours (30 November c. 538 – 17 November 594) Gallo-Roman historian and Bishop of Tours, which made him a leading prelate of Gaul. He wrote in form of late Vulgar Latin; however, it has been argued that this was a deliberate ploy to ensure his works would reach a wide audience. He is the main contemporary source for Merovingian history. His most notable work was his Decem Libri Historiarum or Ten Books of Histories, better known as the Historia Francorum ("History of the Franks"), a title given to it by later chroniclers, but he is also known for his credulous accounts of the miracles of saints, especially four books of the miracles of Martin of Tours.

entries.label: Tower added to St Peter's Basilica
entries.note: AD750? - Tower added to St Peter's Basilica at the front of the atrium.

entries.label: Saint Cyril
entries.note: Saint Cyril (827/828 - 14 February 869) One of the six patron saints of Europe, together with Benedict of Nursia, Saint Methodius, Catherine of Siena, Bridget of Sweden and Edith Stein.

entries.label: Muslims sack St. James at Santiago de Compostela
Knights Hospitaller founded
entries.note: AD1099 - The Knights Hospitaller, also known as the Hospitallers, Order of Hospitallers, Knights of Saint John and Order of Saint John, were among the most famous of the Western Christian military orders during the Middle Ages.

entries.label: Decretum Gratiani
entries.note: The Decretum Gratiani or Concordia discordantium canonum A collection of Canon law compiled and written in the 12th century as a legal textbook by the jurist known as Gratian. It forms the first part of the collection of six legal texts, which together became known as the Corpus Juris Canonici. It was used by canonists of the Roman Catholic Church until Pentecost (May 19) 1918, when a revised Code of Canon Law (Codex Iuris Canonici) promulgated by Pope Benedict XV on 27 May 1917 obtained legal force.

entries.label: Teutonic Knights founded
entries.note: c. AD1190 - Foundation of The Order of Brothers of the German House of Saint Mary in Jerusalem, commonly the Teutonic Order. German medieval military order becaming in modern times a purely religious Catholic order. It was formed to aid Christians on their pilgrimages to the Holy Land and to establish hospitals. Its members have commonly been known as the Teutonic Knights, since they also served as a crusading military order in the Middle Ages. The military membership was always small, with volunteers and mercenaries augmenting the force as needed.

entries.label: Alexander Nevsky
entries.note: Alexander Nevsky (30 May 1220 – 14 November 1263) Proclaimed Saint of the Russian Orthodox Church by Metropolite Macarius in 1547, was the Prince of Novgorod, Grand Prince of Kiev and Grand Prince of Vladimir during some of the most trying times in the city's history. Commonly regarded as the key figure of medieval Rus.

entries.label: Templars disbanded
entries.note: 1312 - Templars disbanded by Clement V

entries.label: Thomas à Kempis
entries.note: Thomas à Kempis, (Thomas von Kempen) (c. 1380 – 25 July 1471) German canon regular of the late medieval period and the author of The Imitation of Christ, which is one of the best known Christian books on devotion. His name means "Thomas of Kempen", his hometown.

entries.label: John Calvin
entries.note: John Calvin ( born Jehan Cauvin: 10 July 1509 – 27 May 1564) Influential French theologian and pastor during the Protestant Reformation. He was a principal figure in the development of the system of Christian theology later called Calvinism. Originally trained as a humanist lawyer, he broke from the Roman Catholic Church around 1530. After religious tensions provoked a violent uprising against Protestants in France, Calvin fled to Basel, Switzerland, where he published the first edition of his seminal work Institutes of the Christian Religion in 1536.

entries.label: Missionary activities of Gregory Thaumaturgus (the Wonderworker)
Church of the Nativity
entries.note: AD325 - Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, ordered by Constantine.

entries.label: Pelagius
entries.note: Pelagius (fl. c. 390-418) Probably British-born Roman ascetic who opposed the idea of predestination and asserted a strong version of the doctrine of free will. He was accused by Augustine of Hippo and others of denying the need for divine aid in performing good works. For him (according to them), the only grace necessary was the declaration of the law; humans were not wounded by Adam's sin and were perfectly able to fulfill the law apart from any divine aid. His supporters cite Deuteronomy 24:16 to deny original sin. He denied the more specific doctrine of original sin as developed by Augustine. Pelagius was declared a heretic by the Council of Carthage. His interpretation of a doctrine of free will became known as Pelagianism.

entries.label: Eastern Church independence in Persia
entries.note: AD 424 - Council of Dad-Ishu declares the Eastern Church independent of Constantinople.

entries.label: Augustine of Canterbury
entries.note: Augustine of Canterbury (c. first third of the 6th century – c. 26 May 604) Benedictine monk who became the first Archbishop of Canterbury in the year 597. He is considered the "Apostle to the English" and a founder of the English Church.

entries.label: Aristotelian theses condemned
entries.note: AD 1277 - Bishop of Paris condemns 219 Aristotelian theses.

entries.label: Knights Hospitaller confirmed by Papal bull
entries.note: AD1113 - Knights Hospitaller confirmed by Papal bull of Pope Paschal II, listing Blessed Gerard (Gerard Thom) as founder, (a.k.a. Sovereign Order of Saint John of Jerusalem of Rhodes and of Malta, Knights of Malta, Knights of Rhodes, and Chevaliers of Malta).

entries.label: Jacques de Molay burned at the stake
entries.note: AD1314 - Jacques de Molay, last Grandmaster of Knights Templar, burned at the stake.

entries.label: Joan of Arc
entries.note: Joan of Arc (French: Jeanne d'Arc, ca. 1412 – 30 May 1431) Nicknamed "The Maid of Orléans" (French: La Pucelle d'Orléans), is considered a heroine of France and a Roman Catholic saint. She was born to a peasant family at Domrémy in north-east France. Joan said she received visions of the Archangel Michael, Saint Margaret and Saint Catherine instructing her to support Charles VII and recover France from English domination late in the Hundred Years' War. The uncrowned King Charles VII sent Joan to the siege of Orléans as part of a relief mission. She gained prominence after the siege was lifted in only nine days. Several additional swift victories led to Charles VII's coronation at Reims. On 23 May 1430, she was captured at Compiègne by the allied English-Burgundian faction. She was later handed over to the English, and then put on trial by the pro-English Bishop of Beauvais Pierre Cauchon on a variety of charges. After Cauchon declared her guilty she was burned at the stake on 30 May 1431, dying at about nineteen years of age. Twenty-five years after her execution, an inquisitorial court authorized by Pope Callixtus III examined the trial, debunked the charges against her, pronounced her innocent, and declared her a martyr. Joan of Arc was beatified in 1909 and canonized in 1920. She is one of the nine secondary patron saints of France, along with St. Denis, St. Martin of Tours, St. Louis, St. Michael, St. Remi, St. Petronilla, St. Radegund and St. Thérèse of Lisieux.

entries.label: John Knox
entries.note: John Knox (c. 1514 – 24 November 1572) Scottish clergyman, writer and a leader of the Protestant Reformation who is considered the founder of the Presbyterian denomination in Scotland.

entries.label: Consecration of St. Peter's Basilica
entries.note: AD 326, November 18 Pope Sylvester I consecrates the Basilica of St. Peter built by Constantine the Great over the tomb of the Apostle.

entries.label: John Cassian
entries.note: Saint John Cassian (c. 360 – 435) John the Ascetic, or John Cassian the Roman, was a Christian monk and theologian celebrated in both the Western and Eastern Churches for his mystical writings. Cassian is noted for bringing the ideas and practices of Egyptian monasticism to the early medieval West.

entries.label: Augustine becomes 1st Archbishop of Canterbury
entries.note: AD597 - Gregory, bishop of Rome, sends a mission under Augustine to convert the pagan Anglo-Saxons of Britain.

entries.label: Abbey of Reichenau
entries.note: The Benedictine Abbey of Reichenau was founded in 724 by the itinerant Saint Pirmin, who is said to have fled Spain ahead of the Moorish invaders, with patronage that included Charles Martel. The famous artworks of Reichenau include the Ottonian murals of miracles of Christ in St Georg, unique survivals from the 10th century. The Abbey housed a school, and a scriptorium and artists' workshop, that has a claim to having been the largest and artistically most influential centre for producing lavishly illuminated manuscripts in Europe during the late 10th and early 11th centuries, often known as the Reichenau School.

entries.label: Imperial Abbey of Corvey
entries.note: The Imperial Abbey of Corvey Was a Benedictine monastery on the River Weser, 2 km northeast of Höxter, now in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. It was first founded in 815 among the recently converted Saxons on a site called Hethis by Charlemagne's cousins Wala and Adelard, with monks from Corbie Abbey in Picardy, under the joint patronage of the Emperor Louis the Pious and the abbot of the older foundation, whence the new one derived its name (Latin: Corbeia nova, the "new Corbie"; Old German: Corvey)

entries.label: Mansur Al-Hallaj
entries.note: Mansur al-Hallaj (c. 858 – March 26, 922) (Hijri c. 244 AH – 309 AH) Persian mystic, revolutionary writer and teacher of Sufism, who wrote exclusively in Arabic. He is most famous for his poetry, accusation of heresy and for his execution at the orders of the Abbasid Caliph Al-Muqtadir after a long, drawn-out investigation.

entries.label: Rising numbers of western pilgrims to the Holy Land
Thomas à Becket
entries.note: Thomas Becket (also known as Saint Thomas of Canterbury, and Thomas à Becket) (21 December c. 1118 (or 1120) – 29 December 1170) Archbishop of Canterbury from 1162 until his murder in 1170. He is venerated as a saint and martyr by both the Catholic Church and the Anglican Communion. He engaged in conflict with Henry II of England over the rights and privileges of the Church and was murdered by followers of the king in Canterbury Cathedral. Soon after his death, he was canonised by Pope Alexander III.

entries.label: Condemnations of 1210 - 1277
entries.note: The Condemnations at the medieval University of Paris were enacted to restrict certain teachings as being heretical. These included a number of medieval theological teachings, but most importantly the physical treatises of Aristotle. The investigations of these teachings were conducted by the Bishops of Paris. The Condemnations of 1277 are traditionally linked to an investigation requested by Pope John XXI, although whether he actually supported drawing up a list of condemnations is unclear. Approximately sixteen lists of censured theses were issued by the University of Paris during the 13th and 14th centuries. Most of these lists of propositions were put together into systematic collections of prohibited articles. Of these, the Condemnations of 1277 are considered particularly important by those historians who consider that they encouraged scholars to question the tenets of Aristotelian science. From this perspective, some historians maintain that the condemnations had positive effects on the development of science, perhaps even representing the beginnings of modern science.

entries.label: The first Jubilee Year announced by Pope Boniface VIII
Zend Avesta is assembled
entries.note: All texts known today derive from a single master copy, now lost but known as the "Sassanian archetype", most likely a product of the 3rd or 4th century. According to tradition, in the 3rd century, the Sassanian emperor Ardashir I (r. 226-241 AD) commanded his high priest Tonsar (or Tansar) to compile the theological texts. According to the Dēnkard, the Tonsar effort resulted in the reproduction of twenty-one volumes, called nasks, subdivided into 348 chapters, with approximately 3.5 million words in total. One final redaction took place under Shapur II (r. 309-379).

entries.label: Martin of Tours
entries.note: Martin of Tours (Latin: Sanctus Martinus Turonensis; 316 – 8 November 397) Bishop of Tours, whose shrine in France became a famous stopping-point for pilgrims on the road to Santiago de Compostela in Spain. Around his name much legendary material accrued, and he has become one of the most familiar and recognisable Christian saints. As he was born in what is now Szombathely, Hungary, spent much of his childhood in Pavia, Italy, and lived most of his adult life in France, he is considered a spiritual bridge across Europe.

entries.label: Consecration of Nestorius as patriarch of Constantinople
Dedication of San Vitale at Ravenna
Basil II negotiates treaty with Fatimid Caliph al-Hakim to protect pilgrimage routes
Cîteaux Abbey founded
entries.note: Robert of Molesme, Alberic of Cîteaux and the English monk Stephen Harding, were the first three abbots.

entries.label: Albertus Magnus (Albert the Great)
entries.note: Albertus Magnus based his systematization of Aristotelian philosophy, and much of his writings on astronomy, astrology, mineralogy, chemistry, zoology, physiology, and phrenology upon those translations made in Toledo.

entries.label: Rebuilding and decoration of the Church of the Savior in Chora (Kariye Camii)
Savonarola’s constitution
entries.note: Savonarola’s constitution proclaimed in Florence

entries.label: Peter Canisius
entries.note: Peter Canisius, S.J. (Dutch: Pieter Kanis, 8 May 1521 – 21 December 1597) Jesuit Catholic priest who supported the Catholic faith during the Protestant Reformation in Germany, Austria, Bohemia, Moravia, and Switzerland. The restoration of the Catholic Church in Germany after the Protestant Reformation is largely attributed to the work there of the Society of Jesus, which he led. He is venerated in the Catholic Church as a saint and as a Doctor of the Church.

entries.label: Saint George
entries.note: Saint George (c. 275/281 – 23 April 303 AD) Born in Lydda, Roman Palestine, was a soldier in the Roman army and was later venerated as a Christian martyr. Saint George became an officer in the Roman army in the Guard of Diocletian. One of the most venerated saints in the Catholic (Western and Eastern Rites), Anglican, Eastern Orthodox, and the Oriental Orthodox churches. He is immortalized in the tale of Saint George and the Dragon and is one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers.

entries.label: Ulfilas
entries.note: Ulfilas (c. 311 – 383) Bishop, missionary, and Bible translator (into Gothic), was a Goth or half-Goth and half-Greek from Cappadocia who had spent time inside the Roman Empire at the peak of the Arian controversy. Ulfilas was ordained a bishop by Eusebius of Nicomedia and returned to his people to work as a missionary. | Nestorius (c. 386 – 450) Archbishop of Constantinople from 10 April 428 until August 431, when the emperor Theodosius II confirmed his condemnation by the Council of Ephesus on 22 June. His teachings included a rejection of the long-used title of Theotokos, "Mother of God", for Mary, mother of Jesus, and were misunderstood by many to imply that he did not believe that Christ was truly God. This brought him into conflict with other prominent churchmen of the time, most notably Cyril of Alexandria, whom he accused of heresy. Nestorius sought to defend himself at the First Council of Ephesus in 431, but instead he found himself formally condemned for heresy by a majority of the bishops and subsequently removed from his see.

entries.label: Armenian Orthodox split from East and West churches
entries.note: Armenian Orthodox split from East and West churches. Armenian Church repudiates the Council of Chalcedon.

entries.label: Peter Lombard
entries.note: Peter Lombard (c. 1096 – 21/22 August 1164) Scholastic theologian, Bishop of Paris, and author of Four Books of Sentences, which became the standard textbook of theology, for which he earned the accolade Magister Sententiarum.

entries.label: Saint Dominic
entries.note: Thomas Aquinas also used many of the translated work to bring Aristotle into his philosophical and theological treatises. Notable Works: Summa Theologica

entries.label: John Wycliffe
entries.note: John Wycliffe (c. 1320 – December 1384) English Scholastic philosopher, theologian, lay preacher, translator, reformer and university teacher at Oxford in England, who was known as an early dissident in the Roman Catholic Church during the 14th century. His followers were known as Lollards, a somewhat rebellious movement, which preached anticlerical and biblically-centred reforms. The Lollard movement was a precursor to the Protestant Reformation (for this reason, Wycliffe is sometimes called "The Morning Star of the Reformation"). He was one of the earliest opponents of papal authority influencing secular power. Wycliffe was also an early advocate for translation of the Bible into the common language. He completed his translation directly from the Vulgate into vernacular English in the year 1382, now known as Wycliffe's Bible.

entries.label: Robert Bellarmine
entries.note: Saint Robert Bellarmine, S.J. (4 Oct 1542 – 17 Sep 1621) Italian Jesuit and a Cardinal of the Catholic Church. He was one of the most important figures in the Counter-Reformation. He was canonized in 1930 and named a Doctor of the Church. Bellarmine is also widely remembered for his role in the Galileo affair.

entries.label: Mani begins his mission in Persia
Mani crucified
entries.note: Prophet Mani crucified, founder of the dualistic Manichaean sect in Persia.

entries.label: St. Augustine of Hippo
entries.note: Notable Works: Confessions City of God | AD384 - 387 Augustine at Milan. AD386 - Augustine returns to Catholic Christianity.

entries.label: Nestorian Christianity becomes dominant in Sassanid Empire
Berengar of Tours
entries.note: Berengar of Tours (c. 999–January 6, 1088) French 11th century Christian theologian and Archdeacon of Angers, a scholar whose leadership of the cathedral school at Chartres set an example of intellectual inquiry through the revived tools of dialectic that was soon followed at cathedral schools of Laon and Paris, and who disputed with the Church leadership over the doctrine of transubstantiation in the Eucharist.

entries.label: John of Salisbury
entries.note: John of Salisbury (c. 1120 – 25 October 1180) Described himself as Johannes Parvus ("John the Little"), was an English author, educationalist, diplomat and bishop of Chartres, and was born at Salisbury. Of Greek writers he appears to have known nothing at first hand, and very little in translations. The Timaeus of Plato in the Latin version of Chalcidius was known to him as to his contemporaries and predecessors, and probably he had access to translations of the Phaedo and Meno. Of Aristotle he possessed the whole of the Organon in Latin; he is, indeed, the first of the medieval writers of note to whom the whole was known. He was a student of William of Conches.

entries.label: Saint Francis of Assisi
entries.note: AD1219 - Francis of Assisi crosses enemy lines during the Fifth Crusade to speak to Sultan al-Kamil; ends with a meal. James of Vitry writes that Muslim soldiers returned Francis and another friar, Illuminato, "with signs of honor."

entries.label: Aquinas writes Summa Theologica
entries.note: AD1274 - Summa Theologica, written by Thomas Aquinas, theologian and philosopher. Landmark systematic theology which later became official Catholic doctrine.

entries.label: Development of Roman diaconate and the catacombs
St. Athanasius of Alexandria
entries.note: AD329 - AD373 - Athanasius becomes patriarch of Alexandria. | Athanasius is exiled five times from Alexandria.

entries.label: Dionysius Exiguus
entries.note: Dionysius Exiguus (Dennis the Small, Dennis the Dwarf, Dennis the Little or Dennis the Short, meaning humble) (c. 470 – c. 544) A 6th-century monk born in Scythia Minor (probably modern Dobruja, which is in Romania and Bulgaria). He was a member of the Scythian monks community concentrated in Tomis, the major city of Scythia Minor. Dionysius is best known as the "inventor" of the Anno Domini (AD) era, which is used to number the years of both the Gregorian calendar and the (Christianized) Julian calendar. From about 500 he lived in Rome, where, as a learned member of the Roman Curia, he translated from Greek into Latin 401 ecclesiastical canons, including the apostolical canons and the decrees of the councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon and Sardis, and also a collection of the decretals of the popes from Siricius to Anastasius II. These collections had great authority in the West and still guide church administrations. Dionysius also wrote a treatise on elementary mathematics. The author of a continuation of Dionysius's Computus, writing in 616, described Dionysius as a "most learned abbot of the city of Rome", and the Venerable Bede accorded him the honorific abbas, which could be applied to any monk, especially a senior and respected monk, and does not necessarily imply that Dionysius ever headed a monastery; indeed, Dionysius's friend Cassiodorus stated in Institutiones that he was still a monk late in life.

entries.label: John Scotus Eriugena
entries.note: Johannes Scotus Eriugena (c. 815 – c. 877) Irish theologian, Neoplatonist philosopher, and poet. He wrote a number of works, but is best known today, and had most influence in subsequent centuries, for having translated and made commentaries upon the work of Pseudo-Dionysius.

entries.label: Hugh of St. Victor
entries.note: Hugh of Saint Victor (c. 1096 – 11 February 1141) Saxon canon regular and a leading theologian and writer on mystical theology.

entries.label: Johannes Tauler
entries.note: Johannes Tauler OP (c. 1300 – 15 June 1361) German mystic, a Catholic preacher and a theologian. A disciple of Meister Eckhart, he belonged to the Dominican order. Tauler was known as one of the most important Rhineland Mystics. He promoted a certain neo-platonist dimension in the Dominican spirituality of his time.

entries.label: Origen succeeds Clement at the Catechetical School at Alexandria
Day of Rest decreed
entries.note: Constantine decreed (March 7, 321) dies Solis—day of the sun, "Sunday"—as the Roman day of rest. "On the venerable day of the Sun let the magistrates and people residing in cities rest, and let all workshops be closed. In the country however persons engaged in agriculture may freely and lawfully continue their pursuits because it often happens that another day is not suitable for grain-sowing or vine planting; lest by neglecting the proper moment for such operations the bounty of heaven should be lost." Constantine's triumphal arch was carefully positioned to align with the colossal statue of Sol by the Colosseum, so that Sol formed the dominant backdrop when seen from the direction of the main approach towards the arch.

entries.label: Consecration of Cyril as patriarch of Alexandria; emergence of Alexandria as the leading see of the East
St. Gregory the Great
entries.note: AD590-604 - Pope Saint Gregory I "the Great", whom many consider the greatest pope ever, reforms church structure and administration and establishes Gregorian Chant, Seven deadly sins etc.

entries.label: Richard of St. Victor (speculative dates)
entries.note: Richard of Saint Victor, C.R.S.A., (died 1173) is known today as one of the most influential religious thinkers of his time. He was a prominent mystical theologian, and was prior of the famous Augustinian Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris from 1162 until his death in 1173.

entries.label: Order of Saint Clare founded
entries.note: 1212 - Founded by Saints Clare of Assisi and Francis of Assisi on Palm Sunday in the year 1212.

entries.label: Bridget of Sweden
entries.note: Bridget of Sweden (1303 – 23 July 1373) Mystic and saint, and founder of the Bridgettines nuns and monks after the death of her husband of twenty years. She was also the mother of Catherine of Vadstena. One of the six patron saints of Europe, together with Benedict of Nursia, Saints Cyril and Methodius, Catherine of Siena and Edith Stein.

entries.label: Waldensian persecution
entries.note: AD1487 - Persecution and crusade against the Waldensians instigated by Pope Innocent VIII.

entries.label: Christian AD calendar defined
entries.note: AD525 - Dionysius Exiguus defines Christian anno domini (AD) calendar.

entries.label: Stanislaus of Szczepanów
entries.note: Patron saint of Poland

entries.label: Peter the Venerable
entries.note: Peter the Venerable (c. 1092 – December 25, 1156) Abbot of the Benedictine abbey of Cluny. Peter became a popular international figure and an associate of many national and religious leaders of his day. He attended many of the important religious councils of his generation, including the Council of Pisa in 1134 and the Council of Reims in 1147. In addition, he defended French theologian Peter Abelard after the latter’s rationalistic Trinitarian interpretation had been condemned by the Council of Sens. He granted Abelard hospitality at Cluny and worked to mitigate the sentence of the council, eventually reconciling Abelard with his principal condemner, St. Bernard of Clairvaux. After Abelard's death, Peter granted him absolution from his sins, at the personal request of Heloise. Peter is well known for collecting sources on and writing about Islam and also as the author of vast amounts of correspondence, reflecting his almost encyclopedic knowledge of theological questions. His writings are counted as some of the most important documents of the 12th century. He took a long sabbatical journey to Spain to study with Islamic scholars of all ranks and published the first Latin edition of the Koran. His Talmudic contributions are tenuous and still under scrutiny. Peter's true brilliance came to light between 1138-1142, especially after his translation of the Koran became required reading to the entire Benedictine world and for all preachers of the crusades. Despite his active life and important role in European history, Peter's greatest achievement is his contribution to the reappraisal of the Church’s relations with the religion of Islam. A proponent of studying Islam based upon its own sources, he commissioned a comprehensive translation of Islamic source material, and in 1142 he traveled to Spain where he met his translators. One scholar has described this as a “momentous event in the intellectual history of Europe.”

entries.label: Henry Suso
entries.note: Henry Suso, O.P. (German: Heinrich Seuse) (1295 - 1366) German Dominican friar, who was a noted spiritual writer and mystic. Suso and his friend Johannes Tauler were students of Meister Eckhart. The three form the nucleus of the Rhineland school of mysticism. As a lyric poet and troubadour of divine wisdom, Suso explored with psychological intensity the spiritual truths of Eckhart’s mystical philosophy.

entries.label: Francis Xavier
entries.note: Francis Xavier, SJ, born Francisco de Jasso y Azpilicueta (7 April 1506 – 3 December 1552) Roman Catholic missionary born in Xavier, Kingdom of Navarre (now part of Spain), and co-founder of the Society of Jesus. He was a study companion of St. Ignatius of Loyola and one of the first seven Jesuits who took vows of poverty and chastity at Montmartre, (Paris) in 1534. He led an extensive mission into Asia, mainly in the Portuguese Empire of the time. He was influential in evangelization work most notably in India. He also ventured into Japan, Borneo, the Maluku Islands, and other areas which had, until then, not been visited by Christian missionaries. In these areas, being a pioneer and struggling to learn the local languages in the face of opposition, he had less success than he had enjoyed in India. It was a goal of Xavier to extend his missionary preaching to China but he died in Shangchuan Island shortly before of doing so.

entries.label: Francis de Sales
