entries.group: Important figures in Hindu culture & Religion
entries.label: Sivananda Saraswati
entries.note: Swami Sivananda Saraswati (8 September 1887 – 14 July 1963) was a yoga guru, a Hindu spiritual teacher, and a proponent of Vedanta. Sivananda was born in Pattamadai, in the Tirunelveli district of Tamil Nadu, and was named Kuppuswami. He studied medicine and served in British Malaya as a physician for several years before taking up monasticism. He was the founder of the Divine Life Society (DLS) in 1936, Yoga-Vedanta Forest Academy (1948) and author of over 200 books on yoga, Vedanta, and a variety of subjects. He established Sivananda Ashram, the headquarters of the DLS, on the bank of the Ganges at Muni Ki Reti, 3 kilometres (1.9 mi) from Rishikesh, and lived most of his life there.

entries.group: Expansion of Hinduism in South-East Asia
entries.label: Lahiri Mahasaya
entries.note: Shyama Charan Lahiri (30 September 1828 – 26 September 1895), best known as Lahiri Mahasaya, was an Indian yogi and guru who founded the Kriya Yoga school. He was a disciple of Mahavatar Babaji. According to the book America's Alternative Religions by Timothy Miller, Lahiri Mahasaya's life was described in Paramahansa Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi as a demonstration of the spiritual attainment that could be achieved by a householder "living fully in the world". A part of Lahiri Mahasaya's face is pictured on the cover of The Beatles' 1967 album Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band.

entries.group: Expansion of Hinduism in South-East Asia
entries.label: Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh (Osho)
entries.note: Rajneesh (born Chandra Mohan Jain; 11 December 1931 – 19 January 1990), also known as Acharya Rajneesh, Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, and later as Osho, was an Indian godman, philosopher, mystic, and founder of the Rajneesh movement. He was viewed as a controversial new religious movement leader during his life. He rejected institutional religions, insisting that spiritual experience could not be organized into any one system of religious dogma. As a guru, he advocated meditation and taught a unique form called dynamic meditation. Rejecting traditional ascetic practices, he advocated that his followers live fully in the world but without attachment to it.

entries.group: Expansion of Hinduism in South-East Asia
entries.label: Sri Yukteswar Giri
entries.note: Swami Sri Yukteswar Giri (10 May 1855 – 9 March 1936) is the monastic name of Priya Nath Karar, an Indian monk and yogi, and the guru of Paramahansa Yogananda and Swami Satyananda Giri. Born in Serampore, West Bengal, Sri Yukteswar was a Kriya yogi, a Jyotishi (Vedic astrologer), a scholar of the Bhagavad Gita and the Upanishads, an educator, author, and astronomer. He was a disciple of Lahiri Mahasaya of Varanasi and a member of the Giri branch of the Swami order. As a guru, he had two ashrams, one in Serampore and another in Puri, Odisha, between which he alternated his residence throughout the year as he trained disciples.

entries.label: Paramahansa Yogananda
entries.note: Paramahansa Yogananda (born Mukunda Lal Ghosh; January 5, 1893 – March 7, 1952) was an Indian-American Hindu monk, yogi and guru who introduced millions to meditation and Kriya Yoga through his organization, Self-Realization Fellowship (SRF) / Yogoda Satsanga Society (YSS) of India – the only one he created to disseminate his teachings. A chief disciple of the yoga guru Swami Sri Yukteswar Giri, he was sent by his lineage to spread the teachings of yoga to the West. He immigrated to the US at the age of 27 to prove the unity between Eastern and Western religions and to preach a balance between Western material growth and Indian spirituality. His long-standing influence in the American yoga movement, and especially the yoga culture of Los Angeles, led him to be considered by yoga experts as the "Father of Yoga in the West". He lived his last 32 years in the US. Yogananda was the first major Indian teacher to settle in the US, and the first prominent Indian to be hosted in the White House (by President Calvin Coolidge in 1927); his early acclaim led to him being dubbed "the 20th century's first superstar guru" by the Los Angeles Times. He published his Autobiography of a Yogi in 1946 to critical and commercial acclaim. The book has been regularly reprinted and is known as "the book that changed the lives of millions". A documentary about his life commissioned by SRF, Awake: The Life of Yogananda, was released in 2014. He remains a leading figure in Western spirituality. A biographer of Yogananda, Phillip Goldberg, considers him "the best known and most beloved of all Indian spiritual teachers who have come to the West".

entries.label: Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama)
entries.note: 563 BC - Siddhārtha Gautama, Buddha-to-be, is born in Lumbini into a leading royal family in the republic of the Shakyas, which is now part of Nepal.

entries.label: 623 BC - Birth of the Buddha according to Theravada countries
entries.note: There is controversy about the base date of the Buddhist Era, with 544 BC - and 483 BC - being advanced as the date of parinibbana of the Buddha. The Sri Lankan chronicles, the Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa are the primary sources for ancient South Asian chronology; they date the consecration (abhisheka) of Asoka to 218 years after the parinibbana. Chandragupta Maurya ascended the throne 56 years prior to this, or 162 years after the parinibbana. The approximate date of Chandragupta's ascension is known to be within two years of 321 BC (from Megasthenes). Hence the approximate date of the parinibbana is between 485 and 481 BC which accords well with the Mahayana dating of 483 BC. The difference between the two reckonings seems to have occurred at sometime between the reigns of the Sri Lankan kings Udaya III (946–954 or 1007–1015) and Pârakkama Pandya (c. 1046–1048), when there was considerable unrest in the country.

entries.label: Marriage of Siddartha Gautama
entries.note: 547 BC - Siddartha Gautama gets married at the age of 16 in Kapilavastu.

entries.label: Parinibbana of the Buddha
entries.note: c. 483 BC - Gautama Buddha dies ('attains parinibbana') at Kusinara (now called Kushinagar), India. Three months following his death, the First Buddhist Council is convened.

entries.label: Four Sights
entries.note: 534 BC - Prince Siddhartha goes outside the palace for the first time and sees The Four Sights: an old man, an ill man, a dead man, and a holy man.

entries.label: Second Buddhist Council
entries.note: 383 BC - The Second Buddhist Council is convened by King Kalasoka and held at Vaisali.

entries.label: Enlightenment of the Buddha
entries.note: 528 BC - Siddhartha attains Enlightenment in Buddha Gaya (modern-day Bodhgaya), then travels to a deer park in Sarnath (near Varanasi), India, and begins expounding the Dharma. 528 BC - According to legend, Tapassu and Balluka, two North Indian traders who lived in a city of Pushkaravat, offered Siddhatha Gautama his first meal after his enlightenment. In return, the Buddha gave eight strands of his hair to the two brothers, who brought the strands to the eastern coast of Sri Lanka and enshrined them in a small pagoda in an area called "Thanthirimale".

entries.label: A printed copy of the Song Dynasty Buddhist canon arrives in Korea
In Myanmar, King Kyansittha reigns; completion of the Shwezigon Pagoda
entries.note: AD1084–1112: In Myanmar, King Kyansittha reigns. He completes the building of the Shwezigon Pagoda, a shrine for relics of the Buddha, including a tooth brought from Sri Lanka. Various inscriptions refer to him as an incarnation of Vishnu, a chakravartin, a bodhisattva, and dharmaraja.

entries.label: Thai Kingdom of Sukhothai is established, with Theravada Buddhism as the state religion
First named but not first known western bhikkhu
entries.note: c. AD1884: Irish-born U Dhammaloka ordained in Burma; first named but not first known western bhikkhu.

entries.label: Maya Devi Temple is erected in Lumbini, Nepal
entries.note: Before 500 BC - Maya Devi Temple is erected in Lumbini, Nepal. It is "possibly the earliest evidence of Buddhist structures ever found and the first archaeological evidence of Buddha's life".

entries.label: Construction of Borobodur in Indonesia
entries.note: c. AD760: Construction is begun on Borobodur, the famous Indonesian Buddhist structure, probably as a non-Buddhist shrine. It is completed as a Buddhist monument in 830.

entries.label: Caodong school of Zen is founded in southern China
entries.note: 10th century AD: The Caodong school of Zen is founded by Dongshan Liangjie and his disciples in southern China.

entries.label: Buddhism in Sumatra declines
entries.note: AD1025: Srivijaya, a Buddhist kingdom based in Sumatra, is raided by the Chola empire of southern India; it survives, but declines in importance. Shortly after the raid, the centre of the kingdom moves northward from Palembang to Jambi-Melayu.

entries.label: Anawrahta captures Thaton Lower Burma, strengthening Theravada Buddhism in the country
King Sithu II of Pagan realigns Burmese Buddhism with the Mahavihara school of Ceylon
The great stone pillar of Ashoka at rediscovered at Lumbini
entries.note: AD1896: Using Fa Xian's records, Nepalese archaeologists rediscover the great stone pillar of Ashoka at Lumbini.

entries.label: Jianzhen reaches Japan and establishes the Ritsu school
entries.note: AD743–754: The Chinese monk Jianzhen attempts to reach Japan eleven times, succeeding in 754 to establish the Japanese Ritsu school, which specialises in the vinaya (monastic rules).

entries.label: Bhikkhuni Order dies out in Southeast Asia
entries.note: AD1017: In Southeast Asia, and especially in Sri Lanka, the Bhikkhuni (Buddhist nuns) Order dies out due to invasions. The bhikkhu line in Sri Lanka is later revived with bhikkhus from Burma.

entries.label: Bhikkhus from Pagan arrive in Polonnaruwa, Sri Lanka to reinstate the Theravada ordination line
Bhikkhus from Kañcipuram, India, arrive in Sri Lanka to revive the Theravada ordination line
Gordon Douglas is ordained in Myanmar
entries.note: AD1899: Gordon Douglas is ordained in Myanmar; until recently thought to be the first Westerner to be ordained in the Theravada tradition.

entries.label: Third Buddhist Council convened by Ashoka
entries.note: c. 250 BC - Third Buddhist Council, convened by Ashoka the Great and chaired by Moggaliputta Tissa, compiles the Kathavatthu to refute the heretical views and theories held by some Buddhist sects. Ashoka issues a number of edicts (Edicts of Ashoka) about the kingdom in support of Buddhism.

entries.label: Persecutions in India
entries.note: 185 BC - Brahmin general Pusyamitra Sunga overthrows the Mauryan dynasty and establishes the Sunga dynasty, apparently starting a wave of persecution against Buddhism.

entries.label: Buddhist practice in China
entries.note: AD 67 - Liu Ying's sponsorship of Buddhism (the two monks Kasyapa and Dharmaraksha) is the first documented case of Buddhist practices in China.

entries.label: Nara
entries.note: AD804: the monk Kūkai founds the Japanese Shingon school.

entries.label: Ashoka sends out Buddhist missionaries
entries.note: c. 250 BC - Emperor Ashoka the Great sends various Buddhist missionaries to faraway countries, as far as China and the Mon & Malay kingdoms in the east and the Hellenistic kingdoms in the west, in order to make Buddhism known to them.

entries.label: Indo-Greek kingdom in north India
entries.note: 180 BC - Greco-Bactrian King Demetrius invades India as far as Pataliputra and establishes the Indo-Greek kingdom (180–10 BC), under which Buddhism flourishes. | 1st century BC - The Indo-Greek governor Theodorus enshrines relics of the Buddha, dedicating them to the deified "Lord Shakyamuni."

entries.label: White Horse Temple in China
entries.note: AD 68 - Buddhism is officially established in China with the founding of the White Horse Temple.

entries.label: (via the Silk Road to China, and ocean contact with India to Vietnam)
entries.note: AD402: At the request of Yao Xing, Kumarajiva travels to Chang'an and translates many Buddhist texts into Chinese. AD403: In China, Hui Yuan argues that Buddhist monks should be exempt from bowing to the emperor. AD405: Yao Xing honours Kumarajiva.

entries.label: Tiantai
entries.note: AD804: The monk Saichō, founds the Japanese Tendai school, partly based upon the Chinese Tiantai tradition.

entries.label: Buddhism introduced to Sri Lanka
entries.note: c. 220 BC - Theravada Buddhism is officially introduced to Sri Lanka by the Venerable Mahinda, son of the emperor Ashoka of India during the reign of King Devanampiya Tissa.

entries.label: Menander I converts to Buddhism
entries.note: c. 150 BC - Indo-Greek king Menander I converts to Buddhism under the sage Nāgasena, according to the account of the Milinda Panha.

entries.label: Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi planted
entries.note: A sapling from the historical Bodhi tree under which the Buddha became enlightened. It was planted in 288 BC and is the oldest living human-planted tree in the world with a known planting date.

entries.label: Pali Canon written down
entries.note: 29 BC - According to the Sinhalese chronicles, the Pali Canon is written down in the reign of King Vaṭṭagamiṇi (29–17 BCE)

entries.label: Fourth Buddhist Council
entries.note: AD 78–101 - According to Mahayana tradition, the Fourth Buddhist council takes place under Kushana king Kanishka's reign, near Jalandar, India.

entries.label: The Kushans establish a kingdom centered on Kashgar
entries.note: 116: The Kushans, under Kanishka, establish a kingdom centered on Kashgar, also taking control of Khotan and Yarkand in the Tarim Basin.

entries.label: Earliest surviving Chinese Buddhist scripture
entries.note: AD296: The earliest surviving Chinese Buddhist scripture dates from this year (Zhu Fo Yao Ji Jing, discovered in Dalian, late 2005).

entries.label: Evidence of Buddhism in Cambodia, Myanmar (Pali inscriptions) and Indonesia (statues)
6th century: Zen adherents enter Vietnam from China
Sutras carved in stone at Fangshan, China
entries.note: Early 7th century AD: Jingwan begins carving sutras onto stone at Fangshan, Yuzhou, 75 km southwest of modern-day Beijing.

entries.label: End of sporadic Buddhist rule in the Sindh
The Chinese Emperor receives two golden statues of the Buddha
entries.note: 120 BC - The Chinese Emperor Han Wudi (156–87 BCE) receives two golden statues of the Buddha, according to inscriptions in the Mogao Caves, Dunhuang.

entries.label: Yuezhi envoys visit Chinese capital and give oral teachings on Buddhist sutras
entries.note: 2 BC - The Hou Hanshu records the visit in 2 BC - of Yuezhi envoys to the Chinese capital, who give oral teachings on Buddhist sutras.

entries.label: First known translation of Mahayana texts into Chinese
entries.note: AD178: The Kushan monk Lokaksema travels to the Chinese capital of Loyang and becomes the first known translator of Mahayana texts into Chinese.

entries.label: Buddhabhadra reaches China to preach Buddhism
Jataka stories are translated into Persian
entries.note: 6th century AD - Jataka stories are translated into Persian by order of the Zoroastrian king, Khosrau I of Persia.

entries.label: Kegon tradition founded in Japan
entries.note: AD736: Huayan is transmitted to Japan via Korea, when Rōben invites the Korean Hwaeom monk Simsang to lecture, and formally founds Japan's Kegon tradition in the Tōdaiji temple.

entries.label: Jataka stories translated into Syriac, Arabic and Greek
entries.note: 8th century AD: Buddhist Jataka stories are translated into Syriac and Arabic as Kalilag and Damnag. An account of Buddha's life is translated into Greek by John of Damascus and widely circulated to the third seal of Jerusalem Christians as the story of Barlaam and Josaphat. By the 14th century knights of columbus, this story of Josaphat becomes so popular that he is made a Catholic saint.

entries.label: Persecution of Buddhism in China
entries.note: AD841–846: Emperor Wuzong of the Tang Dynasty (given name: Li Yan) reigns in China; he is one of three Chinese emperors to prohibit Buddhism. From 843-845, Wuzong carries out the Great Anti-Buddhist Persecution, permanently weakening the institutional structure of Buddhism in China.

entries.label: 10th century: Buddhist temple construction commences at Bagan, Myanmar.
Vietnamese Ly emperors patronize Mahayana Buddhism
entries.note: 1009: Vietnam's Lý Dynasty begins, which is partly brought about by an alliance with the Buddhist monkhood. Ly emperors patronize Mahayana Buddhism, in addition to traditional spirits.

entries.label: A copy of the Khitans' printed canon arrives in Korea from mainland China
Sōtō sect established in Japan
entries.note: AD1227: Dogen Zenji takes the Caodong school of Zen from China to Japan as the Sōtō sect.

entries.label: Arghun makes the Il-Khanate a Buddhist state
First Buddhist mission to the West
entries.note: AD1908 - Charles Henry Allan Bennett a British national previously ordained as a Theravada monk as Bhikkhu Ananda Metteyya in Burma leads the First Buddhist Mission to the West.

entries.label: Chinese General Ban Chao, subdues the Buddhist Kingdom of Khotan
Nāgārjuna
entries.note: Nāgārjuna (c. 150 – c. 250 CE) Widely considered one of the most important Buddhist philosophers after Gautama Buddha. Along with his disciple Āryadeva, he is considered to be the founder of the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism. Nāgārjuna is also credited with developing the philosophy of the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras and, in some sources, with having revealed these scriptures in the world, having recovered them from the nāgas. Furthermore, he is traditionally supposed to have written several treatises on rasayana as well as serving a term as the head of Nālandā.

entries.label: Scriptures taken to Korea; papermaking established in Korea
entries.note: 4th century AD: Two Chinese monks take scriptures to the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo and establish papermaking in Korea.

entries.label: The stupa at Dambulla (Sri Lanka) is constructed
Songtsän Gampo
entries.note: Songtsän Gampo was the founder of the Tibetan Empire by tradition held to be the thirty-third ruler in his dynasty. In Tibetan accounts, it is generally accepted that he was born in an Ox year of the Tibetan calendar, which means one of the following dates: 557, 569, 581, 593, 605 or 617 AD. It is said that Songtsän Gampo was born at Gyama, in Maldro (a region to the northeast of modern Lhasa), the son of the Yarlung king Namri Songtsen. The book "The Holder of the White Lotus" says that it is believed that he was a manifestation of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, of whom the Dalai Lama are similarly believed to be a manifestation. His identification as a cakravartin or incarnation of Avalokiteśvara began in earnest in the indigenous Buddhist literary histories of the 11th. century. During his reign, he sent messengers to India to obtain Buddhist texts.

entries.label: Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Yi Jing visits Sumatra, Indonesia
entries.note: AD671: Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Yi Jing visits Palembang, capital of the partly Buddhist kingdom of Srivijaya on the island of Sumatra, Indonesia, and reports over 1000 Buddhist monks in residence. Uisang returns to Korea after studying Chinese Huayan Buddhism and founds the Hwaeom school.

entries.label: Trisong Detsän
entries.note: Trisong Detsän or Trisong Detsen The son of Me Agtsom and one of the emperors of Tibet and ruled from 755 until 797 or 804 AD. Trisong Detsen was the second of the Three Dharma Kings of Tibet, playing a pivotal role in the introduction of Buddhism to Tibet and the establishment of the Nyingma, or 'Ancient' school of Tibetan Buddhism.

entries.label: 10th century: In Tibet, a strong Buddhist revival is begun.
Atiśa
entries.note: Atiśa Dīpaṃkara Śrījñāna (980–1054 AD) Buddhist teacher from the Pala Empire in Bengal. He was one of the major figures in the spread of 11th-century Mahayana Buddhism in Asia and inspired Buddhist thought from Tibet to Sumatra. Revered as one of the great figures of classical Buddhism, Atisa was a key figure in the establishment of the Sarma schools of Tibetan Buddhism.

entries.label: King Anawrahta of Pagan Kingdom converts to Theravada Buddhism
Hōnen establishes Pure Land Buddhism in Japan
Theravada becomes dominant in Cambodia
entries.note: 13th century AD: Theravada overtakes Mahayana—previously practised alongside Hinduism—as the dominant form of Buddhism in Cambodia; Sri Lanka is an influence in this change.

entries.label: Pagan Empire in SE Asia falls to Mongol invasions
entries.note: AD1287: The Pagan Empire, the largest Theravada kingdom of Southeast Asia, falls due to Mongol invasions.

entries.label: Tsongkhapa
entries.note: Tsongkhapa (1357–1419) Famous teacher of Tibetan Buddhism whose activities led to the formation of the Geluk school. He is also known by his ordained name Lobsang Drakpa or simply as Je Rinpoche.

entries.label: Sri Lanka reinstatement of monks ordination from Thailand - the Siyam Nikaya lineage
Buddhist revival in Sri Lanka
entries.note: c. AD1860: In Sri Lanka, against all expectations, the monastic and lay communities bring about a major revival in Buddhism.

entries.label: Travels of Fa Xian in India
entries.note: AD399-414: Fa Xian travels from China to India, then returns to translate Buddhist works into Chinese.

entries.label: Buddhism introduced to Fusang (Japan?)
entries.note: AD485: Five monks from Gandhara travel to the country of Fusang (Japan), where they introduce Buddhism.

entries.label: Buddhism is introduced to Japan via Korea
entries.note: AD552: Buddhism is introduced to Japan via Baekje (Korea), according to Nihonshoki; some scholars place this event in 538.

entries.label: A Japanese imperial envoy is dispatched to Sui, China to obtain copies of sutras
Padmasambhava establishes tantric Buddhism in Tibet
entries.note: 8th century: Under the reign of King Trisong Deutsen, Padmasambhava travels from Afghanistan to establish tantric Buddhism in Tibet (later known as the Nyingma school of Tibetan Buddhism), replacing Bonpo as the kingdom's main religion. Buddhism quickly spreads to Sikkim and Bhutan.

entries.label: Persecution of Buddhism in Tibet by King Langdarma
Entire Buddhist canon (130,000 blocks) is carved for printing
entries.note: AD971: Chinese Song Dynasty commissions Chengdu woodcarvers to carve the entire Buddhist canon for printing. Work is completed in 983; 130,000 blocks are produced, in total.

entries.label: 11th century: Marpa, Konchog Gyalpo, Atisha, and others introduce the Sarma lineages into Tibet.
All bhikkhus in Sri Lanka are reunited into the Mahavihara sect
entries.note: AD1164: Polonnaruwa, Sri Lanka destroyed by foreign invasion. With the guidance of two forest monks - Ven. Mahakassapa and Ven. Sariputta, Parakramabahu I reunites all bhikkhus in Sri Lanka into the Mahavihara sect

entries.label: Buddhist texts circulating in Arabic translation in Persia
entries.note: 13th century AD: In Persia, the historian Rashid-al-Din Hamadani records some eleven Buddhist texts circulating in Arabic translation, amongst which the Sukhavati-vyuha and Karanda-vyuha Sutras are recognizable. Portions of the Samyutta and Anguttara-Nikayas, along with parts of the Maitreya-vyakarana, are identified in this collection.

entries.label: U Thong establishes Ayutthaya as his capital in Thailand
entries.note: AD1351: In Thailand, U Thong, possibly the son of a Chinese merchant family, establishes Ayutthaya as his capital and takes the name of Ramathibodi.

entries.label: In Thailand, many Buddhist texts are destroyed as the Burmese invade Ayutthaya
Mongol leader Ghazan Khan is converted to Islam
entries.note: AD1295: Mongol leader Ghazan Khan is converted to Islam, ending a line of Tantric Buddhist leaders.

entries.label: Khedrup Gelek Pelzang
entries.note: Khedrup Gelek Pelzang, 1st Panchen Lama (1385–1438 CE) – better known as Khedrup Je – was one of the main disciples of Je Tsongkhapa, whose reforms to Atiśa's Kadam tradition are considered the beginnings of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism. Khedrub Je is considered to be an emanation of Manjusri, the Buddha of Wisdom. Khedrub Je was posthumously decided by the 5th Dalai Lama to have been a previous incarnation of Lobsang Chökyi Gyaltsen, 4th Panchen Lama (1570–1662). Like all the Panchen Lamas, he is considered to be an incarnation of Amitābha Buddha. Traditionally, there were considered to be four Indian and three Tibetan incarnations before Khedrup, starting with Subhuti, one of the original disciples of Gautama Buddha.

entries.label: Oirat Mongols convert to the Geluk school of Tibetan Buddhism
A council is convened in Burma to re-edit the Pali canon
entries.note: AD1879: A council is convened under the patronage of King Mindon of Burma to re-edit the Pali canon. The king has the texts engraved on 729 stones, which are then set upright on the grounds of a monastery near Mandalay.

entries.label: Shantideva writes Bodhisattvacaryāvatāra 'Bodhisattva's Way of Life'
entries.note: Shantideva writes Bodhisattvacaryāvatāra 'Bodhisattva's Way of Life' c. AD 700

entries.label: Attempt to restart Buddhism in Ceylon
entries.note: AD1171: Anawrahta of Pagan upon request of King Vijayabahu I of Ceylon sends monks and scriptures to restart Buddhism in the island kingdom.

entries.label: Chökyi Drönma
entries.note: The Samding Dorje Phagmo is the highest female incarnation in Tibet and the third highest-ranking person in the hierarchy after the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama. She was listed among the highest-ranking reincarnations at the time of the 5th Dalai Lama, recognized by the Tibetan government and acknowledged by the emperors of Qing China. In her first incarnation, as Chökyi Drönma, she was the student and consort of the famous polymath Thang Tong Gyalpo, who first identified her as an emanation of Vajravārāhī, and the consort of Bodong Panchen. The seat of the Samding Dorje Phagmo is at Samding Monastery, in Tibet.

entries.label: An Shigao, a Parthian prince and Buddhist monk, arrives in China
Xuan Zang travels to India, noting the persecution of Buddhists
entries.note: 7th century AD: Xuan Zang travels to India, noting the persecution of Buddhists by Sasanka (king of Gouda, a state in northwest Bengal) before returning to Chang An in China to translate Buddhist scriptures.

entries.label: Naropa
entries.note: Nāropā (AD1016–1100) Indian Buddhist Mahasiddha. He was the disciple of Tilopa and brother, or some sources say partner and pupil, of Niguma. As an Indian Mahasiddha, Naropa's instructions inform Vajrayana, particularly his six yogas of Naropa relevant to the completion stage of anuttarayogatantra. Although some accounts relate that Naropa was the personal teacher of Marpa Lotsawa, other accounts suggest that Marpa held Naropa's lineage through intermediary disciples only. However, the fact that every translation work that Marpa carried out begins by paying homage and gratitude to Naropa illustrates that Marpa definitely perceived Naropa as his Root Lama or main teacher.

entries.label: Düsum Khyenpa
entries.note: Düsum Khyenpa (1110–1193) was the 1st Gyalwa Karmapa, head of the Karma Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism.

entries.label: Mugai Nyodai becomes the first ordained female Zen master
entries.note: 13th century AD: In the Mahayana tradition, the Japanese Mugai Nyodai became the first female abbess and thus the first ordained female Zen master.

entries.label: Buddhists in Persia attempt to convert Uldjaitu Khan
Thangtong Gyalpo
entries.note: Thangtong Gyalpo (1385–1464 or1361–1485), also known as Chakzampa, the "Iron Bridge Maker", Tsöndrü Zangpo "Excellent Persistence", and the King of the Empty Plain. He was also known by a variation of this name, Madman of the Empty Valley. He was a great Buddhist adept, a Chöd master, yogi, physician, blacksmith, architect, and a pioneering civil engineer. He is considered a mind emanation of Padmasambhava and a reincarnation of Dolpopa Sherab Gyaltsen. He founded the Iron Chain lineage of the Shangpa Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, and he recognized the first Samding Dorje Phagmo, Chökyi Drönma (1422–1455), the female incarnation lineage of Vajravārāhī.

entries.label: Güüshi Khan of the Khoshuud donates the sovereignty of Tibet to the fifth Dalai Lama
Jade Buddha Temple is founded in Shanghai
entries.note: AD1882: Jade Buddha Temple is founded in Shanghai, China, with two Jade Buddha statues imported from Burma.

entries.label: Marpa
entries.note: Marpa Lotsawa (1012–1097), sometimes known fully as Lhodak Marpa Choski Lodos or commonly as Marpa the Translator. Tibetan Buddhist teacher credited with the transmission of many Vajrayana teachings from India, including the teachings and lineages of Mahamudra. Due to this the Kagyu lineage, which he founded, is often called Marpa Kagyu in his honour. | AD1100–1125: Huizong reigns during the Chinese Song Dynasty and outlaws Buddhism to promote the Dao. He is one of three Chinese emperors to have prohibited Buddhism.

entries.label: The Bayon constructed at the Angkor temple complex
entries.note: AD1181: Jayavarman VII assumes control of the Khmer kingdom. He constructs the Bayon, the most prominent Buddhist structure in the Angkor temple complex.

entries.label: Sojiji Soto Zen Temple and Monastery established by Keizan Zenji
First translations of Theravada texts into Chinese by An Shigao
University at Nalanda established c. 5th century
entries.note: Nalanda was visited by both Mahavira and Buddha in sixth and fifth centuries BCE. It is also the place of birth and nirvana of Shariputra, one of the famous disciples of Buddha. Many scholars and historical figures of note are associated with Nalanda including: Aryabhata Aryadeva, student of Nagarjuna Atisa Chandrakirti Dharmakirti, logician Dharmapala Dinnaga, founder of Buddhist Logic Jinamitra Nagarjuna, formaliser of the concept of Shunyata Padmasambhava, master of Tantric Buddhism Shantarakshita, founder of the first monastic order in Tibet Shilabhadra, the teacher of Xuanzang Xuanzang, Chinese Buddhist traveller Yijing, Chinese Buddhist traveller

entries.label: The Shaolin temple is built
entries.note: AD495: The Shaolin temple is built in the name of Buddhabhadra, by edict of emperor Wei Xiao Wen.

entries.label: Bodhidharma settles into the Shaolin monastery
Latest recorded use of the Kharoṣṭhī script amongst Buddhist communities around Kucha.
entries.note: 7th century AD: Latest recorded use of the Kharoṣṭhī script amongst Buddhist communities around Kucha.

entries.label: Korean carving of the Buddhist canon
entries.note: AD1010: Korea begins carving its own woodblock print edition of the Buddhist canon. No completion date is known; the canon is continuously expanded, with the arrival of new texts from China.

entries.label: Milarepa
entries.note: Jetsun Milarepa (c. AD1052 – c. 1135 CE) Generally considered one of Tibet's most famous yogis and poets. He was a student of Marpa Lotsawa, and a major figure in the history of the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism.

entries.label: Nalanda University sacked
entries.note: Nalanda was ransacked and destroyed by an army of the Muslim Mamluk Dynasty under Bakhtiyar Khilji in c. AD1197.

entries.label: Eiheiji Soto Zen Temple and Monastery are established by Dogen Zenji
Sonam Gyatso
entries.note: AD1578: Altan Khan of the Tümed gives the title of Dalai Lama to Sonam Gyatso (later known as the third Dalai Lama).

entries.label: Yeshe Tsogyal
entries.note: Yeshe Tsogyal (c. 757 or 777 – 817), also known as "Victorious Ocean of Knowledge", "Knowledge Lake Empress", or by her Sanskrit name Jñānasāgara "Knowledge Ocean", or by her clan name "Lady Kharchen", attained enlightenment in her lifetime and is considered the Mother of Tibetan Buddhism. Yeshe Tsogyal is the highest woman in the Nyingma Vajrayana lineage.

entries.label: Gampopa
entries.note: Gampopa Sönam Rinchen (1079–1153) was the main student of Milarepa, and a Tibetan Buddhist master who codified his own master's ascetic teachings, which form the foundation of the Kagyu educational tradition. Gampopa was also a doctor and tantric master. He authored the first Lamrim text, Jewel Ornament of Liberation, and founded the Dagpo Kagyu school. He is also known as Dvagpopa, and by the titles Dakpo Lharjé "the physician from Dakpo".

entries.label: Khön Könchok Gyalpo
entries.note: Khön Könchok Gyalpo (1034-1102) was the founder of the Sakya School of Tibetan Buddhism, and the founder of Sakya Monastery. He was born in Sa'gya, Tsang. He was a member of the Khön family, and his ancestry can be traced back to Khön Dorje Rinpoche, student of Padmasambhava. He followed his father and brother and learned doctrines of the Nyingma School at a young age, but studied newly translated Vajrayāna texts with Drogmi Shakya Yeshe later. Khön Könchok Gyalpo established Sakya Monastery in 1073, where the Sakya Tradition first developed. His son Khön Kunga Nyingpo was regarded as the first leader of Sakya, and Khön Könchok Gyalpo is known as the first Sakya Trizin.

The Hittites were an Anatolian Indo-European people who formed one of the first major civilizations of Bronze Age West Asia. Possibly originating from beyond the Black Sea, they settled in modern day Turkey in the early 2nd millennium BC. The Hittites formed a series of polities in north-central Anatolia, including the kingdom of Kussara (before 1750 BC), the Kanesh or Nesha kingdom (c. 1750–1650 BC), and an empire centered on Hattusa (around 1650 BC). Known in modern times as the Hittite Empire, it reached its height during the mid-14th century BC under Šuppiluliuma I, when it encompassed most of Anatolia and parts of the northern Levant and Upper Mesopotamia.

Roman Province In Ancient Rome, a province (Latin: provincia, pl. provinciae) was the basic, and, until the Tetrarchy (293 AD), largest territorial and administrative unit of the empire's territorial possessions outside of Italy. The word province in modern English has its origins in the term used by the Romans. Provinces were generally governed by politicians of senatorial rank, usually former consuls or former praetors. A later exception was the province of Egypt, incorporated by Augustus after the death of Cleopatra: it was ruled by a governor of equestrian rank only, perhaps as a discouragement to senatorial ambition. This exception was unique, but not contrary to Roman law, as Egypt was considered Augustus' personal property, following the tradition of earlier, Hellenistic kings. The Latin term provincia also had a more general meaning, 'juridisdiction' Many provinces were under Roman military control or under the rule of Roman clients for a long time before being officially constituted as civil provinces. Only the date of the official formation of the province is given, not the date of conquest.

Eric (1381 or 1382 – 24 September 1459), often known as Eric of Pomerania. Scandinavian monarch who ruled over the Kalmar Union from 1396 until 1439. He was initially co-ruler with his great-aunt Margaret I until her death in 1412. Eric is known as Eric III as King of Norway (1389–1442), Eric VII as King of Denmark (1396–1439) and has been called Eric XIII as King of Sweden (1396–1434, 1436–39). Eric was ultimately deposed from all three kingdoms of the union, but in 1449 he inherited one of the partitions of the Duchy of Pomerania and ruled it as duke until his death in 1459. Eric of Pomerania was a pejorative intended to point out that he did not belong in Scandinavia.

This member of the West Indies Federation was Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla. This was a British colony in the West Indies from 1882 to 1983, consisting of the islands of Anguilla (until 1980), Nevis, and Saint Christopher (or Saint Kitts). Diels–Kranz (DK) numbering is the standard system for referencing the works of the ancient Greek pre-Socratic philosophers, based on the collection of quotations from and reports of their work, Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker (The Fragments of the Pre-Socratics), by Hermann Alexander Diels. The Fragmente was first published in 1903, with a sixth edition in 1952. In Diels-Kranz, each passage, or item, is assigned a number which is used to uniquely identify the ancient personality with which it is concerned, and the type of item given. Diels-Kranz is used in academia to cite pre-Socratic philosophers, and the system also encompasses Sophists and pre-Homeric poets such as Orpheus, who were not necessarily philosophers as-such, but were also active figures in ancient Greece, preceding Socrates. If one takes the Seven Sages as a group of seven and includes the later Iamblichus, Diels-Kranz encompasses 106 named personalities and two anonymous authors. Stephanus pagination is the comparable system for referring to Plato, and Bekker numbering is the comparable system for referring to Aristotle.

Athenian Plague returns. 427 Plataea finally falls to the Spartans after a two year siege. 426 Demosthenes, Athenian general, and Cleon, Athenian demagogue, revitalizes Athenian forces, makes bold plans opposed by Nicias, his first military campaign barely succeeds.
